Pros:
• The solo play campaign is rich, and rewarding. It challenges you to make judgement calls while also offering difficult game play against outrages odds. All of the characters are fun, and definitely offer an escape from reality. Whether you enjoy killing, stealing, or whoring, or a simple game of tennis then this game is for you. You can put off the quests and screw around or do side mission after side mission forever. The ending is a challenge, but it allows YOU to make it which I always appreciate in games.
• Online game play constantly has content updated into it with the "Free" launches of "DLC". Missions, heists, criminal activity, all added every so often to keep the experience new and fresh.
• Nonsense EVERYWHERE. You can play with friends, or randoms, on the very large map. Rarely is their peace between players, but the turf wars can be fun. Sometimes you just want to grind your missions and make dough and you keep getting interrupted but that's GTA for you.
• Rockstar put a TON of time in this game. Their are even TV shows and short films you can watch in the game on your homes TV or cell phone.
Cons:
• Solo play is fun, but doesn't offer you a realistic expectation of the meat of the game: Online. You get rich fast in solo, which leads you to believe it'll be the same in online. WRONG.
• Hackers. Are. Everywhere. Nothing worse than finishing a mission only to be teleported into the sea miles from shore, or have aimbotting asshats spawn sniping you until you leave. And if the hacker is kind, and gives you dosh, report it because Rockstar will punish you and take all your dough, and if you spent it, it'll be compensated one way or another.
• Grinding takes forever, and rarely will people allow you to do your missions to make money. As a CEO I mostly break even from missions because I'm often stopped, my cargo destroyed, or vehicles wrecked by other players. You can make solo lobby's through jumping through loops but eventually others will join and it's a hassle to keep remaking. Do stuff with friends and you won't have as big a problem.
• Content is all the same, missions the same, and no new heists. Some of the vehicles are great, and things look real nice, but it's all just resprayed from a previous thing. The Warstock vehicles are all cool though, so there is that at least.
All and all, I give the game a big thumbs up because I've had countless experiences I've enjoyed and still love booting this title with friends to play with. Just don't buy shark cards, I've bought this game four times over, maybe more, with how much in shark cards I've bought.

For a gameplay video with some thoughts after playing ~20hrs:
Otherwise here is my written opinions,
Ziggurat is the next roguelite to try to tackle the first person perspective. For my personally it is one of the few that has really hit the mark.
Ziggurat combines twitch fps controls with fantasy elements in a seemless way. You fight through randomly generated floors that feature a handfull of different types of rooms, enemies and bosses. As you progress in the game you unlock more items, characters, and abilities that will add to a pool of randomized items, changing the game as you sink more hours into it.
The game has three difficulties, Easy, Normal and Hard. Even on easy difficulty the game takes some getting used to and can be quite challenging. Normal difficulty is where it really starts to kick your butt, however. Hard mode is something else entirely. The amount of content in the game may be concerning to some, as you only fight through five floors which may be off-putting. I can assure fans of the roguelite genre that the game feels whole. Ziggurat is easily my favorite new game I've played in months and I am absolutely in love. Highly recommended to fans of roguelites, first person shooters, or the fantasy genres!

Ziggurat was a surprise for me.  Im not typically a rogue-lite fan, but the spin on putting things in an FPS/wizard setting and the vast variety of weapons/enemies makes it very fun.  Anyone who enjoys rouge lites will like this game, but so will people who enjoy solid FPS style games that require very little commitment but have quite a bit of depth. This game is a prime example of what early access can do for a title in a sea of games that are early access mainly to gain funding, this game did it to help provide feedback and the devs actually listened to the community for once.    That being said, the game isnt without its flaws, some times enemies will clip into the wall, other times ive had saved game problems.
A few things i would love to see in the future:  Online Leaderboards, a small PvP mode and an endless dungeon mode.  I think the addition of one or more of these things would really increase the replayablilty by quite a bit.

So I'm have to start out by saying that I enjoyed my time with this game well enough, but that I feel that I still need to caution potential buyers of this game by not recommending it to them. My reasoning? Well, the short answer is that the price they are asking for at $15 is too high for what you get.
The long:
I bought this off of the recommendation of TotalBiscut after watching his first impressions by it, and I'd say his opinions almost always line up with mine - except in this instance. I think the main problem for this is that all I did was take his first impressions into account and made assumptions I shouldn't have, and thats on me for not researching farther.
One of my biggest problems with this game that I assumed based on his video was that you would be able to play for as long as you could manage with your character. I was surprised to find that it had an end, that you could "beat" the game. Now, ordinarily that wouldn't be a problem, but in this case I found that it was because I felt very disappointed when I discovered how short a successful playthrough actually is (About an hour, in my case). I liked what I had going with my character, and I was having fun with him. Yet, much to my dismay, found I had to stop playing with him after only 5 levels. I hadn't even encountered one of the 4 weapon types, alchemical, yet. So when I defeated the last boss, I thought, can I continue? Can I do New Game+? Continue and restart on a harder difficulty? Or at least just let me continue wandering through random dungeons to see how far I could get? But none of those options were available to me.
So upon completing I received some unlocks for completing certain achievements. Interestingly, some of them were perks that I might have a chance to use upon leveling up in my next run. And there is where I have another problem with the game. Not so much that I can unlock things, like new characters with slightly differing abilities forcing you to play one way or another, but that I realized as a result of this that the game is built with "sideways replayability". What I mean by that is that most of the game's content is centered around the idea that you play many many times, and that each time your start may be a little different and the number of things you have a chance of upgrading your character with expands as you play. This may be fine for some people, but to me it just means that my individual runs' fun factor are severely reduced. Giving you more things to play with over time is fine, but starting you out with a very basic set of possible upgrades and expecting you to grind to have the chance to see others is not, especially when you can't continue for very long even when you get lucky enough to get the perfect build lined up.
I suppose this style of replayability would be fine enough were there more variety in both weapons available and enemy types to fight, maybe even level designs if we are lucky. But After playing through around 5 runs, each with a different character, I am already pretty fatigued. It very quickly became a matter of seeing the same thing over again and using the same exact set of weapons, which in themselves are not all that varied to begin with. And what is my incentive to keep playing? To maybe get lucky and get really far? Well no, that's not even possible, so I cant play with that as my goal. To obtain more starting characters? Well they really aren't that different and basically just force you to use a certain weapon type for the most part... What about the new perks you are getting? Well again, a) you have to rely on chance just to have the option to use them in the first place, and b) then why do you really care if you already know the ceiling is so low? It doesnt really matter if you get a really fun build together, because you wont have a chance to use it for long!
Heres what I would have like to see from this game instead: A larger, more varied enemy pool. More weapons to have access to (How about some actual cool spells to cast, like a flamethrower, or a thunder cloud, or a frost blast? Call me old fashioned, but I wasn’t expecting the only weapon “spells” that would be available to you to just be pea shooters of differing colors where some have dots and some shotgun out more than others). More level variety - for example, not once did I run into a room that had both enemies AND traps in it at the same time. More options or variations on starting characters that make them actually feel different. And probably most importantly, let me play the “long game”! I want to see how far I can make in one go. The game could easily allow you to continue after you “beat” it, and then maybe allow you to unlock things as you go instead of forcing you to restart completely.
All in all, as much as I’m beating up in this game, its still fun. I just don’t want people to get the wrong idea and make it out as “the perfect new rouge-lite” as it seems many have been doing. So I haven’t even talked about its strengths, but that’s because I’ve talked long enough. Check out more positive reviews to see that, but just be warned, you may not end up getting enough bang for your buck in this one.
EDIT: I'm aware that they have since added endless mode. It was not there on initial release at the time of my review. Considering I have no desire to play this game any longer, I will not be revisiting how it affects the game. I would reccomend watching or reading a more up-to-date review than my own should you be curious about this game.

A great polished game for its price, highly recommended for those who enjoy other rogue-lites such as Binding of Isaac.
More specifically, it is a fast-paced FPS rogue-lite with combat similar to Hexen/Heretic (1990's FPS dark fantasy games). For those worried about replayability, do not fret! There is random generation for pretty much everything you encounter in the game.
There's at least 30 different weapons, plenty of perks and monster types to keep things fresh for a long while. Of course there is a bit of overlap between them, for example two bombs, one which simply explodes and the other which leaves behind flames on the ground but they are mechanically different so it feels different enough.
The game's difficulty is definitely tuned towards more experienced FPS players. Health is scarce, do not expect plenty of health packs/regenerating health to save you. Also, the bosses pose somewhat of a threat so be prepared before waltzing into a boss encounter! However, the easy difficulty is very well tuned for those who may find themselves stuck after floor 2 in normal/hard (like myself, the scrublord).
Overall, I am pleased with my purchase of the game and I look forward  to seeing the updates in the future.

• Nonsense EVERYWHERE. You can play with friends, or randoms, on the very large map. Rarely is their peace between players, but the turf wars can be fun. Sometimes you just want to grind your missions and make dough and you keep getting interrupted but that's GTA for you.
• Rockstar put a TON of time in this game. Their are even TV shows and short films you can watch in the game on your homes TV or cell phone.
Cons:
• Solo play is fun, but doesn't offer you a realistic expectation of the meat of the game: Online. You get rich fast in solo, which leads you to believe it'll be the same in online. WRONG.
• Hackers. Are. Everywhere. Nothing worse than finishing a mission only to be teleported into the sea miles from shore, or have aimbotting asshats spawn sniping you until you leave. And if the hacker is kind, and gives you dosh, report it because Rockstar will punish you and take all your dough, and if you spent it, it'll be compensated one way or another.
• Grinding takes forever, and rarely will people allow you to do your missions to make money. As a CEO I mostly break even from missions because I'm often stopped, my cargo destroyed, or vehicles wrecked by other players. You can make solo lobby's through jumping through loops but eventually others will join and it's a hassle to keep remaking. Do stuff with friends and you won't have as big a problem.
• Content is all the same, missions the same, and no new heists. Some of the vehicles are great, and things look real nice, but it's all just resprayed from a previous thing. The Warstock vehicles are all cool though, so there is that at least.
All and all, I give the game a big thumbs up because I've had countless experiences I've enjoyed and still love booting this title with friends to play with. Just don't buy shark cards, I've bought this game four times over, maybe more, with how much in shark cards I've bought.

You play as a boy and his father each with very different and extremely unique abilities. Each pulling each other through the stages. Which lends credence the the emotional aspect. They actually call out to each other taking control away at times letting you know its time to switch in order to solve the puzzle and progress.
The father is the only one that can jump and climb and through the loose narrative the boy has some powers like teleporting and dropping some orb dust to create bridges (in specific locations). There are also these sort of dream scape levels where the boy has the ability to float around where you are tasked with collecting some orbs and avoiding spikes and closing hallways. However these are by far the worst part of the game. If the regular stages range from middling to okay these dream scape stages range from please make this end and why is this happening. They control poorly and unlike the rest of the game where checkpointing is quite forgiving, the dream scape world requires you to collect all the orbs without dying in order to succeed making it unnecessarily stressful.

This is already a solid game.
I have not experienced any bugs whatsoever since playing, that's saying something for an early access(beta) game.
Balancing issues is another story, but the Dev has recognized this and will be implementing a fix in the next patch this coming week.
The provided video and pictures do a pretty good job showing what the game is all about. You don't hear any of the in-game sound effects from the store video but rest assured they are of appropriate quality.
Currently, you start off in your capital ship without a base. You roam the galaxy collecting resources via random generated events such as mining, salvaging and combat. No exploring in this game at the moment.
Once you have saved up some resources and found a suitable spot in the galaxy, you build your home base. Continue to harvest minerals and build up your empire. Make sure to have a sizable home fleet so your neighbors don't get any bright ideas about attacking you.
Continue to level up your flag ship, customizing it to your preferred specifications, build a fleet to take with you, and go conquer the galaxy!
Currently there is little diplomacy, but it's there. Basically you can trade resources and help out when they are being attack by pirates to earn reputation with your neighbors. But they want your stuff, badly. It's that balance issue I talked about already.
There is no diplomacy win at the moment.
This is a fun little game. The best word I can think of to describe it is 'addicting'. He's got the right formula with this one.

Some things have changed since the previous build so the review needs to change as well. As you know the original review was quite negative. But that's the only way things get fixed in games like this.
1.The repair problems have mostly been fixed.
2. Fleets are reduced  in this build.
3. Resources are an issue but it's not so bad the game is bogged down.
4. AI is being worked on, it isn't perfect right now but the developer is making a concerted effort to actually fix the issues with it.
5. Pirates went from a mind-boggling nightmare to a minor nuisance for those with large empires.
Right now all the big issues that were bogging the game down badly have been fixed. The AI and Warp Travel still need a bit of work but it looks like the developer is actually listening and caring, which I was unsure about at first. But they proved me wrong on that issue. I'm very impressed that they fixed several of the most glaring problems in one patch.
There are still some flaws but they aren't so huge I can give the game a negative review anymore. Here they are:
1. Truly huge cities bog the game down quite a bit, even on massively powerful computers (I'm running an i7, 16 gb ram and 970) this is a symptom of it running on Unity.
2. Additional content as far as ships, buildings, new outposts and other depth still need work. That's normal for any early access title and I'm glad they worked on more pressing problems first.
3. Basic polish on the UI, controls and in other areas still needs a bit of work. But that will also probably come with time.
Once the rest of the content is finished the game should be really great, as long as the developer continues with this trend.

This is one of those early access titles that are so much fun that you end up checking for new updates every time you open steam. I simply cannot wait for what the future holds for Beyond Sol!
Pros:
Being developed by, Praxia Entertainment, a Canadian team that used to work for Bioware; Beyond sol has all the elements of a great top down space shooter, combined with the hardcore strategy elements of a 4x empire building game. Throw in some massive fleet battles, tower defense and even some economic simulation, you will find this hard to put down.
You begin the game as a lone cruiser pilot in a small region of contested space and you goal is to quickly build a city where people in the region can live, shop, work etc. You will need to expand your territory by building radar and mining installations that will gather minerals tariffs for your growing empire. While your empire is growing you may also explore the universe freely and without restriction, mining, hunting, performing services for other cultures, salvaging, and even outright attacking your neighbors, if you so choose. There is no restriction on what you do.
Your ship can be upgraded and customized in a variety of ways depending on what corporations you have living in your city. You can buy new corporate ships to fly with you or to defend your cities and stations as well. All things considered, Beyond Sol is amazing already, and it's not even finished yet. I can't recommend it enough!
Cons:
This is an Early access title, so it, naturally has a few issues. I have found some bugs when starting new games where some of the previous game data will carry over, creating some confusing information, like incorrect research and ship levels, more money and minerals than normal etc. The game is also incomplete and there are simply many ship customizing option that are simply just not available yet. The procedurally generated area you begin in is different every time and always interesting, however, there are no options yet to customize it. None of these issues prevent a player from playing the game and enjoying it thoroughly.

You play as a lone captain on his flagship, trying to get your own piece of the solar system.
You settle down in some fine piece of space, establish your city, spend some hours making it grow big and powerful.
And while you do that, you grind... a lot... because the asteroid fields are pretty damn empty. A whole lot of this game is flying around in belts, farming materials to build your city.
Eventually you'll get your own (at first small, then bigger) fleet.
Sometimes your claimed space gets attacked, either by other factions that have declared war on you, or by pirates.
You need to defend yourself, because there aren't any AI patrols available yet.
And that is the big point: Not available YET.
There are a few things missing and seem not right with this game.
A couple of suggestions for the devs:
- Add AI support for the player, like miners and patrols to control your space.
- Nerf the enemy AI. They grow a lot quicker than you and always get into Ragemode as soon as you build near their borders, this needs to be fixed. ! It kills all the fun in expanding when it always ends in war ! Might as well not have my own city then.
- Make the asteroid fields a lot denser. I should be able to fly through at 10% thrust and fill up my cargo but currently it's very VERY tedious and annoying
- Let players play more cooperatively by letting them create a faction, so multiple player can own one city together.
- and a couple more things that I can't think of right now (30°C in my room, too hot to think properly)
Otherwise, it's a great game and could be the one game I've been waiting for for a long time.
Please Devs, make this happen. I love your game, even with it's mistakes, but it could be so much better!

I've been playing Brawlhalla for a long time and I have a good amount of hours racked up on the game, many of those hours were fun but there were also a lot of hours of frustration due to server side issues especially in the past several months. Often times there's delay's when trying to attack, dodge or jump and sometimes things just don't seem to register at all, like for example hitting down + an attack and the down doesn't register. I've hit people multiple times without them dodging and they receive no damage at all. I see people and myself disappear at time for brief seconds, like we are teleporting. These type of issues are what kills game like this.
I know there's people reading this saying, that I'm salty or that I had a bad Wifi or connection issues. The problem is somewhere on Brawlhalla's end and I'll explain why.
1. I have 4 solid green bars on the in game latency meter.
2. Ping tests and traceroutes to the server look great. No packet loss and low 12-16 ms hops.
3. My modem is directly hardwired to my PC. I have run mutltiple line tests and they always come back with great results.
3. There's no issues with any USB ports or devices. I use an XBOX 360 controller to play. The controller is brand new and has no issues on any other game. I've also used other new Xbox 360 controllers to play and the issues mentioned still happen.
It's very clear that with all the info listed I shouldn't be having any problems. There's obviously something going on Brawlhalla's end of things. Whether it be the matchmaking and the servers or a bad input delay application something needs change. While it may not affect some, there's definitely people it is affecting look around the discussion boards and comments. I just want to play the game and have fun but it's really hard to do with the issues happening constantly.
TL;DR Poor optimization and constant server issues kill the fun.

Brothers - A Tale of two sons is the bittersweet story of two brothers trying to save their father. The two brothers must work together to bring back the water of life for their father. After losing their mother to drowning the younger brother has a fear of water which his brother must help him overcome.
The twin stick control is very unique and fun. Its a single player COOP where you control both brothers at once to overcome obstacles that one person could not. The graphics are beautiful and are almost nostalgic in a way., they king of remind me of Shawdow of the Collossus and ICO for some reason.
The story is short and can be completed in around 3-4 hours. But its well worth it as you get a great experience.
Prepare for the feels.

The objective of this game is to click on numbers that appear (out of a bunch of them), that will add up to your "target number" each level. E.g. If your target number = 14, you could click on 8, then 2, then 4, to make up 14. The numbers appear and disappear very fast, and there is a timer every level. You have to make up the target number at least 5 times or more, depending on the level you're on, and the target number gets bigger and bigger with every level.
I found the game to be quite fun, but it's almost impossible to get past level 5 or so, because the game is just way too difficult.
- E.g. With a target number of say, 10, maybe you have clicked on 5 and 4, so you'll need a 1 to complete things. But 1 just refuses to appear. And you can't click on anything else either because that will cause you to run out of time (there is a penalty for "wrong" clicks, and if you choose a bomb, which will reset your sum, you will most likely run out of time - see point #2 below).
Bombs in this game reset your sum. This is helpful if sometimes the number you are looking for refuses to appear. E.g. If your target number is 10 and you've already clicked on 5 and 4 respectively (thus adding up to 9), clicking on a bomb next will cause your sum total to become 0 once more. But after your sum is reset, the only numbers that appear next are either bombs once more, or very low digits, like 1 for instance. So it is nigh impossible, with the timer running so fast, to make up your target number - especially if your target number is big, like 28 for example - within the given time limit.
Given the above 2 points (i.e. bombs costing too much time and the AI refusing to give you numbers you need), levels would be more playable if the timer were lengthened.

A great polished game for its price, highly recommended for those who enjoy other rogue-lites such as Binding of Isaac.
More specifically, it is a fast-paced FPS rogue-lite with combat similar to Hexen/Heretic (1990's FPS dark fantasy games). For those worried about replayability, do not fret! There is random generation for pretty much everything you encounter in the game.
There's at least 30 different weapons, plenty of perks and monster types to keep things fresh for a long while. Of course there is a bit of overlap between them, for example two bombs, one which simply explodes and the other which leaves behind flames on the ground but they are mechanically different so it feels different enough.
The game's difficulty is definitely tuned towards more experienced FPS players. Health is scarce, do not expect plenty of health packs/regenerating health to save you. Also, the bosses pose somewhat of a threat so be prepared before waltzing into a boss encounter! However, the easy difficulty is very well tuned for those who may find themselves stuck after floor 2 in normal/hard (like myself, the scrublord).
Overall, I am pleased with my purchase of the game and I look forward  to seeing the updates in the future.

Worth the money.
Has:

-Very cool atmosphere [even the walkthrough hallways]

-Perk system when levelling up [increased perks the more you play]
-All weapons have main and alt. fire
-You gain a different weapon every time you start the game
-Bosses have different ways of attacking, but susceptible to most if not all attacks
-Decent enemy AI [they have good prediction actually]
Not a lot of playtime right now, but this will increase in the coming days.
Really does feel like a mix of Hexen/Heretic and Serious Sam if they had a cool roguelike kid.
If you like fast-paced first person shooters, this game is for you.
It does get repetitive [like BoI], but it's still pretty damn fun. I've finished the games several times on Easy and Normal [yet to do hard], but still hasn't gone stale.
You will most likely find yourself switching between all your four weapons in most cases, so combat also doesn't go stale. Also: It's not hitscan, it's projectile-based because magic reasons.
tl;dr
If you want a fun, fast-paced, somewhat short first-person roguelike with weapon variety and fun gameplay, get this. Recommended to grab on sale, though, since again it's pretty short. [better stated by one of the higher-rated Not Recommended posts. still fun game]

This game is excellent. If you are a fan of old-style FPS like Serious Sam or Doom, I highly recommend it. If you are a fan of "roguelites" like Binding of Isaac I would also recommend it.
The weaponry is both diverse and balanced. The enemies are diverse as well, with surprisingly good AI. Many enemies even lead their shots. The graphics are also well done and complement the great art style, which really set it apart from other FPS roguelites like Heavy Bullet, which suffer in the graphics area.

It's just good. Smooth, responsive controls, a wide variety of weapons with interesting effects, a level system that makes fighting enemies feel worthwhile rather than just something you're doing to get to the end, and fun, varied perks that you're almost never sad to take.
Great visual aesthetic, phenomenal sound design.
Also if you hate carrots you can kill armies of them. Something for everybody.

Cannot fathom how this game has so many positive ratings.
While it has the potential for fun, it is, ultimately, a trial to enjoy properly.
Almost every weapon in the game feels like a pea-shooter, leading to most of combat being a grind.   Jumping puzzles are extremely difficult to get used to due to a simultaneously overly rigid air movement and unintuitively floaty friction system.  The progression system actually makes the game harder and less enjoyable, as the perk system on level up is, at base, rather beneficial, and then, every time you die, you'll add more and more perks, most of which you wont ever want to take, but'll show up instead of anything you would.
If you're looking for something in this genre, Tower of Guns or Paranautical Activity have a lot more to offer.

Trine 2 – review single player:
Is an action/puzzle/plat former game. You play with 3 characters simultaneously. The wizard can create and move objects, the thief has acrobatic capabilities and a bow, the knight has his sword and shield. As you play you gather experience. With the gathered experience you can ‘buy’ new skills for your characters.
The game is best played with a controller (Xbox One controller was used by me).
It has:
-	Beautiful, colourful and vibrant graphics.
-	Nice sound effects and music – the voice of narrator is also very good.
-	It supports ultra wide resolutions: I use 21:9 2560*1080.
When the main game is finished you can play the included DLC-story ‘Goblin Menace'.
It took me around 14 hours to finish. After that you can replay the levels to find all the secrets or try a other difficulty settings.
The puzzles are sometimes challenging but never frustrating.
I highly recommend this game!

Hello everybody! Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) here to share my thoughts on my latest playthrough for Clouds & Sheep 2 by Handy Games and Headup Games! A review copy was provided by our friends at Headup Games but as with all of my reviews this has no effect on how I feel about the game.
At first glance you may be saying to yourself “But Shaun, Clouds & Sheep 2 is a game for kids, why are you playing it?” and you’re definitely right, the game is a family friendly game geared more towards children. BUT, here at The Indieverse we support games that are family friendly because we feel that gaming is something that can be enjoyed by everybody regardless of age.
Clouds & Sheep 2 is an indie, casual, simulation game where you take care of sheep in various environments. I know the game sounds like it’d be incredibly boring but it’s oddly addicting in a really strange way and I’m not entirely sure why haha.
For those unfamiliar with the Clouds & Sheep series, it first originated back in 2011 as a mobile game. I’ve never actually played the first game so I can’t make any comments on the original, but the sequel sought to improve upon various aspects including a better art style, more customization options and a day-night cycle.
One of my favorite parts about this game is definitely the beautifully drawn art style which is gorgeous to look at. The day-night cycle is definitely a nice touch to the game as well and night time is especially pretty. The game also has a crazy amount of customization as well. You can give your sheep hats, paint them, add environmental decorations or items and many other things.
Taking care of your sheep is the main objective so aside from feeding and sheltering them, you will also need to shear them and keep them happy. Pretty standard simulation game stuff, but there are random quests that you can do to gain experience points to level up which grants access to new environments, decorations and more.
I’ll be honest with and say that this game won’t be something everyone will enjoy. It’s a casual game geared towards children so many adults reading this review might take one look at it and say “nope” and I don’t blame you. BUT, for folks with younger children, this might be a good choice to keep them busy for a while because it’s a time waster and what kid doesn’t love throwing sheep around?
If you enjoyed my videos or this review be sure to subscribe to my YouTube channel! It would also be greatly appreciated if you could share this review or my videos as it would help me get more exposure.
Happy gaming folks! - Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) out!

If you liked Human Revolution then Mankind Divided is more of the same overall. The same main character, some familiar faces, the same sort of gameplay, and the same sort of exploration.
More refined is how I would describe the overall experience. More ways to do things you did in HR.
The new augmentation options are OK but feel a bit tacked on. And by tacked I mean I never used any of them. But they ARE options and I can't fault more ways to do stuff. - Edit: Actually I did use remote hacking - that one is pretty cool.
(For reference I prefer to play non-lethally)
I think the focus on a single city was a great idea. It works much better than trying to split things between Hengsha and Detroit and so Prague feels like a bigger, more city-like place. Also if you like digging into the little miniplots and details, there are plenty to find. The fired disgruntled bank worker, the cashier angry at their boss and reporting them to the authority, the booby-trapped apartment. I love the little details in games like this.
The main plot feels a bit weaker compared to HR - it feels like one of those mid-trilogy plots like the Matrix Reloaded or something. It has a basic beginning, middle, and end, but doesn't really lead anywhere significant. You could sum it up as "Interpol thwarts plot by terrorists to frame pariah political movement for intended atrocities in Prague and London"
Still - because they didn't go for any cliche mid-game "reveals" or other nonsensical plot twists, it works. I fully expect another game that will end with something more conclusive. Unless they go the silly Ubisoft AC route and grind out sequels with an overall plot that never seems to go anywhere.
Regarding BREACH: So this seems to be some mostly fun challenge thing that also compares you to other players. I've done a few of the networks - it is a fun distraction. Totally unrelated to the game (except lore-wise a little).
If you're only interested with the main game you can completely ignore it and all microtransactions related to it. As much as I hate microtransactions, that seems like an OK compromise.
TL:DR -  It's nothing groundbreaking but if you liked HR, you'll like this. Also if you like the Tranquilizer Rifle as much as I did in HR and the original, you can actually get a decent amount of darts now!

Mankind Divided builds on the already succesful formula of previous Deus Ex games and keeps the franchise on high standards. Some people complained about microtransactions but I completed the game without even knowing any details about them apart from their existence. There were also complains about the amount of content in the game and personally I believe that there is enough here to justify a purchase and its pretty well done too.
On the performance side of things, the game is quite heavy but it ran very smoothly (mostly 60 fps) with a few tweaks on the ultra preset on an AMD RX 480 and an intel i5.
Recommended for stealth fans or players that long for a type of game that is rare these days (sadly), where choices are impactful, the gameplay is non linear and there isnt excessive hand-holding.

I enjoy this game, but I have a few gripes with this early access:
Pros:
1) Great fresh idea on the game. Feels like a board game when I get my firends to play!
2) Even though there isn't a tutorial, the game is well-designed and easy to pick up.
3) It looks great. Runs on low hardware.
4) My firend was easily able to connect to me to play coop.
5) You can transfer your ship/profile across different sessions.
Cons:
1) There is zero community. It's hard to even figure out which website or forum is the dev's! Zero active community thus far.
2) You cannot control any settings for your game. Wanna change the sound levels? Nope, better crank up you teamspeak volums bc you have to play this game at the vokume levels they give you.
3) The AI is utter garbage. I get it, I settled near you. Get over it. Just sharing borders shouldn't be enough to send them into a "I must wipe you" rage.
4) When the AI has a multi front war they get an automatic peace treaty from one of their enemies. When it happens to the player? Nope gg gl you gotta fight both those MFs now.
5) The negotiations/diplomacy is pretty barebones in this game.
6) The targeting for enemy ships is messed up. Those tiny ships have to be clicked on while they fly by? Really? That is awful and needs to be changed.
Even with all those issues, the game is fun. Hopefully the devs will start updating it and a community will get going.
Edit: They have actually fixed some of my issues in the first update. They made targeting enemy ships way better, so that is a non-issue now. They have also added settings so you can change sound!
Other things they did on the first update: balanced AI aggro speed and nerfed AI starting city size. They also increased the number of ships players can control. They added another in game event.
All-in-all it's great to see the devs addressing issues in a timely fashion!

Early access so I'm thumbs up'ing it, but I do have some issues with the game at its current state. After about 5 hours, it seems like I've experienced most of the game. I can continue to grind up my city size and expand my borders some more, but it seems pointless to do that since, as far as I can tell, there is no way to kill your enemies. I had an AI city pop up a few sectors outside my borders early on, so of course I had to show him who's boss of my little area and beat him up. So, I destroyed all of his fleets, took over a couple of sectors and he surrenders, giving me a bit of cash (note: Its a forced accept surrender, you cannot decline him). I've done this now on about 4 seprate occasions, except instead of taking over his sectors, I just beat on his city because he is completely surrounded by me. He has 3 sectors left that are spread out, disconected from his city (shouldn't be recieving the tax from those then right?) but everytime I get his city pretty well destroyed, he surrenders again.
So I've gone through the process of destroying his city center and as many population buildings as possible in a mad rush to try and finish him off before he surrenders and I have to wait another 20 minutes to try again. This really wouldn't be an issue if I could subjugate him or otherwise force his compliance, but since I can't I feel the need to keep trying to kill him since he is literally an enemy stronghold inside my borders.
Overall, game is incredably fun, definitely has a lot of potential. List of suggestions that IMO would greatly improve gameplay though:
- Ability to destroy your enemies cities or otherwise pacify them permanently!
- AI comanders for your fleets. Let those massive stock of reserve ships patrol your borders so you don't have to personally respond to *every* minor pirate/enemy incursion.
- Repair option for the ships in your fleet. Right now you can ghetto it by puting them into the reserve and taking them back out, but it doesn't seem like thats intended.
- Asteroid mining base! Lets put those asteroid sectors to work!
- Trade convoys, you can go to distress beacons and see the NPC convoys, why not have our own going around for us to protect? Maybe have them delivering the resources mined from planets instead of them auto arriving?
- Don't let players build their city center on a planet, or at least warn them! I thought I was being clever having my city on a planet I wanted to mine, but instead it made it un-mineable!
Overall, great game and well worth the money. Looking foreword to seeing the future content!

The premise of Pressured is simple but relatively hard to master. In each level, you are assigned a target number. Your goal is to click on numbers that add up to that target number before the pressure meter fills up. As you click on numbers, your current sum is shown on the top of the screen so that you can keep track of how far off from the target number you are. On the bottom of the screen, you'll be advised as to how many times you need to reach your target number before advancing to the next level. Each time you successful reach the target, some pressure is relieved, in essence, adding more time to complete the level. Easy peasy, right? NOPE! The grid where the numbers are located is constantly shifting. Numbers flash on the screen for no more than a second before new numbers appear, bombs randomly appear (resetting your sum to 0) , and a "2X" symbol occasionally pops up (doubling your current sum). Points are earned for each correct target hit and points are lost for hitting bombs or going over the target number. You will need to stay sharp or you will fall to the pressure!
It's insanely addicting and an intruiging game. The game is meant to a quick burst of action but you will find yourself trying to best your score after every game. And for under $3 USD, you can't go wrong!

Yes i had fun with the game, but there are a couple things that bother me about Ziggurat, that other Dungeon Crawlers like Binding of Isaac did much better.
First of all the repetition: it's randomly generated, the problem is there simply aren't enough pieces, that could be put together. Visually after three games you've seen it all, walls over walls over staircases.
Regarding Game Design it's even worse. Not only are there so incredibly few enemies in that game, but also almost none of them require any specific approach. Just shoot, walk sidewards and you're fine. Same with bosses: no "sore" points to shoot, no tricks or strategies to learn. Don't even try beeing fancy, just shoot!
What bothers me most is the shooting itself. It just doesn't feel as rewarding as in games like Diablo or Serious Sam, it's rather very indirect, there is almost no feedback on how hard you've hit or not, or how injured the enemy is. Games which are all about slaughtering hundreds of enemies just need to be satisfying about it, otherwise there's not much left.
In addition the RPG system is rather simple and the weapons pretty much all serve the same purpose.
It's these two things i miss about the game, the replayability and the depth. Otherwise you get a simple, solid Shoot ’em Up as they have always been there.

is a first person shooter Rougelite. You make your way through randomly generated dungeons, using magical weaponary to fight hordes of enemies and gain experience to increase your level and power up your skills in order to defeat the final boss at the end. Think
crossed with
and you're pretty much there.
If you have played any Rougelites like
or
then you should know what to expect. Dungeons, rooms, items and enemies are all randomly generated, keeping the genre's infamous RNG element that can carry you through to the end or completely screw you over and everything in between.
Like
or
,
's combat is built in an FPS format. Unlike many games of its ilk, however,
's combat is incredibly robust. The weapons all feel different enough to warrant experimentation throughout runs, while they are still meaty enough that you rarely feel cheated through being given a shoddy weapon. Every weapon has both a standard attack and an alt-fire, essentially doubling your means of attack. Alt-fire tends to expend more mana, which acts like ammo in other FPS games and can be replenished by picking up coloured crystals of each weapon class's respective colour. You unlock more stuff as you play, including new characters, so repeat playthroughs are highly encouraged.
Movement in
is very fast and fluid, harkening back to the PC shooters of old, so you feel very agile as you dance and weave amongst your enemies, firing off spells left, right and centre. The feeling of speed, the crunchiness of the combat and the gorgeous lighting effects make for a game that is very exciting to play. Even in runs where you don't make it past the second level, you feel powerful and capable of taking on the world. Until you get stomped by one of the tough-as-nails bosses.
is a gorgeous-looking game. It's semi-cartoony aesthetic and gorgeous lighting effects are very pleasing to the eye, and allow absolute clarity for spotting enemies and lining up your shots. Enemies are also refreshingly varied, ranging from sword-throwing skeletons to acid-spitting slimes and screeching banshees. It also runs very smoothly, even with a lot of enemies onscreen (a regular occurance); Milkstone did a stellar job of optimising their game.
The sound design is respectable at best. The music consists of generic loops and enemy sounds are repeated quite frequently. The weapons and spells sound good enough, but the sound design is overall rather unremarkable.
is an excellent game. It's pure balls-to-the-wall fun that surpasses its contemporaries in terms of its combat and is lovely to look at to boot. The controls are tight and responsive, the weapons are great fun to use, and it is balanced in such a way that you are rarely screwed over. The old Rougelite RNG can still stick a spanner in the works of an otherwise good run, so you ought to consider your opinion on this element before making a purchase. If high-octane, spell-casting action is what you're after though,
is the game I would recommend first.

It's easy to get caught up in the satirical laughs, but the gameplay here is also superb with different solutions to problems and intense action highlighted by the Rex 'Power' Colt's constant (and beautifully chosen )one-liners. Ótima sequência do Chips Challenge
10/10

After many years of copyright purgatory, Chip's Challenge 2 was finally released, with more varied puzzle elements than its predecessor and a far better understanding of what makes a puzzle fun and interesting.
With over a hundred puzzles plus usermade puzzle packs, this game will sate anyone's craving for skill and timing based puzzling!

If you're a completionist, this game has many levels that will make you suffer. If you just like touring tile-based puzzles, Chip's Challenge 2 runs smoothly and has quite a few elements. If you're nostalgic for the Microsft version of Chip's Challenge 1 and were disappointed by the Steam version, rest assured Chip's Challenge 2 was designed to run in this engine and thus feels "right".
Unfortunately while the majority of levels have some sort of clever design, some require a lot of trial-and-error or very tight timing. Other levels require using strange combinations of rules or obscure rules that you will have forgotten by the time they're relevant because they were introduced in a tutorial 75+ levels ago.
Despite the frustration I had, and my dislike for some level designers more than others, it was fun enough that I stuck with it for the 30+ hours it took to complete all 200 levels. It's nice that they added bonus flags as optional extras that are harder to get than just solving the puzzle, and that using the built in editor's "Replay" function you can see how the level was supposed to be solved, which is great if you're stuck or just wondering why your solution felt so inefficient.
I'm not sure I'd want to go through it all again, but for the price it was definitely worth it.

This game may have a hilariously bad campaign (seriously, METAL BOXES and SPESS MEHREENS must be seen to be believed), but it's a good game on its own. Different from most RTSs in that the focus isn't on economy management but on battle: thus, resources are gathered automatically by capturing specific points (Requisition) and building generators (Power). The scale of battles is also different, with squads substituting individual units for most infantry and making battles of hundreds of units and a dozen vehicles very much possible. If you're only buying one Dawn of War, it's either this or Retribution. And that's a different monster.
But you can't speak of Soulstorm without speaking of mods. This game has some of the best mods out there. Ultimate Apocalypse is one of many, but it stands out: it makes battles even larger, makes titans buildable, adds several races, adds more progression to vanilla races and makes it all feel like it belongs in the game, barring one or two glaring exceptions. Don't want something as large, but you'd like it if Daemons/(insert Chaos Warband)/(insert Space Marine Chapter)/(insert faction) were playable? There's very likely a mod for it. Mods for Chaos Daemons, Thousand Sons, World Eaters, Salamanders, Blood Angels, Black Templars, Inquisition, Tyranids... they all exist, and that's only listing some of the mods I've downloaded (the ones I remember off the top of my head).
Also, this game has the best unit in any RTS (tied with AoM Titans): the Daemon Prince. Best unit quotes ever, its sync kills are awesome and it has a buttload of AoE attacks. Plus it looks freaking awesome, and when it dies the best evil laugh ever plays.

So, I've played through the intro of this game and done a bit of free roaming with my friend, so I thought I'd give some first impressions. (The Quest Log section may be updated, so you may want to check back at some point if you're interested, which I expect you aren't).
PLOT:
Judging by the intro and the dream sequence at level 5, your character (my first one being the Hobbit Burgular, Mimbulius) is the chosen one (or something like that) whose destiny is tied to the fate of Middle-Earth! The story is set out in quests that vary depending on which character you are (my friend was a dwarf and met Gandalf and Thorin and all the other dwarves from The Hobbit while I was just helping out around this little village that got attacked for five minutes).
GAMEPLAY:
Open World, quest-based gameplay. It is very much like World of Warcraft, but it's still a good MMO.
QUEST LOG:
Day 1: My friend and I set out from Erebor on the free horses they give you for 24 hours after completing the intro, and we decided that we were going to go from Erebor to Mordor, stopping at certain locations to look around. We rode to Hobbiton, where we found Bag End and looked around, then we headed off into the Bree-Lands to find The Inn of the Prancing Pony. My friend thought he could take on a bear, and it chased us all the way into Bree. At the Pony, I got my haircut and got drunk, while my friend sold all his junk items to Barliman Butterbur. We then set off for Weathertop, as my friend did not want to stay the night in Bree as to be safe. Weathertop is in the Lone Lands, what we now know to be as quite a dangerous place for two Level Sixes to be riding through at night. My friend was lucky and actually managed to make it onto the ruins, but I, however, was attacked by some freaking ravens! Meanwhile, my friend wasn't having the best time up on the hill, and he managed to use some magical item or something to teleport back to Erebor. It was just me now, so I rode on, past Weathertop, to try and go through the Trollshaws to Rivendell...I was killed two minutes later, and used my instant respawn, only to be killed again about twenty seconds after. I then respawned at a safe place (the entrance to the Lone Lands) as day began. My ride through the Lone Lands was fine, and nothing attacked me at all. If only my friend had actually listened when I suggested waiting in Bree until morning. I entered the Trollshaws, and the game warned me that this area was Level 30, but I was determined. I rode through the Trollshaws, with monsters chasing me. I reached the river that seperates the Trollshaws from Rivendell, and rode on. I could not see a path to Rivendell, so I rode up a hill to get a better view. At this point, I stopped, and, as I checked the map, the monsters caught up with me and attacked me. I moved away from the monsters, and they chased me. I moved back again, forgetting a crucial detail - I was on the edge of a hill. I fell 200ft, still riding my horse, and died as my body smashed into the same river I had believed to be the end of my worries. I had to use a 'Safe Respawn' that took me to the middle of a place called Archet, on the borders of Bree. I left to go and play Town of Salem instead.

Okay so, first off let me explain something.
There are a lot of reviews here that do not recommend this game, and most of them basically come down to 'this game isn't what it used to be before it went f2p'. This may be true, I will not argue against that. But I only started playing less than a week ago. In other words I have only ever seen the f2p version, and so will anyone who picks up this game now. Therefore, f2p is the game I am reviewing!
The game can be downloaded for free, and it is entirely possible to play this game fully free to play. The game has a huge amount of content available for free without any purchase (I haven't gotten that far into the game, but from what I've seen, there's hundreds and hundreds, if not thousands of hours of gameplay possible without ever purchasing anything).
That being said, there are some clear restrictions to your account that require payment to solve. Most notably, there is a gold cap on 2 gold. When you earn more than 2 gold ingame, any more gold you earn will be put away until you pay to remove the level cap. Also, some characters cannot be started/played before being unlocked by paying for it. And then there are quest packs purchasable that will add so many more available quests to the game to give even hundreds more hours of gameplay.
However, it should also be noted that you can gather the 'paid' currency (Turbine Points) ingame as well by completing deeds (kill 60 orcs, use this skill 500 times, etc). This is not a fast way to gather Turbine points, and unless you're going to put in hundreds and hundreds of hours it won't be enough to unlock a new character type for example, but with a little bit of effort it is definitely possible to remove the gold cap and buy the riding skill (required to use a mount) with only the Turbine Points you got from completing deeds! Those 2 purchases were available to me after only about 30 hours of play, which is quite fair in my opinion.
Taking all this into account, I believe it is fair to rate this game as a truly f2p game that really allows you to remain f2p as long as you're willing to work for your stuff. This does obviously not include the paid expansion sets that will asllow you to move past level 50 and unlock entire new areas. As an f2p game I also believe it has a very fair way to collect Turbine Points without paying, a feature that not many f2p games really have (some will offer a very minor amount of points once every month or so, but this game actually gives you the chance to collect quite a few of them if you dedicate time to it).
Honestly, I have never played this game before it became f2p, and I may have been missing out. But I don't care. Because this game as it is right now, is tons of fun, with loads of quests and very interesting storylines. And it can definitely be played for free!

This is what you want.
Ever wished you could play SPAZ multiplayer on the world map?
Co-op with friends and form alliances with random strangers?
Build cities?
This is basically what that is, a Multiplayer sandbox version of Spaz.

The AI is responsive and intelligent.

Small ships can beat larger ships if they're outfitted right and the enemy ship is outfitted wrong.

All and all
Is it worth it right now at this very moment in time?

GTA V has a greatly told story and its characters are put in the limelight in an impressive way. The story itself however is kinda sexist (against both men & women) which is tried to be eased a little bit by a cynical but at times very rude humour. This game is really misanthropic. Womens are portraied to be shallow, only wanting to be famous and kinda wanting to get laid for this goal. Men are shown as bad♥♥♥♥♥cholerical brutes or total loosers.
Aside from the story there's a hell of a lot to do - so if you're really bored, GTA V may be your thing. However those sidequests are kinda generic and don't add anything to the main story. In a way, GTA continous to be the evil root that is copied by so many open world rpg's.
The multiplayer -GTA Online- contains a bad character costumization, a chaotic inventory and store management with overprised goods, a ridicolous ingame store, the worst lobbymaking ever and a drastically downgraded and kinda empty World (Los Santos) and tons of time consuming sidequests again for bored people. Thinking of those deers in the wild, flying planes and people having a walk with their dogs -all features in the singleplayer-? Nope, not in GTA Online: aside from other players you only see standard pedestrians with no special activities whatsoever.
Oh and did I mention the graphics? The graphics are the most overrated feature in GTA V ever. In nearly every corner you can see pixely textures and bad 3d models (even with Ultra settings). What GTA V does good is lightening and view distance. I've seen a lot of better looking games though that require far less power from your pc.
So, in my opinion, GTA V is one of the most overrated games out there. If ya want a nice gangsta-open world action game, play Saints Row instead.

Although it is considered the black sheep of the original DoW expansions (mainly due to it being made by a different company) Soulstorm is no where near the blunder the bandwagon would ahve you believe. It has critical shortcomings but those do not actually overshadow it's solid improvements over Dark Crusade which can be observed merely by playing the game.
Pros:
-It's just more. Much like Dark Crusade and Winter Assault this expansion just adds more. More factions, more units, more maps.
-Bigger Campaign. Using the same concept as Dark Crusade, rather than a linear narrative campaign this game uses an open-ended "Conquest" where you fight for control of a solar system against every other faction in the game, 1 territory at a time. It does lose out on some of DC's charm however (See Cons)
-The factions we waited for! The Adepta Sororitas and Dark Eldar are considered niche factions in the Warhammer community that dont recieve nearly as much love from Games Workshop as other more known factions such as the Adeptus Astartes and Orks. It was pleasant to finally see them get some screen time in a game (Actually the only game they appear in to this day)
-Mods. Like the rest of DoW mods are a big part of this game's extended playability although admittedly due to the previously mentioned bandwagon not many modder bothered to move away from DC (See Cons)
Cons:
-Enemy/Ally A.I. still sucks. If you ever played any DoW then you know that the A.I. is utter garbage...enough said.
-Imbalance. Soulstorm is the only expansion for the original DoW to mess up the overall balance of the base game. It adds flying units to each army (Except Necrons who have their scarabs ruined by becoming Anti-Air ONLY units) that dont quite work so well. None of them are particularly good units but they punish melee-oriented playstyles heavily just by being present. It seems the A.I. is the only one who would even use them so heavily
-New Resources but there is a catch. The added factions (Sororitas and Dark Eldar) get interesting resources called Faith and Souls respectively which allow them to unleash many awesome powers on the battlefield. Why is this bad? It isnt, but none of the previous factions get any new resources which makes it feel like a wasted opportunity
-No story this time. Although it tried to do what Dark Crusade's campaign did on a larger scale Soulstorm misses the point by skimping-by on most of the awesome dialogue and backstory for the places you fight over. This isnt helped by the fact that the factions dont have the same quality of characters leading them this time around. This results in a campaign that is bigger but a bit more boring
-Less mods. Due to the outrageous meme-filled bandwagon that poisoned this game's repuation many modders never bothered to work on it and just stuck with Dark Crusade. Therefore it is harder to extend your playtime or correct many of the balance issues via mods

Like the first Chip's Challenge, only with infinitely more complexity! You'll laugh, cry, tear your hair out, ponder what you're doing in life, and then cry again!

In short, go play Chip's Challenge 1 instead.
In long, why the heck is this nearly 200 megs? Especially given the lack of features and overall bare-bones presentation. It's ridiculously bloated in terms of memory footprint. There's a lot of new puzzle elements, some of which seem like they overlap a lot, like did there really need to both be one-step tiles that turn into water AND one-step tiles that turn into blocks instead? And the point flags, different colors of theives, and blocks that you can only pass if you _DON'T_ have a certain item? It's ridiculously bloated in terms of puzzle elements as well!
The puzzle difficulty starting out is really strange, too. Unlike Chip's Challenge which has a nice slow ramp to teach you how the puzzle elements work, this game has a really long, boring single level that throws it all at you at once, then come some stages that don't feel like they're part of a cohesive plan, but rather just grab bag picked and strewn about. The difficulty level similarly seems kind of arbitrary.
I have a lot of fond memorie sof Chip's Challenge, and I appreciate that I'm able to go back and experience it again and see that it still was a decent puzzle game, but this sequel doesn't do anything that the first one didn't do as well or better. Take a pass on this one unless you're getting a good deal on a bundle with this and the Editor, because at least that can provide some value.
Otherwise: Pass.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution was the best game I had ever played (until it was lately supplanted by Witcher 3), and I was glad that this, my first review in a long while, would be focused on the sequel to that wonderous title.
Of course I had heard all about the poor reviews of this game - indeed that is why I haven't finished and reviewed it earlier. A recent upturn in reviews and a big sale lead me to take the plunge and stake my tender heart on a game which I had very little reason to trust.
Well, to an extent, I'm glad I trusted it. Mankind Divided delivers, it is not as good as HR - but then again, no other game has ever been, for me, bar one - but it is a solid offering in it's own right which should be experienced.
We reacquaint ourselves with Adam Jensen, protagnoist of the previous game. Jensen damn near died at the beginning of HR, and was rescued by his boss, David Sarif, who stocked his tortured frame with an arsenal of mechanical 'augmentations' before sending him off on a quest to track down the agumented mercenaries who attacked Sarif and Jensen in the first place. The first game ends any number of ways, but in this title an ending has been selected in which all augmented peoples of the world have been momentarily forced to commit unspeakable acts of murder against their will. The resultant universal distrust of 'augs' has lead to the formation of ghettos, brutal police actions and resultant 'terrorist' and/or pacifist movements.
Jensen - sporting mystifying new augs which he doesn't remember receiving - steps into this world as a representative of Interpol, and he navigates his way through a reasonably complex and layered plot, and itinerant side-plots, in what took me - on maximum available difficulty - about 18 metriculously stealthy, pacifist hours to complete. The story deals with poignant concepts of terrorism, and of the use of ordinary people by as tools for violence by extremists, while also touching on overarching powers that be which remain in place following the events of HR.
The positives, then. The game is fun. The levels are not as big as in the previous game, but feature their fair share of challenge, especially one imagines if a player is fighting their way through the game. I personally chose the stealth route as I mentioned earlier. The zones, while being less numerous, varied or extensive as the original game's offerings, are detailed and of distinct personalities. The mechanics of the game are generally tight.
The game, however, got a buttload of bad reviews on release and I would be remiss if I didn't address some of the problems of the title.
I'd like to assert with finality that no matter how good a game this is, it was always more likely than not to fall short of Human Revolution - if only because I went into this playthrough having seen the sheer weight of red downward-thumb reviews on the Store Page. Indeed, it is not the same title. If you haven't played HR you are a fool - a fool! - and must immediately complete the Director's Cut.
So what does the game fall short with? Polish, for starters. A raft of dissapointing features stick out like sore thumbs - stilted, identical seagulls in the opening level that look like they were quite honestly taken from Goldeneye 64 and transplanted into the game, a pixelated JPEG city backdrop in Prague which only looks marignally better than the NYC backdrop of the opening level of the original Deus Ex, a disapointing thinness in terms of variation of models.
I have to make this abundantly clear, the version of the game which I purchased had absolutely zero sense of being a play-to-win title, or a title which is in any way guided by microtransactions. Perhaps the developers took a step back in the face of backlash, but the version I bought a week and a half ago has been completed now without a single prompt or bottleneck presented to me.
There are some things that cannot be beaten from the first game. Their art style was pitch perfect, the story long and worthy, the gameplay challenging and wonderously extended, the settings varied and often awe inspiring, the characters well done, the factions with distinct personalities and challenges, and all things Jensen just right. It was always going to be a near impossible task to beat that, and Mankind Divided has, honestly speaking, failed on all counts. That doesn't mean it's a bad game, only that it isn't perfect. This game is a lot of fun, it gives a lot of scope for players to express themselves, and while it is to HR what Invisible War was the the original Deus Ex, one hopes that the lessons learnt here will ensure that the next title in the series is an excellent one.
Either way, get in on this one when you can afford it, and knock it off, you'll be glad you did because it is a great game, and also because the story of the DE universe is worth living out, step by step.

For fans of the LOTR saga, (and now also the Hobbit saga) this game is right up your street.
It captures ALL the moments from the film, be it items, to characters/npcs, or simply landscape/areas.
Problem is, thats just about where the fun of the game, ends.
It's pretty much the same things that you have to kill, in different zones.
Lots of re-skinned and tougher stats for monstes across the world, and it's really sad to see this, but then of course... LOTRO based their game of the old style WoW... You can see it with so many things which are alike with both gamesit's uncanny.
From the combat, right down to the crafting system, and everything inbetween.
Honestly, getting into a Guild, is normally the way to go with MMO games, as it tends to draw you into the game more, as you form bonds with your guild-mates.
However, for me... This is a game that I would actually like to enjoy Solo, and really experience the world and all it has to offer, for myself.
Sadly, even doing this though, the fact that there are so many re-skins and multiples of monsters which are boring and dull. (Generic types are Goblins, Orcs, Spiders, Wolves... etc)... That was enough for me to finally, after 60+ hours of game time, to put the game down for good.
I can only recommend this game to the hardest of LOTR die-hard fans, who want to immerse themselves inside Middle-Earth.
They can look past the boredom of the combat system, amongst many other simplistic functions of the game.
For everyone else, nope... You will likely hit the wall I have... and look for a more modern day game, which has more variety in it, excluding different skins for monsters.

GTA V has a greatly told story and its characters are put in the limelight in an impressive way. The story itself however is kinda sexist (against both men & women) which is tried to be eased a little bit by a cynical but at times very rude humour. This game is really misanthropic. Womens are portraied to be shallow, only wanting to be famous and kinda wanting to get laid for this goal. Men are shown as bad♥♥♥♥♥cholerical brutes or total loosers.
Aside from the story there's a hell of a lot to do - so if you're really bored, GTA V may be your thing. However those sidequests are kinda generic and don't add anything to the main story. In a way, GTA continous to be the evil root that is copied by so many open world rpg's.
The multiplayer -GTA Online- contains a bad character costumization, a chaotic inventory and store management with overprised goods, a ridicolous ingame store, the worst lobbymaking ever and a drastically downgraded and kinda empty World (Los Santos) and tons of time consuming sidequests again for bored people. Thinking of those deers in the wild, flying planes and people having a walk with their dogs -all features in the singleplayer-? Nope, not in GTA Online: aside from other players you only see standard pedestrians with no special activities whatsoever.
Oh and did I mention the graphics? The graphics are the most overrated feature in GTA V ever. In nearly every corner you can see pixely textures and bad 3d models (even with Ultra settings). What GTA V does good is lightening and view distance. I've seen a lot of better looking games though that require far less power from your pc.
So, in my opinion, GTA V is one of the most overrated games out there. If ya want a nice gangsta-open world action game, play Saints Row instead.

Better than Fry Cry 3. Better than marshmallows. Better than finding a twenty in your jeans pocket after doing laundry.  I knew I would enjoy this game from the very start of it.  Aside from just being an enjoyable experience, this game showcases what a game can be if it strips out the typical open-world busywork, condenses meandering main quests, and limits the map size.
Here's my blow-by-blow:
The good:
- I had a ton of fun playing through this game. I actually laughed, out loud, multiple times throughout this game, and even smiled.  And I hate feeling good about myself, so that's quite an accomplishment. The designers not only satirize the 80's, but the entire open-world RPG genre. For example, after finding one of many scattered collectibles (VHS tapes), the main character says "Great, found another one!" And then, in self-disgust, "What the ♥♥♥♥ am I doing?"
- The retro-futuristic 80's aesthetic, complete with bad one-liners, hits the bullseye.
- The mechanics, animations, graphics, and enemy AI are all excellent, same as Far Cry 3.
- The neon dystopian world the designers built here has more life and aesthetic appeal than any open world game I've played.
- The Blood Dragons themselves are pretty terrifying until you're leveled.
- The crafting system from FC3 was ditched and the skill-tree simplified. Makes for a better experience overall.
- The music is killer.
- The story is straightforward and entertaining. The missions are great fun.
- The voice acting is excellent.
- The map is just the right size.
The bad:
- The game requires installation and execution of UPlay, Ubisoft's content delivery/DRM/social application, over top of Steam in order to play it.  I don't like having to use, or even have, a secondary applications over Steam. It's always clunky and always unneccesary. I read some positive and some negative reviews before buying this game. It was on sale so I figured I'd give it a try.
The game play itself was pretty interesting and I liked the puzzle aspect to the game. I liked being able to switch between the two characters and figure out how to use their abilities. And, of course, the art is absolutely gorgeous.
However, a lot of the game felt very repetitive. It felt like the sort of game you could play for free online, except with better art. The game follows a story but they could have taken the story out and the game would have, more or less, felt the same. Loading a saved game was also pretty frustrating: when you want to load your game you can see all the chapters and choose where you would like to continue. The chapters are named but they are not numbered so it's not really clear whether you are continuing from where you left off or just repeating parts of the game you have already played. It definitely says something about the game if you can't tell whether you are experiencing a new part of the game or simply re-playing content you have already played.
Tiresome in gameplay and narrative.

I think I was perhaps expecting a little too much from a follow-up to one of the rare games that I actually played from start to finish more than once (I do this very rarely, very very rarely). Human Revolution just wowed me and I'd pick it back up from time to time to replay it in a slightly different style, I can't say I feel the urge to do the same with Mankind Divided.
I played HR on a PS3, and MD on a PC with Xbox One controller, so maybe that was the switch, but I just felt the controls weren't particularly slick or well thought through this time around, with moments of frustration occuring e.g. when a simple jump up to a ledge was... fail, try, fail, try, robot sentinel now has spotted you, you're dead.
I didn't really get the overclock system either, extra augmentations are available but you have to disable some for others to work. I never used them and then at some point in the story you get to use all them anyway with no penalty. For those using them, probably a cool thing, for me though it seemed a little pointless to introduce such a mechanic then do away with it a few hours into the game.
I largely enjoyed the story, finished it in about 20 hours, being fairly completionist. If you're going to talk to people and pay attention though be prepared for Jenson's only physical movement being this weird kind of shrug that he does every other line. Voice acting was all pretty good though.
Towards the end the world map will be extremely tedious as you go from A -> B -> A -> B via long loading screens.
Not really a review, just my thoughts as I've just finished it. Yes, I would recommend it, no, not at full price.
