I had great expectations for this game and while some points are positive most of the game is below average.
The graphics are incredible. The first thing that I noticed is the characters clothing is incredibely well defined. The general quality of the image has gone way up from the last game. Due to this, the game is incredibly taxing on the GPU and I had to run the game at High/Medium quality and it was lagging even then.
The sound is great as always in this series. One of the high point of this game is the ambiance and much of that is due to the quality of the audio. The music is perfect, the gun sounds are nice and the characters are voiced pretty well.
From now things start to go down. Quickly. Some **SPOILERS AHEAD** but nothing big.
Let's start with the storyline. It's "okay", nothing more. What I really wanted was a continuataion of the Human Revolution storyline and what we got was a little bit more info and loads more unanswered questions. And I mean a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of questions that remains a mystery, stuff that I really wanted to be explained. Like what's Jensen doing with the Juggernaut collective and why, since he's part of it, why don't know more about them ? Nothing's said about them except that Janus is leading them and theres a useless chick that you talk to from time to time.
The missions that you go on are rather long and there isn't too many of them. They are interesting in themselves but they don't explain much of the "main story". It took me about ~22 hours to pass the entire game and I did almost all the sidequests and visited almost all the corners of the maps. Thats not a lot. Especially since Human Revolution can take up to 40 hours of playtime to go around and can be replayed easily.
The concept of "game hubs" returns in this game but this time there is only one city that you run around with. The other areas are just mission areas that you spend only one mission on and you never see again. The hub of this game is Prague and while it's a bit bigger than Human Revolution's cities, it is fairly boring. I don't feel like the city is alive. Theres a lot of area to visit but most of it is for show. Nothing really happens anywhere except some scripted events.
I found the ending to be a total cliffhanger. Theres the first bossfight and you think that you cleared maybe 1/3 of the game and theres two bosses left. Since Human Revolution split the game on 1/3'rds with each a bossfight. And you are at 15-20 hours in so I thought I had a lot of the game left and felt excited. But nope, the game ends after the first bossfight. What a letdown.
There is DLC that extends the storyline and you are meant to purchase the new episodes to continue getting your Deus Ex fix. That's complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, the DLC is pretty much a single mission each and so far they've revealed♥♥♥♥♥♥about the story. The game is also riddled with other useless crap that you can buy.
Finally the gameplay is alright, not great. They changed the augmentations and I think they are worse than the Human Revolution augmentations. Theres not much useful augs for a stealth playthrough, most of them focus on combat.
Overall, I'm not happy with this game. It could have been so much better. If you are a huge fan of the Deus Ex serie, buy this game when it gets on sale but prepare to be disappointed. If you feel like trying a new shooter, skip this.

On the other hand, there are some decent upsides.

It saddens me to think this might be their last story, when it started as such a ground breaking title all those years ago.

Pressured is a deliciously addictive mathematical puzzle game. The premise is simple - add the numbers on the grid together to match the target number. Easy enough at first but you have to be quick because the numbers you need fade in and out, bombs appear instead of numbers and you are not allowed to use the same sums twice, all the while the clock is ticking! What makes Pressured so addictive though is the arithmetic required is pretty basic but the targets get larger and larger and larger, which means you'll need more and more numbers in your sums then throw some multipliers in... it'll test your limits! It's a killer combination of fast reflexes, quick thinking and of course a bit of luck that'll keep you coming back for more. Move over Sudoku, there is a new kid on the block!
Amazing Puzzle game! Highly Recommend this, and totally different to the norm.

As someone who is not very quick on their feet with the maths, you'd think I would hate an experience like this - but that is absolutely not the case. The music, the art, and the general vibe all come together to form something very special (and the unlocks are just the icing on an already very tasty cake).
Something interesting developed as I played - I got to see what sort of numbers, or sums, I was more mentally inclined to "solve", and which ones I tended to have a harder time with. It's a rare treat that you get to play a game that shows you exactly how your brain is wired in certain ways. So, you could also look at this as a chance to improve something mentally - to raise your own average by tackling something you might not be so good at - and that is AWESOME.
This game is a steal for the price of a coffee drink, and unlike said beverage, you get to keep this forever and ever!

Some thing deeper going on under the hood here, what outwardly is a fun little maths/brain training puzzler turns into something alot darker as you unlock more of the poetry.
I guess in the future (with a bigger budget) this could be pushed alot futher, to "Pye"(Darren Aronofsky) levels, full on Megacd quality cutscenes!!

The premise is simple, imagine a Countdown conundrum, you know, where Carol pulls out a stack of numbers and then tells you you have to calculate an even bigger number. Imagine that, only with numbers that are constantly changing, bombs that appear out of no-where when you're about to click to finish a sum, and a pressure gauge constantly filling up and causing no- end of stress.
In practice, it's involving, addictive, and a bit difficult to put down. Pressured puts you under pressure, but in a nice way, and definitely in a way that you'll come back to again and again.

I'm a sucker for math games, and I love puzzle games: Pressured scratches both those itches in one swoop. I give Pressured a big thumbs up for anyone looking for a game that requires a bit of brain power. It's only a couple bucks, which is a decent investment since it's probably going to take the average gamer around 2-3+ hours to really get the hang of NOT blowing up before unlocking the story (poetry).

Ziggurats are temples built in ancient times having the form of a terraced step pyramid and yet it was a mystery on which purposes they built them. Thats probably the devs used the ziggurat as the dungeon, purposely to fill the gap, which is interesting. Currently the game offers 5 floors (rooms connected with corridors) and more than 5 weapons, tons of perks (unlockable the more you play), different type of characters with different powers (one of the characters have increased firerate for weapons for ex.), ground/flying enemies (monster carrots, flying viking skulls for ex.), traps that are placed outside of battle rooms. Now until here it sounds good and interesting but there are things that i dont like at the moment and looking sceptical for the games some progress but i hope i will be wrong with my worries:
- Devs are open for suggestions but focusing to keep the game ``small`` with tweaking the current problems limiting the games potential in my opinion, they tend to respond to topics and suggestions that are ``worth`` for the price which is understandable but still counter productive for the final version of the game cause many suggestions cant be make true but i can await a compromise here since i have bought the game.
- Floor 1 and 2 are very easy to complete even without perks there is some balancing issues here.
- Lagging on massive enemy hordes.
- Game uses the Unity engine that is not ideal for FPS games, also limiting the games freedom in my opinion.
- Making the game rogue lite instead rogue like makes the game boring at times when you are not in combat. Rogue like would ve bring more variety in the average level structure and some surprising moments.
All in one this game is promising many things in the ``unused`` dungeon crawler FPS section in video games, sub genres are really difficult to make games that everyone would like but this game has the basics to make a unique game. If the devs will be more open for suggestions and making things that they promised this game will be alot of fun. This game is away from wasting your money in the current state but i will not recommend this game for now. If you are interested in this game but are unsure to buy or not, check the forums frequently what have changed for the game.

Know what you're purchasing: This is a first person shooter, not a roguelike. The roguelike elements of this game are procedurally generated dungeons, which seems to mean stock dungeon rooms on a grid in a similar style to binding of isaac. It also has cards you draw after killing a number of enemies, with different bonuses and maluses on them - however, these cards make no substantial changes to how the game is played.
So to rate this game, we must rate is as an fps, not as a roguelike. Sadly as an fps this is also found lacking. It compares itself to Heretic and Hexen, which certainly in theme it matches, but cannot compete with as a game. There are limitations in the room grid system which take away from the experience - you cannot pace a storyline with randomly generated rooms, your level design cannot have much in the way of verticality - and this has led to each room being these very open, very flat affairs, almost like gladiator arenas. What's more, interesting level elements like traps or pits of lava as shown in the trailer are kept to themselves, separate from monsters. You end up going through the game saying 'this is a puzzle room, i need to avoid the dangerous terrain' and 'this is an arena room, i need to keep moving in a circle'. Even boss fights have not been spared this fate, as you strafe around yet more square, open areas.
One thing the game has going for it are the differences in the monsters - they each feel unique, with their own ways of attacking and movement patterns. Certainly when different monsters are combined in a room, it can be a challenging and hectic experience, trying to run from the melee monsters while dodging the ranged monsters. Many of the monsters wouldn't feel out of place in a Serious Sam game, with running exploding berserkers and rocket launching dodos and a guy that summons hordes of carrots. Sadly the interesting monsters fall flat in a flat world, with a flat atmosphere.
I cannot recommend this game, like many unity-based fps games it fails to excite, and the roguelike elements have such a minor effect to your character and such a major malus on the level design that it feels like it's letting down what else is here.

The game it self is a good experiance, I would recommend the story as it has a lot of fun activities. The Multiplayer is a good idea and if you have some friends to play with I would recommend playing with them in a private session and just mess around in the open world  or do some private activities.
However there are a lot of problems in the online public Grand Theft Auto sessions (and some general online problems). One problem some people talk about is the price of everything in the online version of the game. Everything that has some cool features is overpriced as heck which makes no sence. Its not because I am lazy and think that everything is too hard to get. It's because they want you to buy their "SharkCards". Which I can understand that for an online game, developers would like some income from the online servers.  But as someone who has bought some of the features with the in game money. You don't get a lot out of it which kind of disapoints me.
Moving on to the next subject, which I can assume a lot of people are going to expect. The Hacker problem in GTA V is a HUGE problem. 3/10 times I join a session I experiance people hacking in some sort of way or another. That may seem like that its not a big problem because it happens so little. I have only noticed "hackers" or script kiddies when they go on giant teleport and exposion sprees and when they do, it spoils the experiance for the game for me and my friends. Sometimes money drops happens (when this happens I try to leave the session quickly. I will explain later why) and it makes it seem like your earnings that you have been spending hours to get seem usless. Only recently RockStar have added something for players to help spot script  kiddies, and it sucks. The options are not to do anything about reporting script kiddies (the griefing option seems like it was intended for people repeatingly killing players) and when you select the "Other" option, It gives you a character limit of something like 50-80 characters which in my opinion is NOT enough characters to explain why you are making a report on this player. I made a report saying "Killing passive players, invisable, spawning npcs, explo" because the character limit stopped me from explaining the full story, I had yet to say that he teleported players out of vechicles and also giving everyone 5 star rating.
The worst thing about it, RockStar does not seem to give any sort of responce to this at all. RockStar seems to not care about the community opinions. One big reason leading to this is the recent trifle about banning a lot of mods from GTA V. A while back RockStar  tried to take a step in and put a hault to the script kiddies. By shutting down a popular mod launcher. This was a good idea on the scriptkiddies thought, But a jaw dropping terrible idea for the general modding community. A lot of people who used that launcher were using it for fun in singleplayer.
Another example of what they seem to not see is the banning problem in the online session. There was a reason I said I leave the session when money drops happen. RockStar have made it so that anyone who gets a large sum of money without legit ingame ways will be banned. This seemed like a good idea. But then people realised that when they collect money from stuff like money drops (which a lot of the times they are stuck in place to be given money by force) bans them from the GTA V online experiance. This is not how it should work at ALL. RockStar needs to look at the source of the problem and not the results that come from it. Some of you might think that this was to show that they were trying to fix the problem. I say that they could have had an announcement or an interview about this problem. Not a small 2 paragraph talk but a full 2-4 pages about the problem letting everyone know the issues with this problem. I know its difficult to solve these problems and I respect that they are actually trying. But they seem to be taking a less than preffered route to the problem.

Summary:
Torchlight II clings to its Diablo series heritage like no other. It tries to be, at the same time, both fresh and familiar to fans of the genre. In the end, It’s just a cartoony Diablo II clone with elaborated gameplay mechanics. Both gives a mixture that seems appetizing but in reality is just stale and plain boring.
6/10
The Good :
- Many, many weapons and items
- Pets
- Overally polished
- Good music
The Bad :
- Very repetitive gameplay, even for hack'n'slash
- Bland atmosphere and plot
- Feels like cartoony clone of Diablo II
- Dated graphics
I did not finish the game. My review follows these situations rarely. Even more rarely, I’m struggling to like something. This time, it’s Torchlight II.
As serious as I can be, this fight ensued the moment I started the game and ceased when it ended up in a virtual dump. Don’t get me wrong, I adore hack’n’slash RPG’s.
I absolutely loved Diablo I and more so, Diablo II. First part created the genre with gloomy atmosphere and revolutionary gameplay. The sequel had the magic to keep you clicking so many times, one would believe you’re testing mouse manufacturer’s claims of billion click durability. Torchlight II has neither. And here’s why.
Right of the bat, Torchlight II shows resemblance to Diablo II. Made by the same author, the music is unmistakable. At first, I was glad because I really enjoy these notes but at the same time it prevents Torchlight to be unique. Several sounds, like opening a teleport, are basically cloned from Diablo II. Even the sequence of worlds and it’s hubs in TL are the same as Diablo II – wilderness, desert, dense forest, hell. And just like in Diablo II, our nemesis is a mysterious traveler that we’re always one step behind from. All of this takes away from Torchlight II. It’s just too familiar to call it a world of its own. It’s a copy with cartoony overlay which makes it neither dark and gloomy, nor light-hearted.
As years passed, hack’n’slash games had to mutate it’s formula to remain fresh and attractive to gamers. Happily, Torchlight II has some tweaks and non-standard ideas, one of which is company of your pet. Essentialy, it’s your coop friend. There are several pets to choose from, all of which can pick and store items for you, wear accessories, fight, cast spells and last but totally not list, do a little shoppin while you bash evil’s head. You can also fish for, well, fishes that for reasons unknown, can transform your pet into a killing beast.
As It goes for Diablo clones, you have a lot to choose from to do that. Beside leveling, getting a good equipment is the core element of action RPG’s. Torchlight II gives you –collecting sets, enchanting, socketing and putting in gems. Unfortunately, beside collecting and buying spells that can be used by any class, I can’t find anything that discerns Torchlight from other ARPG’s.
Speaking of classes, I didn’t play every class. I focused mainly on Engineer. What I found out, is that I played through majority of the game using only 4 out of dozens. I’ve tried more variety but I’ve always ended up coming back to previous skills as they work best. So it all came down to getting the right equipment. Though you’ll encounter or buy many, many stuff it’s not that easy to find an upgrade. I’ve completed 3/4 of the game using just 3 ranged weapons with a single tactic. Single tactic, because even though monsters seem to vary much, the’re all killed the same. On hard difficulty I didn’t though that Tourchlight II is challenging, not even for a wihle)
That said, it was hard to not get bored. Accompanied by generic maps, plot that isn’t worth mentioning (which I won’t) and repetitiveness with no challenge, I was struck with remorse while playing Torchlight II. Remorse that told me, that time with Torchlight II could be spent way better or at least on a superior game. Torchlight II is an OK ARPG, that excels in mediocrity. If ARPG’s are your thing, you could bite the bullet, especially that it’s dirt cheap now, but don’t say that I didn’t warn you.

Underwhelmed. That's how I feel playing the game. Let's not talk about the occasional loading glitches (although they have costed some success, the checkpoints are mostly generous). I am underwhelmed by the gameplay AND storytelling.
First and foremost, the writing is excellent. Characters are fleshed out fantastically and while I wouldn't like being friends with anyone of them (criminal maniacs aren't my social circle), watching a movie about them would be amazing. Speaking of, the game is more of a movie than a game.
The gameplay is scripted. Heavily scripted. I don't have to listen to anything in the cutscenes as mission markers handold me through every single step. The game even selects weapons for me. The game makes sure I don't fall behind the target I'm chasing, the game makes sure I can't shoot the driver because in this mission, my gun's disabled or the driver simply isn't a hit box, the game goes so far as to control the steering and brakes of my bike to make sure I don't miss that important moment. It's too cinematic, the missions are scripted heavily, it doesn't feel like I'm playing a coherent game but just a series of scenes with different rules attached to each other via cutscenes. Some of the cutscenes are interactive. Way too often, the game has way too much padding in form of driving from A to B with another character in my car or on the phone. The dialogs are great, I give Rockstar that, but they're too long, too much. That's just busywork. Boring gameplay, stretched, to make room for more writing. Way too much fluff and not enough filler. But the fluff is great, isn't it?
Well, no. The characters are excellent, the story not so much. While there is sort of an encompassing story arch, there are many non-sequitur missions. Meaning that stuff just happens. Way too often, STORY missions (I wouldn't bat an eye about this in side missions) start with a random "You go there, another character just happens to drop by and the mission starts". No connection with what I, the player, just did. Or did previously. That "Random things happen randomly around the protagonists" would work great in a movie. A video game is interactive however, I, the player, want the story proggress to be a result of my previous actions. This non-sequitur writing diminishes the player's achievement by implying "Whatever you just did, the next step in the story sort of would have happened anyway". Well, of course not, the scripts says so.
Too much scripting, too obvious breaking of game rules for the sake of the script, too much script alltogether. I wouldn't have bought this game had I known that the "open" part of "open world" is just windowdressing. I've never been to an Ammu-Nation except once because the missions' outfit me with everything. Again, scripts.
Ah yeah, there are the side activities, sure. Too bad they aren't overall enjoyable. Tennis & golf were way more fun on the Wii, paragliding was more fun in Saints Row, meeting the occasional freak ranges from "fun, but again too much padding to fit dialog in" to "forced". Why should I go hunt for mortgage signs from my freak's competitor? Ah right, it's a video game with video gamey open world activities scattered over the place to give completionists a couple things more to do.
The online part is grinding at it's best. Heists are fun, most of everything else isn't as it's just busywork with the progress being the one and only reward. Hey, I have all my perks maxed out in Killing Floor 2, yet I play the game regularly. Why? Because the gameplay's amazing. Not so much in GTA Online.
All in all, not a bad game, but I expected more from what's supposed to be among the best games of the recent years.

Despite having played thousands of hours of the entire series, I was broke around the time this one released, and also wanted to wait and see if the PC version would be improved.

+The different Variants of each character adds lots of variety to each one.
+Though I haven't touched it a lot, the Faction system is pretty neat.
+The game runs completely fine on the highest settings for me with a consistent 60fps.
-The overall character roster is actually quite underwhelming in terms of size. A lot of fan favorites are absent, and some characters from the single player are entirely unplayable (Sindel, Baraka etc...).

I've thoroughly enjoyed GTA (Online) for the past couple of years (three years since PC release). The game offers a variety of gameplays, nice cars (to buy and steal), tuning, races, Missions,...  It's all been alot of fun. But since about a year, the main focus for the creators is to continually and gradually increase profits through sharkcardsales (ingame microtransactions: Simple put: you fork out real cash for fake ingame cash). All prices for every new item ingame have drastically risen and continues to rise. Now you can also earn ingame money and quite a good deal to be honest, but since the last few months it's been very clear that the gaming company wants to maximize your moneyloss. One might say this is the essence of this game (putting people up against people) and that might be true to an extent. But when you have to collect items for quite a few hours and then , during the few minutes of a sale, it gets blown up in a matter of secs by other players, the fun will wear off soon. In current GTA-online, things are all tweaked to maximize your loss (military vehicles/futurustic vehicles,..). This coupled with great new vehicles (including those military vehicles and now new planes) and their huge pricetag will push players towards microtransactions.
Some players decided to 'grind' certain ingame money makers, but since the last two DLCs, it became apparent the ingame money monitoring software was/is buggy. This 'bot' removes illegitimate earned money (due the game being massively hacked the last six months) and while that's a good thing, it also started removing legit and honest earned ingame money from players. Ofcourse you'll always have people crying out innocence, when they're not, but the magnitude and outrage of players crying out right now, speaks otherwise. So then you start filing a formal complaint, aka ticket, to the gaming company to check the 'bot's possible failures... To cut a long story short. There is no support,  you will receive a formal confirmation the removal was correct and due to illegitimately acquired ingame money. No explanation on the when and where and why, so you can at least verify and possibly adapt your gaming. No, if you persist in sending in tickets, the tone of the automated replies turns grim while threatening you with a possible ban if you persist in breaking the EULA.
So instead of an explanation (which is the very least a player deserves when he got robbed of ingame m illions (which do mean quite a few hours of ingame work), you get served a threat.
Currently alot of longtime players are re-evaluating their gaming time within GTA-online. It's still a fantastic game, but once you'll get hit by something that appears fundamentally incorrect wrt ingame earning (= hours of playing the game), you cannot trust the game that it won't happen in the future again, as you'll receive ZERO explanation.
I'm not gonna recommend this game to new players. The ingame money earning has decreased drastically, the ingame price tages increased exponentially and the ingame monitoring is so focused on eliminating players' money, it can't distinguish illegit from legit money. So both get taken away and then you have to their Support. See above for what happens next...
A damn shame, cos there really is no game like this, but it'll come with an ever increasing (real life) pricetag... Just don't assume you can earn it all ingame... You clearly can't... Sad really... Paid DLC would have been a far better choice for players and the gaming company... Not this...

Underwhelmed. That's how I feel playing the game. Let's not talk about the occasional loading glitches (although they have costed some success, the checkpoints are mostly generous). I am underwhelmed by the gameplay AND storytelling.
First and foremost, the writing is excellent. Characters are fleshed out fantastically and while I wouldn't like being friends with anyone of them (criminal maniacs aren't my social circle), watching a movie about them would be amazing. Speaking of, the game is more of a movie than a game.
The gameplay is scripted. Heavily scripted. I don't have to listen to anything in the cutscenes as mission markers handold me through every single step. The game even selects weapons for me. The game makes sure I don't fall behind the target I'm chasing, the game makes sure I can't shoot the driver because in this mission, my gun's disabled or the driver simply isn't a hit box, the game goes so far as to control the steering and brakes of my bike to make sure I don't miss that important moment. It's too cinematic, the missions are scripted heavily, it doesn't feel like I'm playing a coherent game but just a series of scenes with different rules attached to each other via cutscenes. Some of the cutscenes are interactive. Way too often, the game has way too much padding in form of driving from A to B with another character in my car or on the phone. The dialogs are great, I give Rockstar that, but they're too long, too much. That's just busywork. Boring gameplay, stretched, to make room for more writing. Way too much fluff and not enough filler. But the fluff is great, isn't it?
Well, no. The characters are excellent, the story not so much. While there is sort of an encompassing story arch, there are many non-sequitur missions. Meaning that stuff just happens. Way too often, STORY missions (I wouldn't bat an eye about this in side missions) start with a random "You go there, another character just happens to drop by and the mission starts". No connection with what I, the player, just did. Or did previously. That "Random things happen randomly around the protagonists" would work great in a movie. A video game is interactive however, I, the player, want the story proggress to be a result of my previous actions. This non-sequitur writing diminishes the player's achievement by implying "Whatever you just did, the next step in the story sort of would have happened anyway". Well, of course not, the scripts says so.
Too much scripting, too obvious breaking of game rules for the sake of the script, too much script alltogether. I wouldn't have bought this game had I known that the "open" part of "open world" is just windowdressing. I've never been to an Ammu-Nation except once because the missions' outfit me with everything. Again, scripts.
Ah yeah, there are the side activities, sure. Too bad they aren't overall enjoyable. Tennis & golf were way more fun on the Wii, paragliding was more fun in Saints Row, meeting the occasional freak ranges from "fun, but again too much padding to fit dialog in" to "forced". Why should I go hunt for mortgage signs from my freak's competitor? Ah right, it's a video game with video gamey open world activities scattered over the place to give completionists a couple things more to do.
The online part is grinding at it's best. Heists are fun, most of everything else isn't as it's just busywork with the progress being the one and only reward. Hey, I have all my perks maxed out in Killing Floor 2, yet I play the game regularly. Why? Because the gameplay's amazing. Not so much in GTA Online.
All in all, not a bad game, but I expected more from what's supposed to be among the best games of the recent years.

Ziggurat is a fast paced first person shooter set in a randomly generated dungeon. No, you won’t be shooting with guns. In this game you play as a sorcerer and therefore you’ll be using a wand, grenades and spells to complete your task. You have to fight yourself through 5 floors filled with traps, enemies and bosses.
But before you’re ready to take on the final boss you have to become stronger. This is done by killing enemies and collecting their dropped items. Dropped items consist of experience points, health or energy for your weapons. Pick up enough experience points and you’ll level up. Each time you level up your health meter will increase but you’ll also be able to pick a perk that might make things easier for you, or more difficult if you’re looking for a challenge. Unfortunately, the current set of ‘starting’ perks isn’t all that interesting and I wish there was more variety and depth in this system. I think the system itself works very well, by the way.  And on the other hand, the game’s focus lies on skill instead of random attributes so I understand the developer’s choice but right now, whenever you have to pick between two perks, most people will automatically choose the one that makes it easier for them. And rightfully so. But I want the choice between those two to be more difficult or I want these perks to have more impact.
However, I did notice - after completing the game - that there are still tens of perks to be unlocked so who knows, maybe there already are harder choices to be made, but I just haven’t gotten to that part yet.
I shouldn’t forget to mention that you can also find treasure chests and book pages scattered across the levels. The latter gives you more information about the world, the level you’re on or the enemies that you will encounter.
Anyway, energy is used for your weapons; your default wand will automatically recharge when it’s not in use but your other weapons rely on magic fragments that will replenish their meters when picked up. This is a clever mechanic from keeping the game too simple because these other weapons you pick up obviously inflict more damage than your starting weapon. So you have to regularly switch between weapons, depending on the sort of enemy of course.
Let me tell you that this game is just beautiful. It’s beautifully textured, the enemies are well animated and look amazing, but what impressed me most was the bosses. I think they stood out more than anything and the little intro you see before you head into battle makes it even better. I was a little disappointed to see the game had only 5 boss fights (I didn’t know the game had only 5 levels, you see), but I guess more floors, enemies and especially bosses can (and hopefully will) be added later on. And maybe I haven’t seen all there is to it yet, even though I did finish the story. Maybe there already are more floors depending on what character you play with, I don’t know.
The audio is also great. The game has this subtle ambiance. Voice acting for the enemies is generally well done, and the music suits the game, with the tempo slightly increasing whenever a battle takes place.
And yup, you’ve read it correctly. You’ll unlock plenty of stuff by just playing. I finished the game on my first try so there isn’t much replay value for me right now, but should you die often you’ll eventually unlock new characters and perks that will help you in your quest.
A game can be completed within 1-2 hours, if your skill is high enough (even less if you don’t explore). You can then start again with a new character. Unfortunately, there isn’t a whole lot of stuff to do for gamers who’ve already finished it, except for unlocking more stuff and trying to climb up the Leaderboards. It would’ve been nice to see the game mix things up, like adding tougher enemies or extra environmental hazards. You know, to keep things more interesting in the long run. There just isn’t enough replay value at the moment, but I sincerely hope the developers are working on this little dilemma.
In the end I still think Ziggurat is one of the most fun games I’ve played in a long time and it certainly is one of the most polished ones. I can’t wait for the developers to add even more stuff, because I desperately want to play more of it. And if that’s not a compliment, I don’t know what is.

First of all, the full price for a game and DLC of this age is shocking, especially considering that Sims 4 has been out for a fairly long time as well. I definitely wouldn't have bought any of it if it wasn't for sales.
I'm mostly a fan of building stuff and don't play the way most Sims fans seem to play (make families, advance in careers, having babies and all that). I mainly enjoy building on the city map, which Sims 4 does not offer. The ability to recolor really everything is priceless and another feature Sims 4 doesn't have. So for builders, Sims 3 is clearly the way to go. The base game already has a good selection of materials and the various DLCs and mods let you build pretty much anything you can come up with.
But the performance. Jesus Christ, the performance. I have every mod under the sun to make the game run better, I read every forum and guide. And the conclusion is: your PC doesn't matter. Either the game likes you and you can run it on a potato laptop older than the game itself, or the game doesn't like you and would crash, freeze or eternally load even if you put it on a NASA computer. I'm in the latter category. Just starting a new game can take up 20 minutes, depending on the city. Once it runs, it is all consuming and even alt tabbing will crash it. I can only play it in offline mode, too, otherwise the game freezes if any minor thing happens in the background. It runs somewhat smoother in windowed mode, but won't let me navigate the city map - which is kind of important for me.
Since it all depends on luck and if the Sims stars align for whatever system you try to run it on, I don't know if I should I recommend it. It sure is a lot fun for a city building fan to design individual buildings, but it is also frustrating to have your entire progress erased due to some mysterious file corruption from just trying to load it.
If you like to gamble or are dead certain luck is on your side, knock yourself out during a sale, I guess.

The game it self is a good experiance, I would recommend the story as it has a lot of fun activities. The Multiplayer is a good idea and if you have some friends to play with I would recommend playing with them in a private session and just mess around in the open world  or do some private activities.
However there are a lot of problems in the online public Grand Theft Auto sessions (and some general online problems). One problem some people talk about is the price of everything in the online version of the game. Everything that has some cool features is overpriced as heck which makes no sence. Its not because I am lazy and think that everything is too hard to get. It's because they want you to buy their "SharkCards". Which I can understand that for an online game, developers would like some income from the online servers.  But as someone who has bought some of the features with the in game money. You don't get a lot out of it which kind of disapoints me.
Moving on to the next subject, which I can assume a lot of people are going to expect. The Hacker problem in GTA V is a HUGE problem. 3/10 times I join a session I experiance people hacking in some sort of way or another. That may seem like that its not a big problem because it happens so little. I have only noticed "hackers" or script kiddies when they go on giant teleport and exposion sprees and when they do, it spoils the experiance for the game for me and my friends. Sometimes money drops happens (when this happens I try to leave the session quickly. I will explain later why) and it makes it seem like your earnings that you have been spending hours to get seem usless. Only recently RockStar have added something for players to help spot script  kiddies, and it sucks. The options are not to do anything about reporting script kiddies (the griefing option seems like it was intended for people repeatingly killing players) and when you select the "Other" option, It gives you a character limit of something like 50-80 characters which in my opinion is NOT enough characters to explain why you are making a report on this player. I made a report saying "Killing passive players, invisable, spawning npcs, explo" because the character limit stopped me from explaining the full story, I had yet to say that he teleported players out of vechicles and also giving everyone 5 star rating.
The worst thing about it, RockStar does not seem to give any sort of responce to this at all. RockStar seems to not care about the community opinions. One big reason leading to this is the recent trifle about banning a lot of mods from GTA V. A while back RockStar  tried to take a step in and put a hault to the script kiddies. By shutting down a popular mod launcher. This was a good idea on the scriptkiddies thought, But a jaw dropping terrible idea for the general modding community. A lot of people who used that launcher were using it for fun in singleplayer.
Another example of what they seem to not see is the banning problem in the online session. There was a reason I said I leave the session when money drops happen. RockStar have made it so that anyone who gets a large sum of money without legit ingame ways will be banned. This seemed like a good idea. But then people realised that when they collect money from stuff like money drops (which a lot of the times they are stuck in place to be given money by force) bans them from the GTA V online experiance. This is not how it should work at ALL. RockStar needs to look at the source of the problem and not the results that come from it. Some of you might think that this was to show that they were trying to fix the problem. I say that they could have had an announcement or an interview about this problem. Not a small 2 paragraph talk but a full 2-4 pages about the problem letting everyone know the issues with this problem. I know its difficult to solve these problems and I respect that they are actually trying. But they seem to be taking a less than preffered route to the problem.
I could talk about more but right now its a bit long for this review and also the other problems I have have a big chance of being patched in later updates.
I do say that you should get the game, the singleplayer is a great experiance. But the multiplayer needs to be fixed before I can say that its a decent experiance.
Thank you for reading this!

This is a solid entry in the series. The mix of stealth and action options is done quite well. The level design is solid and interesting, as are the missions. The storyline is pretty interesting, and the overall design and style is superb.
Leveling up your character via unlocking augs is great fun, and lets you design your own play style.
The AI is passable though not great.
One serious technical problem I encountered was a drastic drop in frame rates during most dialogues. It was frustrating to get great performance throughout, then have it plummet during the many dialogues.
The microtransactions wasn't a big deal at all as they don't interrupt the gameplay.
The DX Universe app is cool to use, to unlock the documentary vids about the game development. And the Deus Ex Go game is great if you like that sort of thing. Plus it helps you unlock praxis points for your character, if you link your accounts.
Overall, this is an excellent game, and an absolute steal at the sale price I bought it for.

Really Really Good Puzzle Game Even Better With Co-Op And Or Multiplayer !

Amazing gameplay, superb soundtrack, and just heaps of fun! Instead of being a typical platformer, what Trine 2 manages well is to provide players with more than just one method of going through the levels. I played this with one friend of mine, and we constantly 'broke' the game by playing around with Amadeus' magic, or Zoya's flexibility. (Sadly, we only ever use Pontius for his shield.)
(Note: I greatly recommend you play this with a friend or two.)
But what you get are fun-filled moments and a lot of laughter, as you may accidentally kill each other right after helping one another, trap your friend inside a box fort while they leave on a toilet break, or just do stupid things like accidentally slipping off a cliff or jumping to a trap. And when you get to solve the puzzles using methods you know aren't the 'right' way, you will laugh it off and look forward to the next one where you can continue to use your creativity to finish the level.
Overall, I could not recommend this enough. My only regret was that we didn't record it when we were playing.

I have a love/hate relationship with the concept of Early Access. What's my ideal Early Access title? It's a game that, in its current state, feels like it can stand alone as a release. Maybe it's rough around the edges, maybe it isn't fully fleshed out, but it's a more or less finished product that can stand to be improved. Early Access should be like... like when you order something at a restaurant – let's say a club sandwich – and they bring it out and say, “sir/madam, we're sorry but your homestyle sea salt french fries will be out in a few minutes.” And you're like, “oh, that's cool. This sandwich looks pretty good.” And you wait a few minutes, take a few bites out of your excellent club sandwich, and then they present you with your fries. “Ziggurat” is a delicious club sandwich – not too heavy on the mayonnaise and the bacon is crispy. I'm not exaggerating when I say that it is one of the most polished, fun titles I've seen ever from Early Access. And hopefully the fries are incoming.
“Ziggurat” is a dungeon crawler FPS roguelike (say that ten times fast) that has color and style reminiscent of DOTA 2, enemies straight out of the “Zeno Clash” series and “Fable,” and the fast, strafing combat found in “Serious Sam.” You select a character (you'll unlock others as you accomplish feats like 200 wand kills, each with their strengths and weaknesses) and start on the first floor. In the top right corner you have your dungeon map layout for reference. As you explore you'll fight minions (carrot men, floating stone dragons, suits of armor, goblin dudes, leaping bird lizards), dodge traps, and find a portal key that unlocks the boss and exit, all the while exploring a labyrinth carved from stone, ceilings held up by bone columns and looking otherwise metal as ♥♥♥♥. Once you find the end room you'll engage in a boss battle with a unique big baddie. Once you beat it you're shown your score (determined by kills, floors cleared, time) and you're on to the next floor. As you progress you'll find new weapons (you start off with a basic replenishable wand but you'll soon find an ice orb that fires like a shotgun, fire grenades, etc.), perks, and journals that delve into the story of this magical place full of beautiful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t nightmare monsters.
So what else can I say about “Ziggurat?” It just feels cool, y'know? You unlock stylish tarot cards that describe your perks. When you die you'll be frustrated and immediately laugh at the resulting death screen. Floors range from uncomfortably claustrophobic (like when your parents leave you alone in the living room with your handsier relatives) to wide and expansive. The enemies have a variety of tactics, some rushing at you with reckless abandon, some content to fire at a distance like total♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ As you change your tactics – say closing the distance between some distant foe – they'll change their tactics in turn, ground bashing until you beat a hasty retreat or shotgun their♥♥♥♥♥♥face with ice shards. It's highly polished, highly fun, and super pretty like that girl you didn't ask to prom and no it isn't too late JUST GO TO HER SHE'S WAITING.
It might be the prettiest Early Access title yet. The color palette is rich and varied without looking like rainbow vomit – a happy medium between drab dungeon and colorful fantasy. It's challenging without being too big a ball kicker or ball coddler (pick a side, we're at war). And most importantly it feels done. This can only be improved and expanded on. This is something that even if it never saw completion it would still feel like a worthwhile buy. This might be the most excited I've been about an Early Access game in a good while – at least since I've had a decent club sandwich.
Edit: Ziggurat is now available, having completed its Early Access cycle in three months. Early Access devs, take note - THIS is how you do it.

I'm not sure what I was expecting with this game.
I remember watching the trailer and thinking "haha, that seems like an interesting premise. I'll see what this is like"
Then I played the game, and it was exactly what the trailer made it look like, and yet for some reason I didn't particularly enjoy the experience.
There are two major issues with this game:
Firstly, I'm not sure what type of audience this game was going for. The game is a stupendously easy platformer. Any seasoned gamer in any way, shape or form is going to breeze through this game. I feel like I could introduce my non-gaming girlfriend to this game and she'd complete it without too much trouble. Naturally then, you'd think that this game would be for absolute gaming beginners, but the issue was that is that non-seasoned gamers aren't going to understand the myriad of gaming references in this game.
Secondly, the game is essentially one big joke that wears thin well before the ending (which should clock in around 1.5 hours I think). Yes, we're all annoyed at DLC, but all of the comments and complaints can be found on just about every gaming forum, or within the comments section of any gaming article. Not once in the two hours or so that I spent playing this game did I ever come close to laughing, per se. It's almost similar to a really bad pun in real life - you hear it, you smirk a little, then you shake your head.
Other than those two issues, the game was okay. The controls are certainly responsive and the graphics and music were more or less adequate for what they were trying to accomplish. The game clocked in at around 2 hours for me, a lot of which was spent backtracking and looking for the few coins that I missed. The game also has very little replay value once you're done (especially if you managed to collect everything the first time).
Overall, I just can't recommend this game to a wide audience. Not so much because it's not worth the money (I think I bought it for around $0.80 AUD) but rather because I don't think it's worth the time. You'd never want to play this game over a decent platformer like Super Meat Boy, for example.

Metal War Online: Retribution is a game I have been playing a bit recently. I have to say I like it, it plays like a cheaper World of Tanks but it looks scifi. For the layperson the game works by having you queue up into matchmaking as one of a large variety of vehicles in out of 4 classes, scouts (light vehicles) "stromtanks" (tanks), engineers, and artillery vehicles. after selecting your vehicle and gear (smoke screen, scanner, nitrous, etc.) you are dropped into a game. There are a few different game modes, you have modes where you capture points and turrets, capture the flag, and team deathmatch type modes. Concerning the maps, there are a good deal of them, just under 20 at last count. The higher level you get, the more maps you unlock to play, at least from what I can tell.

Really I would recommend Metal War Online: Retribution to anyone looking for a fun free to play vehicle based shooter, or to anyone looking for something to substitute there World of Tanks cravings without actually playing World of Tanks.

I'm all for games that are free and new, so the Indie Scene is something I'd like to start checking out more games from Steam.  While looking last night I ran across a pixilated game called Madagon. Simply based on the artwork (I didn't even take the time to read the description or the story line). 
Its 35 MB and took me 1.3 hours to complete from beginning to end. I didn't expect this to be a very long game, nor did I expect it to have a lot of reputability which is totally fine in a one off game. It was released to Steam on August 4th, 2016 (a mere  9 days ago) and to be honest I am only slightly disappointed.   
The artwork is what initially grabbed me, I grew up with pixilated art style games and have watched the industry grown and leave that style behind. Its only been somewhat recently I've seen some developers go back to that style and really revamp it. I can say without a doubt that what Mandagon felt like, a revamp of games past. 
Its a jumping scroller, that takes place on a single somewhat, seemingly large map. You are a totem that must collect tablets from houses on pedestals and place them in the appropriate slots around the map in order to unlock a door that looks as if it leads to the inside of a palace guarded by 3 identical statues with 4 hands and closed eyes.  Just when I thought "This is to easy" I found myself lost on the map. I couldn't tell where the palace was, or which hut I had missed that held the final tablet. 
But I managed to collect all the tablets and unlock 4 of the 5 Achievements within 1.3 hours, the last one I didn't unlock is sort of what slightly disappointed me. In order to understand the whole story there are Wisdom Totems scattered around the map with a line or two of a story. I'm not sure how many I missed as it doesn't keep count, I could have missed 1 or 10 and I wouldn't know without going back and making my own map. 
There is no health system so if you could find a way to drop from the top of the map to the bottom there is no consequence. But there is also no way to zoom in on the map or check it without being at a tablet deposit to check your location in relativity to somewhere else. So getting turned around is easy. 
Unfortunately with a game made for a one time, short adventure like this one I can't use the rating system I came up with for bigger games. So I will have to tweak it a bit. 
I would give this game a solid 4 of 5 Stars, 
Star 1  Artwork:
I loved the artwork, its got a beautiful Tibet style to it while being pixelated. its what grabbed my attention.
Star 2  Audio: 
I loved the music, it was simple yet serene and calming, I could easily use it to do Tai Chi to or fall asleep. The effects of jumping were there but were not over powering so it didn't interrupt the music. 
Star 3  Plot/Story
The story while it could have been executed a bit different  (perhaps a totem count so you know how many your missing. a better incentive to go looking for the others) 
Star 4 Challenge/ Difficulty 
I wish there was a little more to the adventure, but I also like it the way it is.  Its challenging in its own way without a death/penalty system
The only star its lacking right now is reputability. The only reason I'd go back to play the game would be to get those last few Wisdom Totems I'm missing for that last achievement. And thanks to the way the saving system works, it might not be that hard to.

Crush Crush is a rather interesting mobile-style idle game based around dating anime girls.
People tend to not be very large fans of this style of game, mostly due to the inclusion of micro-transactions that can, at times, range up to and over $100 simply to continue playing and how the game is typically stopped completely for the sake of making you pay more money.
The thing about this kind of game, however, is that you have to come into it with a completely different mindset than you would your normal game.
If you try to sit down and play this for 8 hours and then push your eyesballs back into their sockets with a butter knife as you would with GTA, you'll be bored out of your mind. There's simply not enough to keep you busy during that time unless watching int++ count up is your idea of fun.
But if you simply use it as something to keep your hands busy while listening to a podcast or while checking your YouTube subscriptions on a different screen, playing for 30 minutes to an hour each night simply to check and progress everything as you would on Tomodachi Life or Animal Crossing, you'll end up really enjoying yourself.
The game has micro-transactions however they're not at all neccisairy to make significant progress. And not the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t kind of progress where you either pay $50 or wait 90 days to coninute your game, you can actually end up reaching lover status with the first girl within a few days to a week. The game gets around the idea of a pay wall by using a prestage system whenever progress begins to slow to a halt. The moment it does, you can reset the game while keeping all time blocks, diamonds, purchaces, etc and add a fairly hefty modifier onto all timers and progress bars.
In fact the only real significant things you can spend diamonds on is new outfits or extra timeblocks, the rest isn't neccisairy unless you just really want to get off to seeing lover status on one of the girls, and at that point I'd say you should just use the money to pick up a copy of If My Heart Had Wings and School Days HQ.
It's honest to god a fun little game. It wears the skin of the micro-transaction filled pointlessnes simulators on the iOS store, but it's incredibly playable and it actually kind of keeps you looking forward to what little bit of the game you'll unlock the next time you turn it on. Don't judge the game by it's cover, give it a chance and you really won't regret the little hard drive space it takes up.
UPDATE: So, the devs have released some more content for the game and I've gotten much further than I did when I intially wrote this, so I figured I'd give a bit more insight on what it's like when you reach the late game.
While begining of the game moves fairly quickly after a couple preisteiges, the you still start to hit a wall at one specific point almost every time, that being the point when the few girls you haven't gotten lover with want loads of new cars that cost around 14 billion each. Though it's, surprisingly, never the money that's an issue, but getting the job that makes loads of money, i.e gambling. You almost have to leave it for a week to even have a chance at getting much further.
However, I still reccomend the game since I'm getting to the point where I'm just about over that hurdle. It's not going to be everyone's cup of tea, but it's not trying to be and that's what makes it appealing to those who enjoy it.
Also, full disclosure if that applies here, I did today purchase 240 diamonds for the game. The main reason for this was to support the developers, but having that many extra time blocks is pretty nice too.

This is just a shadow of its former glory, and the few minutes I just spent after my last hiatus gave me no reason at all to ever come back.

Azra is a switch-and-place in game the spirit of old-school PC platform puzzlers like The Lost Vikings. A competant game with some good atmosphere, but also perhaps in need of some polish and balance. The main mechanic is strong, but the level design is begging for someone like, well, Valve to refine it overall.
The focus is on puzzles rather than combat and the slow, awkward attacks make that very clear. Each room has a set number of enemies and pretty specific order to do things with a restart mechanic to drive it home. Think of enemies as tools; this is a thinker, not a fighter.
But then the action picks up or a platform segment is especially tricky and it turns into a Mario game which is a bit jarring. Azra is indie retro the way it should be, but it never quite finds a groove. It's basically excellent for it's scale, but you may find yourself wanting more or noticing missed opportunities. However, if you're new to the puzzle-platform genre, or it happens to be a favorite, you'll be very pleased to give this one a go.

I'm a massive fan of the original Deus Ex, and after Human Revolution I thought Square Enix had permanently derailed one of my favorite game series. Mankind Divided isn't perfect, but unlike the last game it actually lives up to the legacy of its source material.
The maps are sprawling mazes of alternate paths, filled with side missions, lore and secret stashes. There are numerous conspiracies and depictions of how modern society is being corrupted. They've done extraordinarily well considering that this game is a prequal to the original game, meaning they have little room for making new plotlines without rewriting the history explained in the original game. That said, I really wish there was more. The first game was a prescient literary masterpiece, but Mankind Divided is a lot less ambitious with its writing and predictions.
I recommend you buy this game, but wait for a sale. It's a worthy Deus Ex game, for sure, but there are enough flaws that would make you regret your purchase if you paid full price. There are many little annoyances like bad pacing, unnecessary padding, DLC, etc., but overall this is a game that all fans of conspiracies or cyberpunk dystopias should play.

For most part the game is great. It is more than long enough if you take your time to mess around in it (to counter the complaint of a lot of people), the side quests feel like an integral part of the whole and the action is fun. If you liked the previous Deus Ex game, this is more of that and better. However, this game does have a pile of problems that are difficult to ignore.
Firstly, some issues with the story that can make it feel rushed and unfinished. The main story ends in somewhat of a cliff hanger, after a fight with a minor sub-boss: a blatant set-up for a sequel. One of the side quests will be registered as imperfect if you do not follow the “correct” (and I think illogical) order of objectives. Yet, after that mission officially ends, you can still go to one of the “missed” objectives and have a satisfactory ending, but this never gets registered in your mission log. Also, you are occasionally given a stark choice that promises serious consequences for your decision, but those consequences are either negligible or never show up at all.
Secondly, the tacked-on content. There is a mode called “Jensen’s Stories”, which contains small missions available for purchase as DLC. Another available game mode is “Breach” (based on one of the missions from the main game), which is essentially a set of puzzles in an abstract virtual environment, where you have to reach objectives before a timer runs out. Given the aforementioned issues with the story, it is easy to see why some players would be disappointed that the developers chose to concentrate on this other content instead of giving a proper ending to the main story.
Thirdly, the shop. There is a shop accessible through the main menu where you can buy DLCs, credits and praxis kits! Praxis kits are points that you earn in your game to upgrade your character and credits are the in-game currency, and if you don’t want to work for them, you can just use one of several free trainers that you can find online. Of course, the trainers can be problematic, but selling these kits and currency for real money in a single-player game is a little ridiculous.
Fourthly, the graphical optimization issue. If this game looked stunning, then it would have had an excuse for making my system feel obsolete, but there are moments when this game looks like something from a last-gen console and yet I cannot make it run completely smoothly even on the lower settings. Unless you have a properly modern video card, there is always going to be at least a small delay between the movement of your mouse and the movement of your character, which is especially annoying if you want to play this game like a split-second action game. And then there are the long loading times. You may be forgiven for thinking that the game crashed while loading. And it is not like this game has to render huge spaces. The maps are relatively small, though they are packed with items.
The aforementioned 4 issues can contribute to an impression of corporate greed and a lack of willingness to invest the proper amount of work to satisfy the customer. This impression is unfortunate, because the game is ultimately good and had me glued to my computer for a whole week.

The story mode is reminiscent of earlier incarnations of Grand Theft Auto. Same for GTA Online, but the program tends to freeze up on load screens. You have to quit and restart every time this happens, which is extremely aggravating. Also, some of the game mechanics related to flight are extremely difficult to master, because the default flight controls are counterintuitive. Thumbs up for the game overall, thumbs down for load screen freezes and a few annoying minor details.

This game took me about 27 hours to finish, which is actually a good length. I picked the Outlander and loved her!
After you complete an area of the game you can revisit them again, fight the bosses and such, because after you do a few  more dungeons the old dungeons gets rerolled. You could run the same list of dungeons, in order, over and over again if you wanted to gold farm or wanted to level from purely slaughtering stuff.
Areas have random named creatures too which are like mini bosses with random abilities and a whole ton of health. When you kill a named monster you get fame which is like a secondary leveling system. Once you level this you get a skill point. Some of the names I enountered were weak while others were quite hard. A few times I faced multiple named things at the same time. Those were some good fights.
Loot. Unlike other games Torchlight only has common, enchanted, magic and legendary rarity grades, which is a lot less then some games I've played. I always trashed commons and I don't recall ever using enchanted gear after I progressed a bit. Magical gear can spawn as set items which give bonuses in based off how many you have equiped of said set which is additional perks. All items have randomly rolled stats. I never played the Diablo series personally but everyone says its like that. In my mind I compare it to Borderlands though gear in Torchlight II is not as generated as robust as Borderlands. There is still a lot gear attributes to mix and match plus enchantments on weapons, set bonuses, and augments to your class/ skills. Gear all has their own models too so you will be getting new looks. At the end of the game I looked kinda ridiculous in my get-up. Each piece looked alright by themselves just it didn't go very well together.
You also have town serives. Enchanting is a cool one: pay gold to get random rolls, pay gold to strip them off and reroll. Enchanters are also in the wild and offer special types of enchantments like fire or can put 3 enchantments on an item. There is a merchant where you buy items thatare complete gambles. I've gotten some GREAT stuff from him and a lot of rubbish too.
Oh! Ya you have a pet and it actually does not suck. My pet was superemely helpful to me. Pets get 3 special pet gear items and 4 spell slots... there's also spells you can learn in addition to your class skills...
You know what? I'm rambeling. Look it comes down to this. Torchlight II has a lot of features. A lot of enemies. A lot of areas. Tons of loot. The combat is good, balanced, well done and statisfying. I paid $2.99 for this during the summer sale of 2016 thinking I'd enjoy it some but maaaaaaan I totally understand why this game has an 'overwhelmingly positive' review. Steam points 'games like this' to Borderlands and in an odd way it is completely like that! but top down with randomly generated maps and a horbar.
I enjoyed my time so much I will be playing this one again with mods. Porb the best action loot based dungeon crawl I've ever played. This one made it to my favorites list. I give Torchlight II a well deserved 5/5

I was questioning whether or not I should had spent $0.74 on this game, as it is very old and didn't look very deep in its gameplay. However, I decided to put my csgo skin money into this game, and was surprised. This game has solid driving controls and is not very hard to play. It is very much an arcade racer. It has much more content than I anticipated, containing 26 tracks and 49 cars to unlock. It features 5 game modes.
-Quick Play: As you'd expect, just hop into a car, track, and racetype of your choice and have at it. Nothing more.
-Ford Competition: The bread and butter of this game. Features many different cups in different areas of tracks and cars; whether its classic street racing or off road battling. Here you will unlock different cars and tracks to use in quick play and Ford Collection.
-Ford Challenges: I have yet to touch this mode, but from what i understand it features challenges such as staying on racing lines. This mode will unlock vehicles such as the classic Thunderbirds.
-Ford Collection: Where you can view all of your unlocked goodies and take them out for a spin.
-Multiplayer: No one plays it, so it doesn't matter.
Overall, this is a great classic game and a bargain at 74 cents.

"Uniqueness" is an extremely rare adjective within the world of platform video games. Trials of Azra is a puzzle platform hybrid that accentuates the phrase "stands out among the crowd"... The story begins with a young lad named Sam playing "fetch" with his pet pug. It's a fantastic day for fun n' games until a storm front moves in... All of a sudden, lightning strikes and we find Sam and his beloved pet deceased on the ground. Somehow Sam recovers and is able to possess the body of his pug, using him to help out with the tutorial puzzle. Unfortunately, Sam is unable to make his way inside due to a vortex portal swallowing him and transporting the boy to an outer worldly realm. Upon arrival in this strange new world, Sam learns (from a cloaked individual no less) that he now has the ability to possess the corpse of dead creatures, which will prove useful in his travels through this strange domain.
Trials of Azra's crowning jewel is it's core gameplay mechanic... Possessing the prowess of different creatures in order to safely navigate Sam through the many labyrinths in the game is essential to succeeding. At one point you may need to possess a human-like corpse; then find a way to turn said corpse into a skeleton in order to use it's ability to toss bones from it's body. Figuring out the advantages to each possession, and it's purpose for advancement, is one of the game's best feature. It's a tremendous brain teaser, from start to finish, with most stages having upgrades that provide Sam with a myriad of magic powers. Learning what power-ups effect each creature proficiently is all part of the wonderful gameplay experience that Onion Core has masterfully conjured up. There's even boss battles at the end of each stage that abandon the core mechanic for the more traditional platforming mechanic. I can't rave about the mechanics enough within this title. The controls are extremely responsive with no lag input issues at all. A very well crafted and designed title in my honest opinion.
The art and sound is superbly charming, reminding me of those classic video games found on the NES way back in the late 1980's... I truly adore the soundtrack, with each stage boasting a unique melody that fits the mood and tone ideally. If you're a fan of retro pixel titles with top notch puzzle/platform elements, I suggest you try Trials of Azra... It's definitely worth your time and gaming effort!!!

Trials of Azra is an innovative puzzle platformer that relies upon the player's ability to control dead enemies in order to progress through a series of increasingly difficult levels.
The controls are solid and playable, although perhaps lacking the precision found in indie games like Shovel Knight. The graphics are an effective return to 16-bit era art without being a distraction. The music is well-composed and nicely suits the setting of each level.
The game characters all feature their own unique abilities, which keeps the levels from feeling repetitive. The reward system also prevents the frustration of repeating levels already solved, while still providing additional benefits to players who die less frequently. The final boss also included some novel elements compared to other games in the genre. The story itself is kept minimal and mysterious, although the ending still provides adequate resolution to the adventure.
The style of gameplay reminded me of a combination of the Mario series with the Incredible Machine series, with elements of adventure/RPG's sprinkled into the mix. This is the right kind of game for platformer enthusiasts looking for a memorable new twist.

This is a platform/adventure puzzler with 16-bit graphics. Before you say "meh" and move on, let me tell you that this game is so much more than its label suggests. I confess to having always been biased against low-res games like this in the past, I've always thought pixel graphics = basic gameplay but WOW, have my eyes been opened!
You play as a boy named Sam who enters a platform area. You shoot enemies and then possess their bodies (one at a time) to use their abilities to navigate past the various traps and obstacles to reach switches, pressure plates and walls to eventually make a path for Sam to reach the exit and move on to the next level.
Dead enemies drop gems to be picked up by Sam which increases his gold profit. At the end of each main area the gold can be spent at the market stall of the mysterious hooded man (who reveals himself at the end of the game) to purchase powerups (increased weapon range, more health etc), making Sam stronger to tackle subsequent areas.
Sam has 2 power bars: the normal red one for health, and a blue one to represent Mana which depletes as Sam uses his special Spells. New Spells are acquired by picking them up on certain rare levels.
Split-screen local co-op is available. You can recruit a friend to play the possessed enemies while you control Sam.
Up to 1920x1200 res, window or fullscreen. The pixel graphics are clean and sharp. I wouldn't go so far as to say beautiful but there's enough artwork to make it pleasing to the eye. The many enemies are imaginatively designed and instantly identifiable.
Background music is outstanding. There are various different tunes as you progress through the game, they are all catchy and really suit the 16-bit mood. I left it on instead of playing my own music, which is very unusual. They're the sort of tunes that stay in your head and you find yourself humming them later on.
Smooth and responsive on both Windows and Linux. One or two disappearing-enemy glitches are easily fixed by restarting the level, rare and hardly worth mentioning. With low-res graphics this is likely to run well even on potato-class hardware. Good settings menus, everything is tweakable. Fully cross-platform.
Puzzlers are my favourite thing, I've played many and consider myself a bit of an aficionado so I have a lot to compare against. The brainwork here is never easy. It starts off as medium and ramps up through difficult and very difficult. In some cases, part of the challenge is working out how the abilities of a new enemy work and how they interact with the puzzle - there are some Eureka! moments as new game mechanics are revealed. The general aim is to a) kill the enemies one by one (often using them to kill each other), b) work out a route to the exit and c) decide which enemies are the right ones to tackle each part of the puzzle and how to apply their abilities.
Controller skills: the game can be played with mouse/keyboard but I'd say a controller is mandatory. There is little or no challenge in the first 2 areas, it's very easy. The 3rd area starts introducing some difficulty and by the 4th area I was having trouble with some levels. I'm no expert with this type of thing, if you're used to coordination-oriented games you'll no doubt find it easier than I did. This aspect of the game is secondary to the puzzling anyway.
Bosses: at the end of each area is an old-school boss, the type that's very difficult at first but once you understand their attack patterns it becomes a matter of routine. The final boss (the Grim Reaper himself) is really tough!!
The only negative thing I can think of to say about this game is that during the first playthrough there's no indication of how many levels there are or how far through the game you've progressed. I've given you this info below, so now there's no con :) The devs have told me they're considering adding some kind of progress indicator in future.
Once you complete the game you can repeat whole areas (starting from the first level of the area) by going through doorways from the main entrance but there are still no numbered levels to select. This does at least make it feasible to chase the no-death achievements.
60+ levels in 4 main areas. According to the leaderboards it can be completed in 7 hours but it took me a lot longer, at a leisurely pace with a good amount of head-scratching and restarts. There is replay value in tackling achievements for no-death runs and missed pickups etc. It's not just the quantity though, the quality of puzzle design is also top-notch, the wide variety produces constant challenge so it never feels stale.
Well worth full price.
8 trading cards; 30 achievements; cloud; leaderboards. It's got the lot.
Don't let the pixel graphics put you off, this is a highly accomplished puzzler and it's a joy to play. I've been waking up in the morning eager to tackle more levels and discover new enemies. You'll be hooked in no time.

Mortal Kombat X has some flaws, but I think it gets just enough right to make it an overall good game. I've finished the story mode and done some other solo play stuff and plan on playing some couch co-op with a friend soon. The story mode has some of the most painfully cliche writing and events but it's hard not to love. I honestly enjoyed it quite a bit, especially since it showcases most of the new playable characters. I really think the character design is great, Cassie Cage's X-Ray move being so obviously a combination of Johnny Cage and Sonya Blade was awesome. Ferra/Torr is really cool too. The animations are super smooth and X-Ray moves continue to be overall fantastic, same goes for finishers.
Online play is dead for all I can see, I played it once before the netcode patch and it was unplayable so I imagine not enough people returned to it after the fact. It's certainly a testament to releasing a fully functioning game, rather than "fixing" it much later. Most people just won't bother giving it another chance. So yeah, if you're looking at buying it for online play, you probably won't have much luck. Another big complaint I have is the DLC fiasco, I bought Mortal Kombat X with the first Kombat Pack because NetherRealm or WB announced they weren't going to release Kombat Pack 2 on PC, which outraged some but I was like "okay well I may as well buy it if it's complete since I hate buying the first version of a fighting game only to have 12 dlc packs get released thereafter". A few months later they announce Kombat Pack 2 will come to PC )) And now it's more expensive to buy the Kombat Pack 2 standalone than it would be to just rebuy the entire game again. That's just absurd. I just want to play Bo Rai Cho and vomit on some kids but to do that I have to spend the same amount I paid to get the ENTIRE game. Way to kill my nostalgia. I get the feeling WB don't have much love for the PC audience and if that makes you outraged then you're justified in feeling that way. It's a scummy practise and I'm not so desperate for Bo Rai Cho that I'll buy into that nonsense.
Regardless, it's a good game. It's flawed and marred by little to no concern for the PC audience or early supporters of the game but Mortal Kombat X itself is of a high enough quality that I can recommend it. Didn't have any noticeable performance issues other than some occassional FPS drops, generally ran at a smooth 60 FPS. Just one last time though, it's $20 for the one DLC pack I'm missing and $10 to buy the entire game again with both DLC packs. WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥
