Although Heroes and Generals seems interesting at first, it quickly becomes tedious and not even fun. You start out playing with bots and struggling to find a game because you can only play one map, then you are allowed to play skirmishes, still with bad matchmaking times. When you finally unlock assault battles, the most populated staged (as opposed to war) battle type, you face people with one-shot rifles that can kill you from hundreds of meters away and classes other than infantry that you will have to grind hours and hours for.
After you finally earn a sizable amount of credits playing many challenging but still somewhat fun games, you realize you can't purchase many things because you lack the ribbons (badges for doing certain things) needed to buy them. After you grind for those, and you purchase a new weapon or weapon modifications for your starting gun, you will still get destroyed by tanks, etc. unless you spend money on anti-tank equipment or hide in a corner sniping the entire round, not contributing to your team. When you buy your first non-infantry class (for this example, pilot), you will quickly realize the sheer magnitude of the grind this game puts you through. Now, in order to be on par with a majority of players in a war battle, you have to grind hours to unlock ribbons and credits to purchase a better plane and weapon, otherwise your weak recon plane will get demolished by fighters/heavy fighters - it is like this for every class. Every single thing you can accomplish in this game takes many, many battles to, or money, which I will explain later. Unless you are content with sticking with your shovel and recon plane with your pilot, or with your starter rifle for your infantry, you will be subjected to this punishment.
If you are actually okay with the grind, which some people are, and are excited to test your new tanker or pilot in a war game - where everything you do has an impact - you will probably not find a battle. You will notice you have to use auxillary seats to be able to use your class in a war battle that allows planes. But then, when you queue, you get placed with someone multiple levels lower than you who does not have access to auxillary seats (a "Squad Leader Cadet", as they care called), or you get placed with someone who does not choose the auxillary seat that allows you to play your new class you bought, which can be incredibly frustruating.
While I was grinding, I thought, is there a way to quicken the process? And yes, there is, but it requires heavy financial devotion to the game. Gold is the premium currency, it costs a lot for a small amount and you can buy everything with it, but if you want increased credit gain, or an extra slot for a boost, such as damage reduction, you have to buy Veteran, which can be bought with credits or even more gold. If you don't want to spend lots of credits on repairs for equipment you must have to consistently support your team and be able to switch your in-class role quickly (such as tanking down a APC or tank, or driving to a far-off command point to defend it), gold is the answer. Want to buy a fully-leveled tanker? Use gold, but you still have to grind for ribbons... unless you use more gold.
Overall, this game is not enjoyable unless you devote either much of time or money. H&G is an obvious cash-grab, taking money from those wishing to speed up the grind by just a few hours...

I don't know what some of the other reviews are talking about; this may not be the best rogue-like if you're a R-L snob, but I found it pretty entertaining. I got it bundled with a few other games, so it was a steal, really.
Basically, you're exploring the surface of a planet that shifts every time you visit it. There are loads of different items, and events on every level. Somewhere on each level is a portal to take you to the next 'distance', and on explore mode every three distances gets you more points for buying better equipment/upgrades.
You can also find the means to upgrade/buy equipment on each distance. There are potions that you pick up as well, but each one has to be tested by throwing it or quaffing it, each go around, because the effects shift. This adds a strategic layer, because some of the potions can be very useful. For instance, there's a darkness that grows and gradually consumes the whole level as it follows you, but one of the potions will blow up a few square blocks - you can use this to stop the darkness' progress for that distance, and give yourself the freedom to explore the whole level at your leisure.
I also found the events pretty interesting. You usually have two ways to react to the different events you run into, each with stat checks - so you can end up with some nice bonuses, or a title that follows you until you die.
Anyway, I think that it's a pretty interesting game. If you're looking for an absolute blockbuster, this isn't it, but it IS a really well put together, beautiful indie game that is fun to play.

Shattered Planet leaves a lot to be wanted, as the mechanics of the game are very enjoyable, but the execution is incredibly poor. Although you may have fun with this game for a few hours after you purchase it, you'll find that during your later gameplay, you'll be feeling a lack of depth that doesn't really deserve to be there. Like another user said, binary reviews like this are bad for games like this, but I'll have to give it a thumbs down until other things are implemented.
For those who don't know, Shattered Planet is a rogue-life, turn-based strategy game in which your character travels to distant planets. These planets are the equivalent to dungeons in any other rogue-like; you find items, gain currency, and inevitably die only to return and do a little better each time. To Shattered Planets strong points, this game has several things to collect and playthrough, but that's the extent of depth you'll end up getting.
- Very visually pleasing.
- Comical lines of dialogue.
- Level design is great.
- Extensive amount of gamemodes.
- Not enough items.
- Small pool of abilities.
- AI on companions lack-luster.
- No crafting stations.
- Expensive upgrades.
- Sometimes dull grind.
The things that Shattered Planet does right is in its visuals. The game deserves to pride itself on how aesthetically engaging it is, considering the variety of biomes you can explore and the massive level design that continues to produce original and fun maps over the several hours I've played. I've not once felt annoyed to go into a certain point in the level because no specific artwork bores me, unlike other games like Tales of Maj'eyal and Dungeons of Dredmor.
However, there is a massive shadow looming over this game that makes it not enjoyable after a certain amount of hours. You can experience this with the substantial lack of items, small pool of abilities, horrible companion AI, and almost zero ability to craft your own items or at least upgrade them to a better weapon. This can sometimes make it a very difficult grind because, without much customization, the game falls flat quickly.
When you first play the game, finding all the weapons are pretty fun. All seem to have their own traits, like increased punctured damage or critical hit, but that's about all the depth you'll get with the weapons. It would be nice if the developers would add a crafting bench, another currency sink other than simply spending tons of money on static weapons from the store.
I imagine that adding this bench would allow you to spend currency in order to put different upgrades on your weapons or smelt them in order to get different resources in order to make your own weapon. Since enemies in the game have specific weaknesses and they appear on predictable levels of the game, having this type of crafting bench would be very important for people wanting to breeze past the first levels. Right now, you'll struggle through every run-through, which can be dull.
There's also a very small pool of abilities. What I mean by that is, you don't have any active abilities, the characters that you choose have passive abilities. Some are much more strong than the other characters, which almost defaults you to a couple of playstyles, which sucks for a rogue-like. It would be great to add some more abilities, even active ones, that players could use to enhance their gameplay. Right now, all you do is chop with subpar weapons and try to take as less damage as possible before going to the next floor.
AI's suck. They're supposed to be companions that attack for you, defend you, and stop you from taking damage. 9 times out of 10, they don't listen and they rarely attack unless you force them into a position to attack by moving several spaces. It can be tedious, especially when you're surrounded with tough enemies and your companion is doing nothing but snoozing in the corner. You'll die because of this - several times, and that just adds to your misery.
...and this all adds up to a boring game, giving you very little for what you're putting in. With how expensive some of the upgrades are (health, dodge, and attack) and how insignificant they seem to be in-game, you're going to find that you'll get bored of grinding the first few floors until you just switch the game off and uninstall. The only reason I haven't done this is because I'm an achievement hunter and look to collect them all, haha.
All-in-all, I don't recommend this game just because of the systems I wish were added. The weapons are simple, the characters are simple too - it just leaves so much to be wanted and it's unfortunate for a game like this, a game that is very pleasing and has so much potential, but falls flat on its face because of developers that aren't attentive to quality designs. Find another rogue-like to play, mates, this isn't a good one to sink your time into.

Shattered Planet is a fun, enjoyable and for the most part non-taxing casual rogue-like-lite. Though its an iOS port With a simple formula, its solid design and addictive gameplay offer a range of unique experiences ensuring the somewhat repetitive nature of gameplay doesnt detract with each playthrough.  With multiple game modes and a host of research items to discover it will keep your interest high for weeks if not months.
If you enjoy taking a character to explore small randomly generated maps, exprience many unique events, collect a vast amount of unique items, while fighting off enemy monsters then this could be something for you.  With minimal RPG elements, basic character skills and inventory management the game is a great little time killer between those larger budget games you no doubt play.
2.5D Isometric, adventure, lite rogue-like, mobile port.
From your starship orbiting a strange unsurveyed planet, you take on the role of an expendable clone  created to conduct exploration missions and discover what is on the planet below.
Once you step into the teleporter on your ship you are beamed onto the ground below.  Your mission is to explore the different areas of the planet which are split into levels. Arrayed across the map you will meet the indiginous people, an assortment of random and varied enemies to defeat, items to collect, events to experience and obstacles to overcome.  Your aim is to discover and catalogue serveral hundred elements unique to this world and in some modes reach the end level of the mission.  Standing in the way of progress is the deadly invincible blight, that follows you from the beginning of each level ready to infect and overcome every living being in its path.  To avoid succumming to its effect you must locate and reach teleporter that will transport you to the next level.
There are four types of game mode: the basic quest - Daily Challenge (10 levels), the Exploration Challenge (150+ levels) and the two harder Signal and Old Blood Challenges (10 levels).  All with their own objectives.
Though the games biggest draw is the element of exploration resource collection and harvesting plays a big part.  Perhaps the game's greatest strength is the numerous gameplay mechanics included with its uncomplicated design.  Numerous playable archetypes(character types), several recruitable allies; melee and ranged combat with dozens of varieties of weapons, armors for protection, resistance and immunity to certain elements, collectibles for healing or boosting character stats and abilities.
The starting area of the starship contains several consoles and dispensers from which you can setup options such as character archetype, starting inventory for the next game.  They also allow you to upgrade character stats, choose your ally and, buy weapons, armors and item from dispensers using two resource types.  Resources include metals to upgrade stats and minerals which can be used to make other purchases.
There are too many to name here but the variety of enemies means it will take you a while to discover all of them and what their weaknesses are.  Sometimes you will not have the perfect weapon or item to quickly take care of them, so you will either have to improvise or flee.  The most common enemy types are: Crabs, Robots, Humanoid Natives and Plant-life.
Levels consist of four or more areas defined by terrain.  Areas can number from four upwards depending on the game mode or the depth of level entered.  Terrain can be destroyed with weapons.  Levels are covered with events and collectibles provide the player with tough choices.  What to do or what to keep in order to remain intact and progress as far as possible.
The A.I controlling the various npcs and enemy monsters does a good job of randomingly sending them towards or away from you so until you get too close they seem to be oblivious to you.  Unless you attack them of course.  As there is little interaction by the computer controlled critters the A.I is basic but good enough for the job.
Good basic keyboard and mouse controls.  For an iOS port, mouse control is up to the standard you would expect for PC games.
The graphics are well-drawn and cute, if rather basic.  Overall the aesthetics are functional and nice.
A simple repeating melodic tune which changes when combat starts is the mainstay of the games sound.  Its apt but nothing to write home about.
Minimal but used to good effect during the tutorial and at key levels during certain game modes.
The game has a useful tutorial at the start.  Progression is measured almost perfectly with a learning curve that will match most players commitement to the game.  In addition achievements mark significant events so if you go after them you will learn more about how the game mechanics work and what you should be doing.
Only a very few which required a restart at most.  More annoying than game-breaking.  Sometimes the tooltip for held inventory items can become stuck and take up part of the screen.  Only moving the mouse pointer over the item fixes this.
A few minor bugs with interacting inventory when buying items from the randomly located robot trader.   Sometimes this will lock up you game and you will be unable to move.  Can be fixed by restarting the game but any progress for that level will be lost.  Annoying but not game-breaking.
Actually a great mix of achievements.  A few teach you the games basics. Most though can be categorized as: Kill x y z; Complete each game mode; Complete n amount of research or upgrade character stats.  Just be warned that two to three achievements will need many hours to grind - at least and most likely more (2x kill 10000 critters).  Be aware that one achievement is unobtainable.  Complete ALL research is bugged with and events items not in the game. Unfortunately the game looks abandoned so dont expect any fixes.
EDIT: 16 Mar 2016 - broken achievement removed.  Now 100% completeable.
There are no dlc and none planned.
You could play most of what the game has to offer in around 25-30 hours.  That includes the 4 major game modes.  Though you would probably need to play around 50 hours to get your character up to the sort of level you will need to get to level 50 and beyond on the Exploration mode.  I have 100 hours with 70/71 achievements, the only remaining one is the bugged research probably requiring many more hours to get all the available research items. Something Im not bothered with.
There is a massive amount of longevity and replayability in this game.  Yes the nature of gameplay is repetitive but which game isnt...  the game seems to be designed around this (as you'd expect) to a certain degree as its a mobile port.
Anyone who likes rogue-likes or doesnt mind good mobile ports will enjoy playing this.  Though if you dont like casual games of a somewhat repetitive nature then it wont be for you.  Even though it has lite RPG elements I dont think there is enough for players who may want something deeper.  It really is something you can play for 5-15 minutes each day but no more than an hour or so.  Short spurts of fun.
Excellent a full price even if you only play twenty or so hours.  In a sale its a bargain.  If you intend to play this well-made game for longer then you'll get many weeks / months of entertainment for peanuts - no sweat.

I'd give a plot synopsis, but really, there's not much more to it then "you're a badass cyborg on an island killing pretty much everything while you save the world for the USA." If the humor the game uses were enough to make up for the flat plot, this might be exclusable, but there were countless groaners that really fit the genre... too well. Guys, there's a reason we don't right corny as hell plots like this anymore.
Alright, so the story is flat and schlocky, how about the gameplay? Well, it's basically just Far Cry 3, except... detached. You've got maybe 6 hours in the core game, 16ish overall if you get all the collectables. They didn't add much new until really the end of the game, and really, half of what was so fun about Far Cry 3 was you ascended your character from weak chump to badass over the course of the game, discovering new skills and abilities. Here, you just start out a badass becoming a bigger badass, fighting hordes and hordes of bland, faceless enemies... It just kind of became boring. Vast murder and tons of explosions became boring. That's half the selling point of your game!
The only stuff I really took enjoyment in was the stealth and the mobility, which is surpisingly good. The environments may not be all that pretty, but at least moving about them is a fluid and kinda pleasant experience.
All in all, unless you really want some kind of new Far Cry 3 experience? Just avoid this one. I'm surprised I stuck with it as long as I did.
Imagine if FarCry 3 was 1/3 as long, but had 10x as much heart, soul, and humor.

I came from a position where I NEVER played a Grand Theft Auto game before. I had niether high nor low hopes, and entered the game completely neutral. And I thoroughly enjoyed it.
GAMEPLAY:
You can really tell that the developers spent a great deal of time designing and perfecting how the game feels, and it a quinticential 3rd person game. It handles movement and viewing tremendously. Never does it feel awkward or annoying. 100/100
GRAPHICS:
Stunning, to say the least. Even with a PC that boasts a budget GPU like mine, it ran well over 80 FPS even on the highest settings. The graphics makes Los Santos pop, and it really feels like a living, breathing creature of a game. Graphical glitches were not noticable, if there even was any. 100/100. Incredibly well optimized.
SOUNDTRACK: Each musical queue felt fitting and energizing, and the inclusion of a radio in cars makes the world feel that much more real. 100/100.
STORY (spoiler free):
This is where the game comes across a lot of criticism and controversy. YES. I KNOW. THERE ARE CHARACTERS THAT DO BAD THINGS AND SAY BAD THINGS AND SUPPORT THE SAYING AND DOING OF BAD THINGS. WELCOME TO REALITY. PEOPLE CAN BE MEAN. WOOPTY-F*CKING-DOO. But the game really has a funny and fun story, with characters that, while they aren't morally sound, are fun and interesting nonetheless. Trevor Phillips' character is a great example. He's a completely sadistic b*stard, and his voice acting, modeling, and missions fit his character to a tee, and he has since become one of my favorite characters in gaming. The story is fun, interesting, with twists and turns and is of decent length. It has some annoying, repeatative, and bad missions, no doubt, but thats the only failing feature of the story. 90/100.
PRICE: I hate the price of this game. It is amazing, but it is NOT worth $60. I got it on sale when it was $35, and I would encourage anyone who wants the game to wait until it is on sale before purchasing it. 70/100.
OVERALL: 83.75/100. When on sale, that bumps up to 95/100. Just get in on sale, and enjoy.

A great game if you like puzzles and challenges.
Personal rating 9/10
The environment you move in is detailed and although it is 2D this does not feel like a limitation but more like a nice reminder of an earlier age of games, as you puzzle and challenge your creativity in order to overcome the challenges and obstacles of the game. There are a number of traps and small or large puzzles at each level and each character has a different set of interactions and skill trees that can be applied in order to complete each level (so there are basically 3 puzzle challenge maps pr. level if you want to challenge yourself in this regard).
If it seems to be too hard, just turn down the difficulty, if it is too easy just go hard and just in case that is too easy as well just enable hardcore mode at the same time.
I had a great time playing it solo and it was even better when teaming up with a friend due to the teamwork aspect of the game, and the easy by which some of the characters overcomes some challenges but struggles with others, especially when you decide to go experience bubble hunting for each map :)
I especially like the fact that you can regulate the interaction possibilities and interchangeability of the characters (all going paladin, archer or mage or keeping it nice and classic with max. 1 of each). Personally I would recommend going the classical style due to the challenges it places on the party, and do not worry if a particular experience hunt needs a specific character you can always change with your teammates (providing that the character is not dead of course :) ).
All in all a great experience, funny characters and character comments.
The only downside might be that the story is a bit simple but then again it allows you to focus upon the game itself and all the fun it has to offer, while allowing for some good laughts ranging from the slightly puzzled surprised laughs to the more direct laughs (WARNING! it might feel a bit weird at first to laugh by yourself, but do not worry, laughing is healthy so just go with it or play with friends so that you have someone with whom to share the joy :) ).

First off, I need to say that this is my favorite game I've found on Steam, so I'm a bit biased.
Jumping right into what you want to know:
Gameplay/Story: Simple; easy to learn very fast. Choose a clone, each with their own skillset and buffs, and traverse the ever-changing shattered pieces of an ancient planet crawling with monsters and tribals, littered with loot and new weapons to help you on your way as you progress onto harder and harder levels that are different every time. See how far you can get before the flora, fauna, or your own mistakes spell your end. You will die. A lot. But don't worry; your clone can pick up where you left off to start the adventure all over again with all the information and levels that your last one was able to earn before his untimely, and probably sudden, demise. But you're not always alone in this, you might sometimes also find it in your favor to either purchase or tame a companion or pet to help fight with you on your next trip to the surface. If you'd rather have a goal to reach instead of pushing the limits of your clone endlessly, there are 3 other difficult missions for you to complete with cool rewards for each, but you'll fare better practicing in endless first! Grab some scrap and crystals (money) in there to buy yourself some fancy murder-tools before pushing your luck in the missions. Travel a lot and you'll find it lying all over the place!
Graphics: Clean isometric environments come together with soft, painterly-esque textures and crisp characters to make for an interesting but pleasing-to-the-eye adventure. Animations are smooth, but your clone's walk cycle usually seems a bit short or abrupt, but it's nothing too jarring. Waddle on, fresh meat.
Sound: Adjust sound and music to your preferences or turn them off completely. Tranquil and sometimes ominous music follows you on your travels, each pretty decently set to match your current environment which changes every few levels you progress through to mix it up and give you different enemies and events to find. Every time you stumble into a fight, though, you'll get a more rambunctious action clip to keep you on your toes, though this one only has a few variations based on the enemies you're fighting. I like the music in this game a lot and it's not too invasive or annoying. The fight music does sometimes make a jarring jump in volume compared to the other tracks, however.
Controls: The controls were obviously made for mobile platforms but everything is, thankfully, operated with the mouse. There are no key binding options, which is a shame as right now you need to click every tile you want to travel to and you can only see so many ahead of you. This game would greatly benefit even from simple arrow-keys or WASD walking controls, but the clicking-to-walk isn't really a deal-breaker; it's just a little annoying until you get used to it. The camera keeps your clone the center of focus, though, and sometimes I find my eyes feeling a little dizzy the way the environment moves but I stay riveted in the center of the screen, which probably isn't a problem for most people. Think Pokemon Mystery Dungeon.
Notable/Other:
- The devs removed the achievement that required finding all the items, some of which were broken and undiscoverable, instead of fixing the broken items, but that works, too, I guess.
Overall: The game is fun, addicting, and easy to play; other than a few tiny annoyances, I feel Shattered Planet is well worth your time and attention, and even a few broken achievements don't make it unplayable. Believe it or not, some players enjoy a game with or without achievements. Personally, I love achievements, so it's a disappointment that a handful of them are broken, but truly, that's not going to keep me from playing this and having fun. I recommend nabbing it on sale.

I was new to the roguelike genre when I picked up Shattered Planet on a Humble Bundle deal.
The game is a roguelike that focuses on exploration, progession across a shattered, austere, galactive environment while discovering unique breeds of enemies, different kinds of companions, new items, flora, fauna, landscapes, and novel experiences/events. These are all logged in a Datalog, which is curated and worked on by a scientist (who is the only other character you get to interact with.) The premise of the game places you on a spacestation/research lab as a disposable clone that can be upgraded with boosts as you play, hopefully increasing your survivability. Your goal is to get as far as you can, and collect/experience as much as you can. The standard mode has endless replayability, but it may seem to get repetitive if you're new to the genre. However, as long as character progression continues, you will oftentimes break farther and farther into the shattered planets, and hopefully uncover new things!
There are alternative game and challenge modes, and endless litte things to discover. The game has an enjoyable art style, with a laid-back and humorous attitude. The music goes mostly unnoticed to me, and I find this a relaxing sort of experience to play! It may not stand up to hardcore/serious roguelikes, but its an enjoyable way to pass some time!

So Brawlhalla. Brawlhalla is a fun and fast paced game with online and offline features and Improvement options (Training mode).
The game is inspired by the Super smash bros. Franchise. And I think it's really well done, You have ranked 1v1 which features an ELO system which means, Everytime you play a game of ranked 1v1. You can gain or lose ELO. How higher the ELO how higher ranked the players you will meet. It's a good system because you will meet players on your level. Training mode includes, A bot system, With damage on him, hurtboxes etc. It also let's u see the damage you can do with an attack or combo. But this game also features something with your friends. Like 2v2 Ranked, which is an ELO based gamemode where u can earn ELO but with your friends in a fight.
So why do I play this game you may ask, Well:
I play this game because it's a really fun game to play with friends but also to improve your skill level, you can buy new things in Shop (Mallhalla) like skins and weapons skins etc.
You can also make a clan for friends or competitive wise or just join a fun and good clan.
Also, I think the game is getting bigger with events which I really like to watch cause of the good players with the amazing plays, It's really fun to see how they develop and how u can do that too.
So, I really really REALLY recomment this game if you like fast-paced fighting games and up-to-date things, and of course watch the pro players to improve your skill.
And as always. Keep on Brawling!!

This is a neat little game set in the DCU where can manipulate people and objects with near omnipotence. The game is about a kid with a magic note book and his sister trying to get home, inorder to do so they must help DC's superheros over come villains aided by someone with the same powers as yourself.
I bought this rather than the first game since it's set in the DCU, so I can't compare it to the original. I picked this up on a steam sale, which is where I recommend you buy it.
Pros: simple lighthearted fun, plenty of material and details for DC fans, the ability to mess with things like your mr mxyzptlk
Cons: poor mouse controls, grinding to pad out the game,  overly scripted boss fights, occasional glitches/bugs
The drawbacks to this game are that the mouse is sluggish, this can be a problem when you're trying to click items in the game. This is not a game breaker by any means, and the game is easy anyway, but its an annoyance when you first start the game. Another problem is that new missions are unlocked by in game points rather than beating prequesite missions meaning that you may have to grind them with sidequests late game. The side missions are really where the game shines because you can get creative and/or fail them without consequence Boss fights mostly feel like their holding your hand and telling you exactly what to do which can be annoying since you want to get creative. I undersand this is for kids, but a higher difficuluty for adults would be appreciated. I've found one mission where the game doesn't give you back control unless you mash enter and/or space, reading the forums alot of other people also have this problem.
All and all I would recommend buying it, though for me it's not worth $30 US(that said I'm on a budget so decide for yourself if you want to pay full price) It's a neat little game that rewards creativity and experimentation. Despite it's flaws the game is definitely worth checking out.

Soulstorm continues expading the Warhammer universe with some new units, a new race and a "new" campaign which feels like nothing but a remasking of Dark Crusade. Now this isn't a bad game, but it's age shows and how does it. Between incredibly predictable AI and what quickly becomes a tedious if not repetitive campaign, innovation wasn't what the developer must've been looking for. But then again, if it isn't broke, don't fix it. While the gameplay can be satisfying to some extent, victory can still feel hollow even on the harder difficulty due to the AI's general stupidity and inabilities to do anything surprising outside of scripted events. As for the game mechanics, this is basically a copy of Dark Crusade in almost every manner possible. Sure, the gameplay has had some tweaks here and there, but nothing to really blow you out of the water and just wow you or anything.
Now note, I've spent way more time in this game than recorded on Steam, as I'd gotten this game on it's release and had my fun with it, dropping well over 100+ hours in, playing as every race and in too many cases almost effortlessly dominating my enemies. That is why I just can't play it anymore, for an RTS, the challenge just isn't as heavy as it should be. But the graphics still look alright and the art designs stay in tune with the Warhammer universe. However it should be noted this game must have some compatibility issues with Windows 10. Resolution doesn't display properly, stretching the screen in ways it shouldn't, even though the resolution is set correctly. I've ran the game in compatability modes and this doesn't make any difference, so in the ten hours I've played this on Windows 10, I've had to deal with a large black border around the game on my monitor. Though after a bit, you can work past that and focus on the game.
Overall, this isn't a bad game, but you can do much better in an RTS. But if your a Warhammer fan, I'm sure you'll have your fun and enjoy yourself. That and the price is fair as well, which does make this something of a bargain. So if you're looking for a somewhat fun RTS and have $14(USD) to burn, go for it. Just don't expect the AI to put up much of a challenge.

Please don't be discouraged from playing this game from its Mixed review score aggregate. While understandable, that rating is about gaming politics and the circumstances of the game's release, not about the game itself.
If you are a fan of cyberpunk and/or Deus Ex, you will love this game. Yes, the ending is abrupt and obvious sequel baiting, but what IS here is really really good. Great atmosphere, awesome gameplay. The main hub, Prague, while the only hub in the game, is enormous and full of content - easily more than Human Revolution's two hubs put together. The graphics are insane (hint, playing the game in Exclusive Fullscreen gave me +10 fps) and the sound and music are typically excellent as we've come to expect from the series.
I've seen a lot of complaints regarding the game's length, but I think this is more about the abrupt way the story ends. Despite the game actually being as long as the first, give or take a couple hours, Mankind Divided ends in what feels like the beginning of the third act. It's disappointing, but it doesn't change the fact that what's here is absolutely excellent and well worth paying full price if you're a genre or series fan. If you're just curious about the series, I recommend starting with Human Revolution.

I've put nearly 200 hours into this game now, and while, being incredibly competative and love the 2D platforming fighter with its own little intricacies, it is horribly flawed.
First of all- counters. Certain weapons have a standard moveset for light attacks and special heavy attack for the character you're using. Some weapons are significantly better than others, and their regular movesets can ABSOLUTELY zone you out. Bows and pistols, two of the weapons I consider to take actual SKILL to use, can be completely blocked out and countered by katars, spears, and lances. ♥♥♥♥ING lances.
Second- this game does not punish spam. Spamming is your best friend, and the idea that some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t true combo that's inescpable, has a pretty large range to catch you in, and can be repeated over and over again, can be your entire moveset, just doesn't make any sense to me. Where's the fun in using the same attacks over and over and over again?
Third- some weapons are just BETTER. There seems to be, and many I've talked to, very little balancing when put into the weapons. When I mentioned counters before, weapons just happen to have either a move diverse and range moveset, and create more of a hurtbox than other weapons. The lance is an unstoppable spamming machine, with nothing being able to stand in its way, quite literally. I've personally won MANY games on gold and platimun level just spamming side to side, while keep my positioning in mind. It's absolutely broken, and you can and should consider certain weapons "overpowered".
Fourth- character stats. Characters are supposed to be unique with not only their own signature moves, but their stats as well. Attack damage, attack speed, movement speed, health, etc, are all slightly or significantly varied on characters. But here's the thing; WEAPONS NEGATE ANY STAT THAT COULD BE CONSIDERED USEFUL. I played this game from the time when Evendim was first introduced up to when they released the Helm's Deep 'expansion'. In that time, it was my primary game. It was great. Kins, raiding, PvP. It was all I wanted in a MMO, with a Lord of the Rings theme. Unfortunately, the game went down hill.
The first expansion was Moria and was a good expansion. Probably the height of the game. We got loads of instances, a lair raid, a legendary weapons system and two new classes. They even gave us a few more updates with some instances and a couple of raids.
The second expansion was Mirkwood. It was marketed as a 'mini-expansion', and though it was smaller than Moria was, it was still much larger than anything we had later. We got a new instance system called 'Skirmishes', where we got soldiers and about a dozen instances to fight with them in. It was good, it filled it out. Mirkwood also came with 3 x 3 man instances, 1 x 6 man instance and a 3 boss raid with a gauntlet at the start. It wasn't as good as Moria but it was cheaper, so we accepted it.
Then came the biggest issue: Turbine was bought by Warner Brothers. Only a couple of months after this, the game went 'free to play' (you can play for free, but it's heavily restricted and you need to pay to unlock things). The community was a little concerned, thinking that it would mean the reduction in quality of the game or finding lots of 'pay to win' items. Turbine assured us it would be alright.
They released a large update with about 4 or 5 instances and a raid. It was a good instance cluster, but it didn't come with any level cap increase so loot wasn't that desirable. It also came about 6 months before the release of another expansion.
Rise of Isengard was our first expansion since F2P. And cracks were beginning to show more and more. They released it without any instance cluster initially. Only a single buggy lair raid that was originally promised as a free update and later tacked on to the expansion to fill it out. Then, slowly, we got the instance cluster and raid. It was an alright raid but it felt hollow. We'd waited a long time and then got nothing more than a mini-expansion had provided before, especially when it cost twice as much as Mirkwood did.
After that, we got Riders of Rohan. This 'expansion' was the biggest joke of all. Originally, they didn't tell us what was in it when they released pre-purchases. Then, after people bought it, they revealed it wouldn't have any instance cluster. No raids. The only end-game would be a daily grind to rebuild a town. That was it. The community kicked off. Eventually, they gave in and said they'd include an instance cluster. But the instance cluster was about Erebor (the mountain in the Hobbit) and not anything to do with Rohan. It was clear it was intended as a cash grab for people who watched the Hobbit films. We got the first half of the instance cluster a few months after the expansion first released. Then we got the second half. Both times they gave us these instance cluster halves, they called them 'updates'. Usually, updates had new content in. This time, it was just delayed content that was supposed to be part of the expansion. The downside being all of the instances were terrible, the raids were 2 lair bosses and a gauntlet (so less than the Mirkwood raid), and people gave up.
By this point, Turbine had also gone out of their way to monetise what they could. They ignored complaints about lag, grinds, and broken old content. Instead, they began selling more store-only items. They milked what they could from the playerbase without caring what sort of content to deliver. It got to the point where the community was so divided between fanboys and people hostile to Turbine that the forums became a propaganda-fest. The CM banned dissenters left and right.
With customer trust erroded, Turbine finally announced their next (and my last) expansion. Helm's Deep. They didn't have any instances, only these things called 'Big Battles', which took away any importance of class and relied on generic big battle upgrades. They also did the thing that killed the game for many people: Trait Trees.
Before, you could trait your character how you wanted. It made hybrid builds viable and widely varied. You could make a class built for survival, or DPS, or whatever you wanted. But Trait Trees took all of that away. They gave generic builds to everyone. Now, you couldn't run a hybrid build because you could only choose one line and the skills it came with. They literally locked our skills behind 3 different lines. Where a person might have a few healing abilities in their DPS build, they were now locked behind the healing line only. Sure, you could put points in other lines, but it didn't give you the skills you wanted like before. In effect, they took everyone's characters and made them generic, cookie-cutter builds.
After this, they said they had no plans for another expansion. A few small updates here and there, but it's basically maintenance mode now until Mordor. A cash cow to squeeze, not a game to please.
And now we're at the point where they've driven so many people away that they're having to merge servers to save cost and to make the population look busy again. 29 servers cut down to just 10; 5 US servers, 5 EU servers. It says a lot when a game is forced to make such drastic changes, while pretending it's doing fine. Not only that, they've been unsuccessful with actually transferring characters between servers, so in true Turbine form they've got no clue what they're doing.
TL;DR: Do not play this game. It's no longer what it once was. It's a broken, hollow, generic shadow of its former self, and Turbine are only using it now to milk the few remaining loyalists for all they're worth.
Edit: To clarify, I have a Lifetime account. I get full VIP perks forever because I paid a large amount when I first started playing. So my complaints are from the perspective of someone who doesn't even need to pay for it, yet still can't bring themselves to play it.

First of all, like most reviews, this is completely opinion based.
I highly respect BMG and their thoughts on this game, but I believe they can have some improvement.
I have seen over reviews about this game, and I agree with some, and disagree. So, props to BMG for creating a great community.

*What can be improved:
ELO SYSTEMS: The elo system created in this game is completely dumb. It can go either way, being good or bad. I believe BMG could have done a better way to program this, because the most ridiculous things can happen. I can play 1 game, and get 13 elo, (Pretty Normal) and I can lose a game, and lose 40 elo. (WTF BMG?) The game barely rewards you, and mostly takes away. I believe that BMG could have made the ELO system more balanced, and not punish players so greatly.
MATCHMAKING: Ok, this is just ridiculous. Last season I was in the ranking Platinum. Recently, there was a new feature added to the game called "Experimental 1v1s." This is basically a way for the community to respond on different things that may or may not be added to the game. This sounds good, right? Nope. The gamemode is nice, and a new way to look at the gamemode like a PTS, but the matchmaking is completely screwed up. I find diamonds all fo the time in it, and sometimes even player who just got the game. The matchmaking could be better, but I'll leave it at pretty good for now, because I do not have problems while playing Ranked or Strikeout.
*Good Job, BMG!:
THE ENTIRE GAME: This game is very fun, and easy to learn to play. (In my opinion)Any player from anywhere can play the game, due to the game having different servers such as US-E, US-W, EUR, SEA, ASIA, AUS, and BRZ. New players can play in the training room to find a Legend and playstyle they like, so nobody is completely confused on how to play the game. So, good job BMG!
NOT PAY TO WIN: This game is completetly play to win. BMG did a good job of this because they didn't want rich to very wealthy people just being able to overtake new players or players who aren't capable of buying Mammoth Coins. The entire Mammoth Coins concept was a great idea, because this gave players who wanted to support the devs and makers of Brawlhalla and were able to show off some style with skins. There are a few different things you can buy with Mammoth Coins, for example, K.O. effects, Sidekicks, Taunts, and Skins for characters. These give no advantage gameplay wise, but they are fun to show off and use, because each skin is special in its own way. Even though there are some things that can only be gotten through special packs such as the Valhalla pack, Collecter's pack, and the soon to be BCX pack. There still aren't many exclusive things though, so there is no need to worry.
SEASONAL AND RANKED ITEMS: In brawlhalla, during specific seasons or after the ranked season has reset, you can buy special items. For example, the ranked currency is Glory, in which you can buy Skyforged items. During different seasons or holidays, for example Halloween, there will be a patch with exclusive items that you can buy with mammoth coins or gold. (normal currency) You can keep these items forever, and will look stylish with your exclusive items.
*Summary:
THANKS FOR A GOOD GAME, BMG!: Overall, Brawlhalla is a great game that everyone should consider getting and just playing for a bit. There are some things that I believe should be fixed or things that should be the same, but that is just my opinion. I have loved Brawlhalla since I got it, and I have met a handful of wonderful people while doing so. So please, if you get the chance, just take some time to get to know the community and play the game.

Based off of my currently limited experience with this game, I would love to give a neutral response, but that is sadly not an option.  The Sims 3, on it's own, is a great game.  The customization is acceptable, the graphics look nice but aren't over the top, it runs on my outdated computer, and I enjoy playing the game.
Here's my problem with the game.  There is a large quantity of really good content locked behind a very large quantity of money in the form of DLCs.  While for most games this isn't a big deal, I feel like The Sims 3 DLCs don't provide enough bang for their buck.  I personally cannot afford to be throwing twenty bucks into one game just because I would like to access some new furniture or game mechanics.
If EA games were to take a hint, I would suggest that they make the DLCs free, or at least put a huge discount on them, once The Sims 4 begins to surpass The Sims 3 in revenue.  Most people are going to move on to The Sims 4, so why not make it easier for those people with outdated computers to enjoy the full Sims experience?
I would gladly put at least $100 into this game, but the combined prices of the DLCs and the game far exceed this limit.  It is still a great game that deserves plenty of playtime, but if you're on a budget, prepare to be dissapointed by the massive quantity of good stuff you just simply can't afford.

You may complain about the price now but have you even seen the prices for the sims 4 and it's expansion packs? Nowadays, each and every game pack and expansion pack costs 20 to 40 dollars, and the packs only offer something that is far more exclusive than the games before it. Making them well, more expansive.
I grew up with the sims, and my naive child mind, despite dodging every single innuendo the game threw at me, always had a soft spot for this franchise and its a shame that EA threw it into this rut, milking it for what it's worth. Shattered Planet is a charming rogue-lite in which you play as a disposable clone sent to discover and explore fragmented Alien worlds. The core gameplay loop is simple - Click to move, click to attack, and wander around the map discovering new items, enemies, and events. You will inevitably die, losing all of your equipped gear and items and hope you earned enough resource to upgrade your stats, or unlock a new pet or character class. Then buy a new set of random gear from the vending machine, and head out for another run. Shattered Planet captures the spirit of a classic rogue-like, but it’s extremely simplified mechanics, soft-core difficulty and lack of strategic depth will leave fans of the genre wanting more. I give it a thumbs up, as it held my attention for a good few hours.
Shattered Planet is fun in short bursts, and slightly addicting. The engine and art style are fantastic, so they really could do great things with this game if they continue to support it. But as it stands, the lack of depth and dumbed down mechanics don’t hold my interest for very long. I would say Shattered Planet is worth a buy at around $10, or if they patch in a new content update. If you do give it a go, be sure to stick with it for at least 2-3 hours to get past the slow start.

A casual roguelike that has a odd combination of rewarding exploration and getting through the area as quickly as possible. The different character classes are unlocked by finding enough new stuff. Each enemy, item, area, and event are recorded in a journal of sorts, and after discovering enough, your Research Level will increase, which unlocks the characters and gives you a randomized bonus item. You play as a clone, and when you die, you get 'resurrected/cloned' back at the base.
The classes, of which there are 5, are mostly a different skin with a different passive ability and a limited use skill. For example, the Assassin has better range with Guns(which is this games version of Wands), and increased damage with them, along with better unarmed damage.
The Items themselves are not randomly generated, they're all premade, though what you'll find and where is still random. All of them have a unique appearance, along with a description that often proves amusing. Also, a lot of them reference something: Like Master Chiefs Helmet, a Lightsaber, and a Stormtrooper Helmet. As for types of items, there's consumables, which come in either food, or Canisters. The Canisters work exactly like Potions in other roguelikes, where there's only so many different types, but in the beginning of each run their appearance and name is random, and only by using or tossing them will you discover their uses, and btw, the food is for healing, though there are healing canisters too. Guns work like Wands, in that they do certain damage and/or effects.
Equipment is kinda limited in my opinion. Well there's certainly a lot of different ones, but their restricted to the Weapon and Helmet category. They DO appear on your character visually, but I wish there were body armor and boots/gloves to deck your character in. Also, once you die in a run(which the default mode has no end, so you WILL die eventually), you lose your equipment, including the ones you brought on the run with you(you can equip your self back at the base/ship). This isn't too much of a problem, since there's enough items of good quality to acquire fairly easily.
You have a home base. as Ship in orbit, that you return to between runs. This is where you get most of your equipment, upgrade you character, etc. before a run. There are 2 currencies in the game: Scrap and Gems. Scrap is used to permanently upgrade your clones stats permanently, and btw, upgrades are tied to each of the classes, so if you buy 3 Strength Upgrades for the Assassin, your Renegade wont get those unless you buy them for him too. The price of the upgrade scales at a set amount, so first upgrade is 25 Scrap, second is 35, etc.. Gems are used for the R.O.S.E. machine thing in the base. I forgot what the acronym stands for, but it randomly generates Weapons and Helmets using Gems. Each equipment in the game is rated from 1 to 5 stars. At the ROSE, the Tier 1 generates 1-2 Star Items, Tier 2 generates 3-4 Star Items, and Tier 3 generates 4-5 Star items. They're fairly priced at 5/20/50 Gems respectively.
You can also have companion pets that help in battle, which are created/cloned at the base for Gems.
The 'get through level quickly' mechanic I mentioned earlier is sort of Creep/Corruption, called Blight. It's a black goo that slowly spreads through out the level, which hurts to step on, eventually spawns Blight Creatures which are fairly strong,
I'll stop rambling now, but this is definitely a fun casual roguelike with nice graphics and and SFX/Music. The $15 price tag is a bit steep for the quality of the game, personally I feel it would be better in the $5-$10 range, but it's a must get on sale.

Shattered Planet is a fun little roguelite (quite light) with a nice mechanic of ever-encroaching blight to keep a little tension.  Levels are very quick to complete and have a nice 'one more level' flair.  Itemization is fairly diverse in flavor, but limited in impact.  There's a ton of random events, but unfortunately (again) they have little real impact (temporary stat boost).  Progression is tied to boosting stats based on resources collected during runs, and the needed amounts increase exponentially.  After about five to ten runs, you'll have more or less effectively maxed out your character.  This is a fine mechanic while you're still progressing, but the wall comes too quickly and too hard.
Unfortunately, the game is its own worst enemy, as the mechanics break in really stupid ways.  Blight adds tension, but a common item makes it completely trivial and avoidable.  I enjoyed the game 100 times more when I didn't realize you could stop blight progression.  Also, enemies are easily teleported off into space, instakilled no matter the strength...what's the point in fighting and developing stats if you can just safely kill everything without a fight?  More importantly, anything past a certain level WILL one-shot you if you try to attack, no matter your stats.  Again, why bother with combat at all?  And finally, resource collects increase by level, so the best strategy is to simply teleport everything, get to the next level and collect random dropped items.  It's far more rewarding than doing it the 'right' way.
For the list price, I wouldn't say it's worth it.  I got it in a bundle (as the only thing I wanted in said bundle, but it was substantially cheaper) and am quite happy with that purchase.  I would've been much happier with it had there been an expansion pack (it's a little repetitious, even for a roguelite) and if the game was better balanced.  I did really enjoy it for a few hours.  Good setting, fun graphics, some interesting things to unlock earn it a reluctant thumbs up.  But ultimately, it's a bit too shallow and self-defeating for any lasting appeal.

A long-enduring ever-expansive homage to the alternative history that is Middle-Earth, that will absolutely bury you in its many miniature gameplay mechanics steadily accumulated and tweaked over its now 8-year-long course.  And while it my look like an overwhelming ammount of content to go through to a new player, the fact that this game is most proud of is, be you a level 1, 30, 50 or 100, there always seems plenty to do to feel rewarding, and a time well spent.
Mechanically, its a by-the-numbers MMORPG game, very much entrenched into evey known trope of an early 21st century online game. But its style and gameplay hasn't yet been hampered by it, rather built around it. There's the standard 50+ skillbar of each fairly ballanced class which compliment eachother in a D&D kind of way (the tanky one, the squishy dps one, the buffer, the healer, the run-around-do-whatever-you-like one), working together without ironic subtext, since Tolkien basically
(ugh...) inadvertently defined the classical dungeon crawling class system anyway. You TAB around the monsters presented and diminish their red bars. Alternatively, you gather materials, craft, randomly explore, complete numerous deeds, roleplay (it is, obviously, an extremely RP frienldy game), buy junk, sell junk, play through story mode, pvmp, do instances (scalable) do quests, do quests, do quests........
The strongest parts are indeed the stories of numerouns inhabitants of the world, gated behind and propelled by your typical fetch and kill x quests. You could do a lot worse then reading through abysmal ammount of text walls of these chatty NPC's, and, if you're a fan of the setting, it will be a treat throughout the game. It is skippable of course, but this is a text heavy game.
The FTP model can safely get you through 1-50 without much hassle, and the remaining content is gated behind purchases, but, by then, you'll already decide if its worth your money and time. As stated above, there's plenty to do in Eriador anyway, before venturing forth through Moria into Rhovanion, Rohan and Gondor.
Tip: Get a mount as soon as you can, it's a massive game. And don't venture into Prancing Pony drunk.
Oh yeah, grinding is, for the most part, optional.
Highly reccomended.

This game was just not what I was hoping for.
I will admit I didn't go in with very high expectations. I remember there being some controversy over bad reviews being hidden at the time of its release as well as pay-offs for good reviews from "reputable" sources. That being said I really tried my hardest to go into the game with an open mind. What I got what just a non-immersive bland story between two characters. I'm not saying the game is all bad. The visuals are somewhat pretty, the gameplay is interesting at points, and I think some of the ways the game progressed were cool. But overall this game just lacked in basically every department.
The first and main complaint I have is that the game is story driven. I can tell the developers really wanted to create something that everyone could connect with on a deep emotional level. Their attempt at this resulted in the characters having a made up language, the logic for this (I can only guess) is so that people of any language could connect without having to worry about translation or anything like that. The thought, however good, makes the two main characters come off as silly Sim-like beings. And because of this I had a very hard time connecting with the characters on any level, which significantly takes away from any sort of emotional connection that the developers most likely intended. And I'm a huge fan of story driven games, even when there really isn't complex gameplay (games like Walking dead, Life Is Strange, or Heavy Rain) so I would like to think that I would have some credibility when recognizing a good specimen.
Also I think it's important to note, I played this game with my brother. We were both hoping to get something out of the experience being brothers, even going so far as to have one person controlling the one brother with a controller and the other with the keyboard. Honestly we really tried to give this game a fair chance.
Other small issues with the game were things like the simple controls. Now don't get me wrong I'm not saying that this is always a bad thing, but I really felt limited by the ones in this game. The puzzles themselves were simple enough but sometimes we would have trouble solving one simply because we couldn't figure out how to get something to work properly. They were also quite dull, in my opinion. It is possible to have exciting or at least somehwat fun puzzles but this game bordered on monotonous. We played through the game on my brothers steam account and I think only took us about 2-3 hours but even with that small amount of play time it really doesn't feel worth it. I just don't feel enriched like I normally would from other good story driven works of art.
I'm not trying to say it's a horrible game, or anything like that. I bought it for $3 so I don't feel too jipped, but if someone asked me if I thought it was worth it I would probably say no. Put your money toward something better. Not to sound like a jag but I don't understand how so many people can think that this game was so amazing. Maybe this is the only one of its kind that they have played.
But seriously, play something else.

So I've just finished Transmissions: Element 120. It's a singleplayer source mod that was released Jun 16, 2016, and takes place in the Half-Life universe, seperate from the main plot. The beginning is creeping and mysterious, with a fantastic mechanic that can bring out tense and pumping moments, even with the familiar enemies and predictable AI.
"The wolf moves freely amongst the flock, veiled in the black of night."
The latter half of Transmissions, you obtain a form of the Gravity Gun unique to this source mod. It turns combat from a boring bullet sponge-'em-up to something much more involving and fun to execute. Alongside this, the latter half better displays the enviromental design, and the love and care that went into every detail of the maps.
My only complaint about Transmissions: Element 120 is that there isn't more. The pacing of the first half should have been much longer - I enjoyed the mechanic and I wish there was more of it used, alongside more creative ways to bounce around with the Propulsion Gun; the climax of the game came far too fast.
I say it's worth the costly price of zero quid, and it's relatively short, so give it a try

This game is perfect if you're in the mood for pure puzzle solving without a grande story behind it or having to talk to a bunch of characters. It's similar to Myst – but without the mystic atmosphere.
Some wealthy oil dude with a big love for safes has died, and his family has hired you, a master safecracker, to find his last will hidden inside the mansion.
Technically, it didn't run well at all due to nasty flickering, until I found a Steam community guide that shows you how to disable fullscreen mode. Smooth sailing from there.
There's a great variety of puzzle types, ranging from mathematical puzzles, to sliding puzzles, to simple letter decryption, and more – even some unique stuff I've never seen before. Though at the end of the day, you do find yourself dealing a lot with 4-digit codes.
I've already had an affinity for Snooker, so I kinda accidentally blasted fairly quickly through the Snooker puzzle. But I'd like to know what other players thought of that one. I can imagine it being hard to comprehend.
Speaking of hard: the Polybius square puzzle was by far the worst, imo. The way you're supposed to read those numbers is very unintuitive. Other than that, I'd say that these puzzles are satisfyingly challenging. Certainly not easy (as a whole).

This game is one of my favorite PC games. I know I don't have a lot of hours at the time of writing this review but have had it in my library for a while, making that seem like a bit of a bold statement. But hear me out: this game is worth your time. I usually only get to play it between my classes but I usually get caught up in it in my free time too.
So have you ever wanted to play Super Smash Bros on your pc and have it right on your steam account for easy access? Well, here you go. This is very much alike to that game, but with a few of it's own original twists. The rules are the same: get the other players off the map to kill them, earning you a point and deducting them a point. Several powerups and weapons help the gameplay vary. There's also VERY many gamemodes (free-for-all, 1v1, stock, holiday events, etc). You can also play single player if you don't want to wait to find a server.
The AI is a bit stupid at times, though. Even on hard mode, they sometimes pause thinking of what to do next, letting the player kill them immediately. Probably need to work on that.
Honestlty, it's free, so why don't you just try it for yourself?
edit Jan 11 2017
The community is slowly pulling me away from this game. Lots of awful people, but there's some nice ones too. Though if you want to play ranked, get a thick skin. Or you will bawl your eyes out. I don't mind permanent unlocks in my rogue-like, but this isn't how you do it.
In traditional "proper" rogue-likes you could win the game on your first attempt, but you won't, because you lack the knowledge required that comes from your previous attempts.
In Shattered Planet you could never win on your first attempt, because you need to unlock permanent stat upgrades that are acquired by playing, collecting a few resources to buy upgrades, and then dying and starting over again.
This fundamentally breaks a large part of what makes rogue-like games compelling, your skill and knowledge counts for nothing against the need to grind.
The graphics are quite nice, and I like the idea of being perpetually pushed forward by the encroaching corruption, but the mechanics ruin it.
Maybe you can reach a point where you have capped the stats, and then it's just your wits vs the game, but I'm not prepared to grind it out to find out.

Shattered Planet is a fun little turn-based roguelike when you first begin playing. The setting is interesting -- you play a clone who has been sent forth to a mysterious planet to map the terrain and relics found on the planet... or, more likely, die trying. The planet is the game's single dungeon -- it consists of a series of randomly generated levels which get progressively harder. Items can be found scattered throughout the levels and are generally interesting. You also collect minerals and golden triangles that serve as currency to make your future runs easier. When you die on the planet, you keep your currency but not your equipment, and you must use the currency to buy future equipment, permanent upgrades for your future clones, as well as monster companions to help you.
There are two main things that make this game not very enjoyable. Firstly, the game is seriously unbalanced. Between dungeon runs you can buy different levels of gear: bronze, silver, or gold. When you buy an item this way, you get either a weapon or a helmet at random (the only two equipment slots in the game). Gold gear is the highest tier in the game, and it's cheap enough that you can buy this gear after a run or two while completely ignoring the bronze and silver tiers of items. You're guaranteed a high quality item that will allow you survive long enough to buy many more gold items after additional runs, so the pleasure of finding better equipment while exploring the dungeon is very low as you walk in with some of the best equipment right away (although you can still find nice usable items and guns).
The second problem is that you'll quickly find there is not a lot of strategy to the game. While the items are generally nice to discover, they add little depth to the gameplay, which generally consists of explore/whack monsters/ collect loot/repeat. Once you amass a number of guns in your inventory, instead of whacking monsters you shoot them. While there are a few things that you can do to protect yourself and take less damage, none of them feel particularly clever, usually just tedious (like waiting for your guns to recharge ammo after a battle, which takes time).
Overall, the game is pretty fun at first. But it doesn't last too long, and gets old quick.
Pros:
Cool items
Nice sense of exploration with random events
clean, easy interface
Cons:
Not much variety in level design
Not much room for strategy, good strategies can be tedious
Access to high tier equipment comes way too fast
Verdict: It's not a bad game, and I enjoyed playing it for a while. But I don't think it's worth more than $5-$8.

Trine 2 is an excellent platformer, the difficulty settings accurately reflect what you sign up for, the soundtrack is again excellent, the visuals are breathtaking - and some of the puzzles clever and fights challenging. My only gripe is the ability to refund and re-spend ability points at will. It is great for experimentation, but honestly removes any sense of figuring a clever way around some of the puzzles. For example, you often run into a puzzle that you know you could have easily solved had you spent your points on platforms instead of new arrows. Rather than work out some ingenious solution around it - you reshuffle your points into platforms - pass the puzzle, and put them back where they were.
It's a small mechanical decision but it dramatically effects my investment in play. There may be a mod to fix it, but this is a review of the base game and that's my only complaint. Other than that, worth the money if you like platformers. Check out the gameplay if you're unsure - it is exactly as fun and whimsical as it looks.

This is definitely my favourite MMO that I have played to date. I have played it before getting Steam, so I have way more game time than it actually shows.
This game is basically WOW, except less limited in the free to play.
You can unlock everything in the game just in F2P, and there is no difference, except for a few perks, between a player who is F2P or not. There is one location that requires you to be VIP : a location for Player vs Monster Player fighting, but there is another location for that.
The graphics are not disappointing, considering this game was initially released in 2009, but could use an upgrade to bring them to modern level.
Speaking of updates, these are happening constantly, with bug fixes, but also new areas and locations, quests, and other content.
Now for the quests. Well, to be completely honest with you, while the main epic quest is loads of fun, and actually had me engrossed in the story for quite some time, (It's really good !), the intro quest for the Elf start is.... lacking.
Sure the beginning of it is, kind of awesome, in the middle it is just pure boredom. I had to spend several different day doing it, simply because I was bored with the walking - talking - walking - fetch item - walking quests. That would literally be nearly half of the quests in the tutorial, which takes an HOUR to complete. That being said, the end of the Elf tutorial picks up the pace once again, but - not really that great.
Combat is absolutely fine, no issues with the abilities of any kind, Hunters' focus system is to be enjoyed with the balance. Different combinations of the abilities can be used to fight different monsters and also people. There is a PvP system - you can spar outside of major cities.
The map is just spectacular. You can explore the entirety of Middle-Earth, with different regions corresponding to different skill levels so you always have something to do in the game.
Overall - 8/10, really fun game, but a few of the quests are boring and repetitive, with a few bugs.

Let me just preface this by saying that I bought the game in large part because of TB's (TotalBiscuit's) review. And my own curiosity, of course. One of the things that really swayed me was that TB expressly says in his review that you SHOULD NOT just watch the gameplay/story on youtube or some such, he says that you must PLAY to get the full experience. To this, I EMPHATICALLY disagree. I'll try to tell you why.
Graphically the game is decently styled, if a bit basic. The video "settings" are non-existant. The camera angles CAN be a little off/misplaced at times, but are usually fine. Performance-wise it does fine, but that's as it should be with these graphics.
The gameplay/story itself; I found the twin stick contolling of both characters at the same time a little wonky, but manageable. Honestly the controls sort of detract a bit from the story the game obviously wants to tell, because half the time you are trying to play twister inside your brain instead of immersing yourself in the story, and yes, I did use a controller. I agree with TB on the necessity of using a controller, and frankly, anyone that gives a review playing only with a keyboard has done it wrong has no place mentioning contol scheme as an issue. You pretty much NEED to play with a controller (says it's a requirement right in the description, by the way). The story itself is alright, I suppose. Obviously quite a few people find it compelling, but I just didn't. Seems pretty basic, and relies quite heavily on tugging on heartstrings (or TRYING to) to foster an involved feeling in the player/viewer. In addition the made up language in the game I found to be more distracting than anything else. I get that the game is supposed to sort of just convey the feelings without actual words, but obviously that means that a lot of poorly animated gestures and pantomimes are used throughout the game, with a distant camera that has relatively basic controls, in addition to people gibbering away in baby-talk while you try to puzzle out what they're actually getting at. A bit annoying and distracting rather than emotional or helpful.
Summary? It's good, I suppose. Nice little puzzle game. I got it on sale for $3, and I totally agree with that price (about 2.5 hours of entertainment -1 playthrough- for $3 seems fine, if you're into the whole value for money thing), but I would not recommend this at full price. Just go watch the story if you're curious. You really won't miss anything. Sorry TB, swing and a miss here, feels like you got too subjective, rather than staying objective. But then... Brilliant mechanically, story is wasted potential.
Mechanically this game is brilliant (although just like in Human Revolution invisibility is ♥♥♥♥ing broken), and it's merging of old arcitecture and new technology is an uncommon aesthetic. Sadly the story goes nowhere and feels like a short story as opposed to a novel unlike the other games, it's really hard to not spoil yet it doesn't really go anywhere, so I'll talk about it's themes. Or rather, theme.
Once again the story revolves around augmentations and the world's nonsensical, yet unceasing obsession with them. Augmented are forcefully seperated from the unaugmented population who didn't really see much point in augs when you're dependant on an expensive drug made by one company just you can have cool abilities you won't even use, and that's assuming that augs work the way they do in the game. The world's obsession with augmentation being utterly nonsensical and heavy handed is was a problem in Human Revolution too, and the writters have doubled down on this one nonsensical theme. Using augmented people as a metaphor for racism is bad, but it's portrayal of a cyberpunk Apartheid is even clumsier. I was in a hurry once and went down the wrong half of the staircase and was minorly inconvienced. And that's the worst it ever gets.
Things in Deus Ex that are still relevent are basically ignored save for the occasional instance of corporate greed, only really seen in emails you read every now and then. There is actually interesting, well written moments, but they're still tied to the omnipresent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Finally, since the game fails to really do much on it's own, how does it fair as a prequel to Deus Ex? It doesn't. Just like Human Revolution this game blatantly makes retcons to an existing franchise because it's creators or publishers thought it couldn't stand on it's own. It actually feels like more like that one mod for the original X-Com that took place in an alternate timeline where X-Com lost and you play a bunch of all-female mutant air pirates. And that handled racism MUCH better than this game despite being rather silly, and knowingly so. Seriously, it had a faction of racist humans that had uniforms based on Wolfenstein 3D's NAZIs, use WWII era weapons and fly in UFOs SHAPED LIKE GIANT ♥♥♥♥ING SWASTIKAS. GIANT ♥♥♥♥ING SWASTIKA UFOS.
...And that those all-female mutant pirates? According to the creators if they don't intake a certain substance they get LOLIFIED.
And that game mod STILL manages to both handle racism more seriously then this. So it's a bit absurd that for a game so utterly focused on racism metaphors, it's handling of said metaphors is so clumsy.
Do I recommend it? Yes, as there is potential, and there is good ideas, and fairly good gameplay. But if you're looking for a good main story you won't find it here.

I really tried to like this classic Point 'n' Click adventure. It has most of the ingredients of a funny PnC from the golden era of LucasArts, but heavily fails to deliver - and it is one hell of a bugfest.
There are a few threads about game-breaking bugs in the forum, and I also encountered a few. The game saves at the start of every chapter - but when a bug occurred beforehand, it is saved as well! So I was left with a game-breaking situation, never able to finish the dialogue at the start of the last chapter because of an overlapping dialogue bubble and an actor that was placed in the room way too soon, thus crashing the game. Every. Single. Time.
The developers have been made aware of those bugs, but their only reaction was that they cannot reproduce them and they would "look into it". Well, it's been three years and nothing happened.
All those bugs wouldn't even be there if the game (and automatic save system) had been designed properly. It's entirely possible to soft-freeze the game in a few situations where other characters are acting, your character can be controlled, and a scripted action fails because the game is not correctly scripted for concurrency. Well, in that case, what about locking controls until that scripted action has finished?
I'm frankly surprised that there aren't more people who ran into those bugs.
It's a real shame. The graphic style is not for me, but the mini game had me laughing quite a lot.
If the game ever undergoes a major software design overhaul, I might change my review.
