This is a weird game!
I don't often gravitate towards satirical games, as far as I know the only other game I've ever played that remotely fits the genre was Microshaft Winblows 98. Obviously that was Gates-bashing, and this is DLC-bashing; satire tends to reflect whatever the fashion of the public's disdain happens to be. For DLC Quest, their attempt to both mock and highlight the major game company's use of DLC to extract more money out of the end user is apt and well thought out.
The first part of the game is an outright taunt at the concept; starting with no ability to attack, animate, jump, even move left, you need to use the in-game coins to purchase any of these things as DLC. From there the basic abilities become available and thus establish the foundation of the game, you need to return to the seller to get more DLCs in order to progress. The more stages of the game you complete, the more DLCs you're likely to need to continue further. A second part becomes available when you complete the first game, which is designed to be more like an actual game, complete with a story, a collection of stock characters, a bad guy and indeed more DLCs. I have to give the guys credit for making a semi-coherant storyline and plot progression through this part of the game and the jokes are good, but the game brakes the fourth wall way too much, which I don't mind in the first part - it makes the most sence there.
4 out of 5. This is a weird game that I'd recommend to anyone who likes a quirky satire that's more interested in sending a message than looking good.

It's a fun little parody, but don't expect any replay-ability.

Getting this on sale for $2.00 after coming from Dawn Of War Dark Crusade (which I also reviewed, finding it very lovely), what does this do to enhance the expirence further?
Is the game as glitchy as people say it is?
Can it's campaign hold a candle to that of Dark Crusade?
Are the new races worth it?
Let's begin:
Races:
New to the series are the Sisters of Battle and the Dark Eldar, and at first I was a little cautious of these newbies because something about them seemed.... pointless?
However I quickly realized that these new races add a massive amount of strategy to the game.
Sisters of Battle rely on faithfullness and the power of flame to scorch the enemy to a crisp. They have a massive buff against vehicles and can turn the Impieral Guard's horrid overpowered Baneblade into a pile of dust with a well placed Melta Gun to the face. My only gripe with the Sisters of Battle is that they have a horrid start up during battles, with their main infantry requiring a totally seperate building in order to train them. Wanna know what that means? If you don't start with that building, your screwed. Whatever you are fighting will bum rush you before you can do anything to combat them.
Dark Eldar on the other hand... Ho boooooooooooiiiiiii. Have you ever wanted to be a sadistic, egotistical, slave monger? The Dark Eldar embody all of that, with their main gimic being to use powers that can totally destroy the enemy and if you build up early on, nothing can handle you if you bum rush the enemy. Don't mistake that as a bad thing however, as the Dark Eldar are both fun to play and to fight. I would say though that it is important to be aware that the Dark Eldar have only a melee unit as their starting fighter, which means that Chaos can run them to the ground in a matter of seconds if you aren't paying attention.
Now, onto the changes present in the old races.
The features claim to have air battles but they are so undercooked it acts more as a way to make the campaign your ho ho ♥♥♥♥♥. The com has no answer to you just building five aircraft (especially Tau) and then bombing everything in sight. This leads to a sort of forced progression in certain missions where the aircraft are the easiest way to harass an enemy or prematurely end a mission. This isn't much of a complaint though because the aircraft can still be shot down, unless you are the Orks. Deth to the false orkyboy.
But hey, speaking of that campaign.
You aren't just taking a planet, but rather several "planets".
It's honestly more akin to that of "I own a continent, therefore this planet it claimed for all of Chaos", more than it is a matter of the entire planet a la No Man's Warhammer.
Once more I stress that this isn't a complaint, as it actually feels quite fun to take a planet, especially if you can directly rush an enemy. I will admit that between this, and Dark Crusade's Kronus, I prefer this. It's much easier to try and take a planet without every nation trying to cram their Baneblade, Kroot, Daemon, and Tomb spyder up your♥♥♥♥♥ so that's a plus.
The game runs fine, I've encountered exactly one glitch while playing but it was so minor it may as well not be mentioned. It was just that the build icon appeared over busy Hertics while being absent over free ones. That's not too difficult though if you know how to play already.
If you liked Dark Crusade, you'll enjoy this. If your new to both Warhammer and the Dawn Of War franchise, I recommend this as a jumping point, or Dark Crusade if you don't mind lacking the Sisters of Battle and Dark Eldar, as well as the aircraft.
This game is a great way to help familiarize yourself with the utterly insane universe of Warhammer 40K, and I will say that I completly love the franchise now, going so far as to buy the real codex's and study the wiki page for fun. This universe is insane and heavy metal as hell, and I love it for that. These games help ease you in and make you want to learn more and more about this twisted universe and what it holds in store.

Let me just preface this by saying that I bought the game in large part because of TB's (TotalBiscuit's) review. And my own curiosity, of course. One of the things that really swayed me was that TB expressly says in his review that you SHOULD NOT just watch the gameplay/story on youtube or some such, he says that you must PLAY to get the full experience. To this, I EMPHATICALLY disagree. I'll try to tell you why.
Graphically the game is decently styled, if a bit basic. The video "settings" are non-existant. The camera angles CAN be a little off/misplaced at times, but are usually fine. Performance-wise it does fine, but that's as it should be with these graphics.
The gameplay/story itself; I found the twin stick contolling of both characters at the same time a little wonky, but manageable. Honestly the controls sort of detract a bit from the story the game obviously wants to tell, because half the time you are trying to play twister inside your brain instead of immersing yourself in the story, and yes, I did use a controller. I agree with TB on the necessity of using a controller, and frankly, anyone that gives a review playing only with a keyboard has done it wrong has no place mentioning contol scheme as an issue. You pretty much NEED to play with a controller (says it's a requirement right in the description, by the way). The story itself is alright, I suppose. Obviously quite a few people find it compelling, but I just didn't. Seems pretty basic, and relies quite heavily on tugging on heartstrings (or TRYING to) to foster an involved feeling in the player/viewer. In addition the made up language in the game I found to be more distracting than anything else. I get that the game is supposed to sort of just convey the feelings without actual words, but obviously that means that a lot of poorly animated gestures and pantomimes are used throughout the game, with a distant camera that has relatively basic controls, in addition to people gibbering away in baby-talk while you try to puzzle out what they're actually getting at. A bit annoying and distracting rather than emotional or helpful.
Summary? It's good, I suppose. Nice little puzzle game. I got it on sale for $3, and I totally agree with that price (about 2.5 hours of entertainment -1 playthrough- for $3 seems fine, if you're into the whole value for money thing), but I would not recommend this at full price. Just go watch the story if you're curious. You really won't miss anything. Sorry TB, swing and a miss here, feels like you got too subjective, rather than staying objective. But then... I suppose that's the whole point of this "game"- make people feel like they're FEELING.

Loved DX:HR and was hoping for more of the same. This is unfortunately a shadow of the previous title and a buggy shadow at that.
Stealthing around, performing takedowns, and getting into gunfights is still heaps of fun and the levels are decently designed with some great visuals.
Combat can quickly become frustrating when wrestling with the controls. Cover has become somehow clumsier to use and responds to inputs inconsistently. Mouse sensitivity is incredibly high by default and feels a little weird even after extensive tweaking.
The dialogue, and the plot itself, are so far below the quality of many pulp novels and well below the DX:HR and even the original game. (edit: played more and the writing is up and down, shoddy at the start but some of the world building gets a lot better, characters are thin but dialogue and plot improve a bit too.)
There have been no crashes, but a the game has frozen, controls have stopped responding, odd visual glitches, and other bugs have forced a reload of a save or a restart of the application. (edit: the game has since crashed to desktop.)
I only paid $20 for this and it is worth that price. It's surprisingly flawed though and I can't recommend it at full price.

Português:
Este jogo é algo bastante diferente do que se costuma encontrar no mercado. É um jogo estilo Point & Click em que focamo-nos em descobrir pistas e resolver crimes. Quando digo diferente, não é propriamente o seu género, é mais o estilo em que é apresentado. Isto é o verdadeiro jogo á TUGA! A comédia está lá, as personagens e as suas personalidades são bastante engraçadas e variadas, a banda sonora combina perfeitamente com o tema do jogo, há pequenas brincadeiras e Easter Eggs que os desenvolvedores criaram, para quem é português vai achar muita piada e vai se entreter bastante a completar esta pequena pérola portuguesa como eu gosto de lhe chamar. Em termos de gameplay, é muito simples, não há muito que se possa dizer, é um jogo Point & Click e acho que é escusado explicar o porquê. Concluindo, aprovo este jogo e parabéns aos Nerd Monkeys! ;)
English:
This game is something quite different from what is usually found in the market. It´s a Point & Click style game where we focus on finding clues and solving crimes. When I say different, it´s not about the genre, but more like how it´s introduced. This is a game that really focus on my country Portugal and everything about it, so probably foreign people are not going to identify themselves much with this game as a portuguese like me. The comedy is there, the characters and their personalities are really varied and funny, the soundtrack fits perfectly with the theme, there are little jokes and Easter Eggs that the developers made, I think even for folks who are not from here they´re gonna find this quite fun and entertaining to complete this little pearl as I like to call it. About the gameplay, it´s very simple, there´s nothing much to it, it´s a Point & Click game, I don´t think I have to explain why. Anyways, I approve this game and congratulations to the Nerd Monkeys! ;)

This game was in my Steam wishlist when Steam user Eri! unexpectedly decided to send it to me as a Steam gift. Thank you for that. Unfortunately, as that version was region locked, I regretfully had to rebuy the game instead of enjoying the gift.
Detective Case is not only a private investigator, but also a typical, good-for-nothing protagonist with a big mouth, an inflated ego, and no clients. His sad, daily routine gets unexpectedly interrupted when Clown Bot, a mechanical domestic helper, shows up in his office. The machine explains that it is willing to work as the hero’s new sidekick, but actually aspires to be a real clown one day. Unfortunately, it still doesn’t fully grasp the human condition and thusly depends on the detective to show how people interact with one another. When Captain Garcia then suddenly asks for help in a suicide, all of Case’s problems suddenly seem like things of the past. The game has a great setup and both protagonists have their assigned functions. While players interact with other characters or the world as Justin Case, Clown Bot saves the in-game progress, gives hints, allows one to fast travel, but also delivers the occasional lame joke. Furthermore, the robot’s interior happens to have a portal to another dimension where Johnny, the tentacle monster, takes care of the protagonist’s inventory.
In addition to the colorful duo, the whole game further features an interesting gameplay mechanic: Unlike other point & click adventures,
doesn’t bring the typical “use object X with object Y” construct into play, but instead all collected thingamabobs are handled as pieces of evidence. As soon as one has collected enough items (typically three), it is possible to question certain characters on their whereabouts during the murder or their connection to the victim. For this, one will have to select the right question to ask and combine it with the corresponding item. If done correctly, the interview will progress, if not, one has to start all over. Players can even conduct these inquiries as either Detective Case or as Clown Bot to spice things up a little.
With that said,
has some minor sequencing issues. As stated, players can start the interviews as soon as they have collected the right items, which means that they can do so, even when they have never talked to a suspect before. The inquiry will simply start as if the protagonist and the other person know each other, even if that isn’t the case. Additionally, at one point around the middle of a playthrough, I had already collected all items and finished interrogating every available suspect, so I assumed that I needed to talk to Captain Garcia to continue the plot. Therefore, I went to the police station, where he then told me to investigate further. I immediately returned to Case’s apartment thinking I might have overlooked something, but once there, the telephone suddenly rang and Garcia told me to go to the station to talk to him. So, I went back. Both of these issues could have been addressed with a “check if variable exists” command, which can easily be overlooked while playtesting a game.
To make up for these shortcomings, the game has one of the most incredible soundtracks in any indie game out there. Unfortunately, I don’t know a lot about music, so I don’t think I could do the renditions any justice by talking about them, but the effort put into the songs is very noticeable. Apart from that, most of the pixelart is quite charming as well. The set pieces look really nice and do remind one of titles like Day of the Tentacle (1993), especially with the blackened foreground. Regrettably, the same cannot be said about the characters. While most of them follow the same art style, those that are based on real humans appear to have been rotoscoped, while the band members at the Gaf Bar are drawn in the manner of cartoon modern. These characters even have very different body proportions from the rest of the cast, which makes them stick out even moreso.
Apart from that, two of the three biggest drawbacks to
are the difficulty as well as the playlength. Genre veterans will finish their first playthrough of this in about the same amount of time it takes Kate Winslet to get on board the Titanic, survive the iceberg, and drop the rock in the ocean. (So, around three hours; four if you accommodate for commercial breaks.) There aren’t that many puzzles and they are far too straight forward to pose any challenge, especially because everything the detective can pick up is directly related to the plot. Creating puzzles is a time-consuming chore that might exceed an indie developer’s budget, and so, given the admission price, these shortcomings really aren’t that bad. However, Nerd Monkey should have targeted a game this short and easy at younger audiences. Yet, similar to how
(1997 ongoing) might be mistaken for a children’s show,
may look family friendly, but really contains a lot of offensive jokes coupled with adult themes.
With that said, the English localization is this game’s biggest issue and, unlike in the foul-mouthed cartoon, a couple of gags might leave players in unruly bewilderment.
was originally written in Portuguese and Nerd Monkey decided to only have one translator convert the entire game into English, which was certainly a mistake. Point & click adventures depend heavily on language, which means that the poor translator was confronted with a Herculean task. They should have employed at least  one other person to proofread the finished result. But since that didn’t happen, players will undoubtedly notice just how exhausted the translator was by the end. The English rendition is plagued with spelling errors, several jokes got lost in translation, and grammatical mistakes sometimes make it difficult to follow some of the dialogs. While this is certainly a non-issue to EFL and ESL learners (English as a Foreign/Second Language), I know that the quality of English translations matters to a number of native speakers.
Overall,
is a title best meant for those that wish to support aspiring independent developers. It may have sounded like I wanted to give the game a beat down, but that is certainly not the case at all. Detective Case has a number of shortcomings and some the jokes are not necessarily the best, at least in English, however, the developers seem well-meaning. The dynamic between the two heroes is certainly a good foundation that I would like to see more off in the future, most of the pixel art is lovely, and the soundtrack is phenomenal. The dialog mechanic too is a great idea, but is currently held back by a localization team that was just too small.

Movement was just annoying. You could walk from location to location (in a huge circle) or you could take the cab. Of course the cab would show up anywhere (even inside buildings), but it would only drop you off outside them. It wouldn't even always drop you at the door. Normal conversations were weird at points as well. Perhaps I did something out of order, but several times it made no sense what people said... It was as if the conversations for an actor who wasn't present were mapped to an actor who was.
While I am slightly curious how it will end, I half expect there will simply be a THIRD twist which further stretches the game...
Perhaps a true point and click fan will appreciate it more, but I certainly did not.
I applaud the devs for the efforts, but for me it didn't deliver.

I tried this game years ago and only played the free areas. It was patronisingly easy and dull at the beginning but it got better as it went on. When I'd finished all the free areas and hit the currency cap, I moved on to a different game. I always remembered how much I enjoyed it though and recently I bought the expansion packs during a sale. It's much more enjoyable paying for access rather than grinding for Turbine Points. With the expansion areas unlocked, it's a lot easier to get TP too. After a couple of quest pack purchases, the whole game can be unlocked painlessly through regular play.

I strongly recommend this game for any classic MMORPG & LOTR fan.
LOTRO has an immense amount of side story & lore vs. the traditional movies.
Although this game is quite old now, the graphics are still considerably good.  DX11, DX10, DX9 settings allow backwards compatibility with older machines & laptops.  Choose to download HD textures, or not.  Choose to play at 1080p, or not.  It's your world for the taking!
For a free to play game, you start off with everything you need.  A decent amount of character creation selection, a decent amount of storage space, access to all beginning area quests, as well as access to two more area quest packs.  Once you're in your LvL 20's is when you will need to purchase quest packs.
To purchase quest packs, you have four choices:
1) Go VIP & get access to them as part of VIP.
2) Purchase packs from the LOTRO store/Steam directly.
2) Use real money to buy in-game premium currency to purchase them.
3) Create a grind character to grind TP (Turbine Points) to purchase them.
You will earn in-game premium currency (Turbine Points) just by playing the game.  Completion of certain quests, or deeds, will grant a set amount.  Deeds are "passive" quests.  Example, kill 100 wolves would be a deed.  Use a certain skill a certain number of times is a deed.  I was able to grind 150TP in just over 1 1/2hrs.  One hint, it involves creating a second character, Elvish, and doing certain quests & deeds.
If you're a crafter, this game has a very in-depth crafting system.  It is also simple to wrap your head around.  An added bonus, certain crafted items allow you to name them.  Every item you craft, the characters name who crafted it will be in the item description.
If you just like a quick jump into battle then log off, there is a feature called Skirmish.  This is a closed mission/dungeon where you can take other players with you, or go it solo.  Either way, you can just hack n slash.  Skirmishes are unlocked around lvl20.  Although you don't get drops off of the foes, you do earn Skirmish Marks.  These are spent in Skirmish Camps.  You can purchase armor, weapons, rare crafting materials, cosmetic attire, etc.
Here is a video, from 4 months ago, that I recorded when doing a solo Skirmish:
If you like to play in a group with other people, there are two types.
1) A Fellowship.
2) A Kinship
A fellowship is your standard everyday party/group.  You're just out to do a quick quest.  A standard fellowship has a maximum of 6.  A raid fellowship has 12.
Raids can be extremely difficult, or, extremely easy.  You will find, as usual, most PUGs (pick-up groups), will fail unless they have a much higher level player, or a very experienced veteran player, leading the way.  Raids are also only ever done at end-game.  Unless you're in a kinship.  Many hours can be wasted during a raid with nothing in return other than a very costly repair bill.
A kinship is your standard everyday guild/clan.  These are the groups of people you prefer to do raids, quests, events, etc. with.  Kinships also gain levels based on time.  A kinship can reach a max level of 10, with a max number of members at 1,000.  Every character you create can be in a different kinship.  A kinship can also have a Kinship Home.  Similar to a guild hall.  This comes at a fairly steep cost at lower levels.  A kinship is only allowed 1 home.  The kinship leader decides on access rules, though all kinship members generally have full access.
Every LOTRO account is allowed to have 1 home for their characters.  You can purchase, & find treasure, cosmetic gear to spruce up your place & make it look just how you want it.  You can also purchase additional storage chests to keep extra special items.
All in all, this game is FREE!  Download it & try it!
If you like casual, but still exciting, playing at your own pace, or even just only crafting and never doing anything else, this game is for you!
P.S.
Although it says I've played less than 100 hours, I never really had a need to use Steam.  I only ever played LOTRO & nothing else.  Played it straight for nearly 4 years & also Beta tested it.  I've seen this game change so many numerous times, but I still hear it's call in my dreams...trying to drag me back...back to a neverending world of lore.

Shattered Planet is a turn based rougelike based on exploration. Much in the way that rogue legacy has, each life you are collecting resources that you can use to improve your characters (I feel this game improves on this by allowing you to keep resources between lives). I really enjoy how the game is exploration driven, you get points and progress through the game by discovering new items, enemies, and environments. Another fun element you explore are "events" where you are given a choice and that affects your game play. For example, in one event you encounter a strong enemy who is injured and you're given the choice to kill it or heal it. If you heal it, then it becomes a companion animal and attacks your enemies.
The game has a great sci fi flavor, the art is great (and not pixel art which is nice), and most of all it's really fun to play. Roguelikes are all ready about adventure (mostly loot based) but this is the first game I've seen that actually makes the adventure the primary drive for the game. Definately worth checking out.

I like the humor of the game, I like the art. But I can't recommend it because of one glaring problem: there isn't much game.
There are some different classes and a range of abilities. The problem is that everything is gotten through grind and that there's only about two tactics: walk up and bash things that you have to while avoiding others or manage to get a gun and kite things. The first way is the way you go because you don't have a gun. You try to survive as long as possible and die due to attrition. Skill is not going to save you here. If you have a gun and a shovel on the other hand you can survive anything. You'll eventually die simply because you get too bored to keep paying attention.
A level basicly goes like this: enter a level, get as many goodies while taking the least possible damage and find a teleporter to get to the next level. If you're successfull, the game will quickly run out of things to throw at you. Expect to see the same levels and enemies time and time again, just in a randomized layout (which doesn't really change much)
The only thing that stands out in this game are the random event tiles. Stones or stumps that look slightly different. If you click on them, you get an event, followed by a choise and a skill check. This is the best part of the game.
In the end, the game relies a lot on grinding and doesn't offer enough variety or gameplay depth to back it up. You can have fun for an hour or two. You can pick it up at a very low price, but I recommend you quit playing once it's starting to feel a bit boring because it's not going to get any better. Don't buy this at full price.

In this game you are a detective, inherited a clown robot from a deceased relative, and together, you are assigned to investigate a murder in Hotel Lisbon. The game is point and click, detective mode. You have to check the scenarios, find clues, and interrogate characters.
The game sounded interesting to me. But in my first minutes playing this game, I only hoped to complete it as soon as possible. It is not worth USD 6,00 and I will tell you why:
Cons
* The game is all based on dialogues, portuguese humour, and it could not be translated very well to english. I played on both languages (english, and native portuguese, tho im fluent in brazilian portuguese). All of the texts are nonsense chitchat, forced jokes (a lot of sexist), so be ready to spam your mouse clicks to skip them repeatedly, all the useless conversation will grow you tired.
* The script is not very well elaborated, you will have to interrogate people using very poor worded questions mixed with lame jokes. You have to select the correct clue and along with the right question, until you progress to the next step. This part makes the game slow and boring.
* Although the crowdfunding seems to be not working anymore, you will meet the gaming studio crew in a scenario, and they will ask for a donation, pretty absurd.
* The laughing audience while the characters make jokes are annoying.
Pro
* The game is short. There is one main quest, and three side quests. My personal POV, I found it better this way, because I could not take this game anymore.
* The game soundtrack is good. The best thing on this game was the Fado bando in the restaurant.

Other than the poorly written dialog (which makes it difficult to discern which dialog choices to pick - apparently someone being interested in "material" things means they don't care about money???)  Probably the most glaring problem is how unabashedly sexist the game is. I don't mind *characters* who are sexists - I love me some Game of Thrones, but the game itself is really pretty awful. I couldn't get myself to finish playing it. There aren't many female characters and those that do exist are pretty terrible stereotypes that aren't treated well by other characters. Many of the 'jokes' are at the expense of women and it's just not funny? Maybe if you are in middle school it would entertain, but the jokes aren't even creative or decent quality.
As for the plot, eh, who cares. That's how I feel about finishing the game. The story was completely unoriginal - someone murdered, let's investigate with an annoying sidekick.

If you're tired of "roguelikes" like Rogue Legacy and Pac-Man (who the hell tagged Pac-Man as roguelike?) and want a game that is actually LIKE ROGUE, this is it.
Shattered Planet plays a lot like Rogue, but with a point-and-click interface, as opposed to using arrow keys. Honestly, this is the first modern game I've played that I would even BEGIN to compare to Rogue. If you haven't played Rogue, stop reading because the rest of this review won't mean anything to you.
Start with Rogue. Between games, add a sort of home base where you respawn after every death and buy equimpent for your next run. Here you have a storage locker to keep things you buy at the store (you can't keep things you find during a game, except for money and money (there are two kinds of money)), a place to cohose your class and pet for the next game and a place to buy permanent stat upgrades for your current class.
Now put in a few different quests. Of course there's the main "quest:" run until you die. There are also a few other game modes that I haven't really gotten into yet because the novelty hasn't worn off the basic game yet. In addition, there's a daily quest that you can only run once that picks your starting equipment for you and challenges you to make it through ten levels before dying for a nice reward.
Add some fun graphics and average sound effects and you've basically got Shattered Planet.
Seriously. If you ever loved Rogue, you NEED Shattered Planet. And there's a mobile app as well. It's free, but significantly watered-down.
Shattered Planet gets an A+ from me. If for no other reason than the simple fact that someone has FINALLY made a modern "roguelike" that actually feels LIKE ROGUE.

Great UI. Great music. Good variety of items, from glorious to plain silly. Descriptions are often humorous, as are in-game events (Hitting enemies with a rolled up newspapers grants a bonus to Wits/crits. Because you are better informed... and i wont even mention the time i sang a song to a hatching egg).
Gameplay is slick. True, it will get repetitive after a while, but it will be a good while and the ride is fun while it lasts. The visual presentation and lighthearted athmosphere keep the game going and you might struggle to put it away. Rougelite elements include equipment unlocks for future playthroughs, so-called permadeath, inability to pick exactly what items to start with, and several character classes to indipendentely level-up. As a nod to SOTS, diffrentely colored potions have diffrent effects on each playthrough.
On occasion the game struck me as overly simplistic, but that may be because of concessions made to touch-screen devices. Gameplay is well designed and above all, fun! I thought i'd get 5 minutes of fun before moving on, but it's better than that.
Strategic depth is not as great as other similar games, but the flipside is faster-paced gameplay, less confusion and a learning curve more focused on fun aspects of exploration. You won't need volumes of crafting guides for this game, and that may be a very good thing.
Lack of tooltips has been mentioned in some reviews. Feedback is there it's just implemented another way. Damage types are color coded for example. While more information on damages or resistances would be nice, the game designers choose not to clutter the UI or make it too complex. Most of the time detailed information is not needed, as you would expect plant lifeforms to burn easily or robots to be vulerable to electricity.
Overall, the gameplay is rewarding and fun which ofsets some simplistic design choices. Level layouts are fairly simple and screenshots do not present the game too well. I have no idea why it has no demo on Steam or anywhere else. Considering the asking price, it's a very good game.
Recommended.

After reading alot of the player reviews I was expecting to be sorely disappointed when finally getting around to purchasing and playing the addon to DAWN OF WAR. Fortunately this turned out to be a case of people complaining too loudly about minor things.
The Sisters Of Battle are really done well and properly fleshed out. The sound effects for them are amazing bringing out the extremism of their religious fanaticism. The male troops such as the Confessors are also given the treatment sounding just as devoted in their faith.
Graphics are top notch and much more better then they were in the Demo version. The Penitent Engine is highly detailed with a very intricate mechanical look. Yes the sound effect as one excellent reviewer has mentioned does sound obscene but then again it fits in perfectly with the holy euphoric rapture spoken so much about in religious books on how serving God will be as being in a constant state of ecstacy. So I have no qualms with the sound effects for the Penitent Engine.
One sound effect which really caught me off guard in its menacing beauty was the artillery unit called Exorcist which fires from its church organ like tubes creating a very buetiful church organ musical sound. Having many of these firing at slightly different rates side by side is quite inspiring.
Graphics for other units like the Sisters Of Battle,The Confessor, The Missionary, Sister Repentia Squad etc are stunning and capture the look of the Warhammer40k universe perfectly. Especially notible is the Living Saint the giant angelic Godlike being of the Sisters Of Battle which one can summon after having build many other needed structures to lay waste to enemy units. Vehicles are also top notch and its nice to the Rhino taking a prominent place in combat once again.
Music is great with some new tracks adding to the religious mood of the Sisters Of Battle.
Combat seems much more balanced and reminds me of the unpatched version of DAWN OF WAR. For the first time in ages I could play on standard difficulty and not have to worry about it becoming a bum rush situation with the Sisters Of Battle being able to hold huge numbers of enemies at bay. Why they changed combat in WINTER ASSAULT and DARK CRUSADE to a bum rush situation after the first patch I dont know. Am just happy to see combat once again feeling balanced without having to resort to playing at the Easy setting.
Complaints about aircraft are a bit exaggerated but I do agree with them being more like hovercrafts land units then actual air units. I was expecting some cool strafing runs and fly by bomb drops but there were none which was a surprise since they had this in a previous old Warhammer40k game called FINAL LIBERATION. Other then this I have no complaints about this expansion and it is well worth the money I paid for it.

Fallujah[a] (Arabic: الفلوجة‎‎, al-Fallūjah  Iraqi pronunciation: [el.fɐl.ˈluː.dʒɐ]) is a city in the Iraqi province of Al Anbar, located roughly 69 kilometers (43 mi) west of Baghdad on the Euphrates. The city grew from a small town in 1947 to a population of 275,128[2] inhabitants in 2011.[3] Within Iraq, it is known as the "city of mosques" for the more than 200 mosques found in the city and the surrounding villages.

If you've ever played a little Flash game called "Upgrade Everything", then this game'll feel pretty familiar. But it adds its own little twists on it. The game's entire point is satire of the gaming industry, judging by the title you can tell that the game mainly capitalizes major titles including most of its content or fixes in paid DLC (I'm looking at you, EA). Purchasing DLC is absolutely imperative to the game; everything from having music, animation and being able to walk to the left to getting an extremely overpowered gun, and minor DLC's such as making everyone wear a bikini or a top hat.
The game is well designed and its satirical form of humor is quite welcome. Making fun of everything from titular downloadable content, to the recent uprising of games with silhouette graphics (To, as the game puts it, "make games more artsy and trendy") to people that won't stop spamming the same lines like "Do a barrel roll!" or "All your base belong to us".
The game is fun, although I'd rather get it when it's on sale (You can get it for 75 cents on HumbleBundle (Another thing that the game makes a vague reference to) right now). It's a neat little indy collectathon with tight controls, fun pixelated graphics, well-done (although slightly repetitive at times) music and a fun sense of humor. Although, even with getting all the DLC, coins and achievements (Or "awardments"), it's still short and you can finish the game quickly. Though, you still can get a few hours out of it. So I recommend it.

I had a bit of a difficult time using the controller to control the two brothers but that's more a "me" problem than a game problem. The concept in itself is quite unique and by the end of the game I was getting a good handle of controls.

A bittersweet and haunting game . . . very much about grief and love, and determination! Unusual gameplay, can get a little tricky so try and keep the brothers on their respective sides of the screen despite the camera turning . . . but it keeps you on your toes! There are so many things I loved about this game, the art, the style and storyline - all the little things you can interact with (like rocking an old lady's chair so she laughs, or playing a harp!) It's beautiful and heartfelt. Yes, I cried very close to the end - it was a good cry.

An outstanding example of Narrative, Interactivity and Mechanics working in perfect harmony. A masterpiece in game design.
I was thoroughly unprepared with what Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons offered up and it's an experience I won't forget for a long time. The game begins with a fairly interesting mechanic, allowing you to interact with its world and puzzles in a unique way. It then extrapolates upon this mechanics to such a degree, that by the end, it is pulling at your heart strings.
I have been a die-hard Keyboard & Mouse fan my entire life, however, it is absolutely CRITICAL you play this with a controller. Otherwise, you are severely hampering your experience of this game.
This is not a game you can watch a 'Let's Play' of, it's not even a game you can watch your mate play whilst sat on the sofa next to them! The controller has to be in your hands with you controlling, if not, then the connection you build with it over a short 2-4hours of play simply won't happen.
I would recommend Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons to anyone and everyone. Worth every penny.

If you didn’t know already Crush Crush is a clicker game. If you don’t know what a clicker game is either then let me tell you. It’s a game where you click to earn currency or different kinds of value and upgrade and buys things to progress the game. All clicker games are the same in some manner since they all have the same goal and the same way of getting to it. The difference between this and other clicker games are mostly the theme which is you are trying to date girls and that you upgrade stats and have jobs to buy presents. This game is not so much about upgrading from currency, which is more focused on, and more common in other clicker games but about unlocking from waiting. The way you progress is from your "skills" and from buying presents but you don’t spend anything on upgrading, all upgrading comes from waiting. This is kind of interesting and not so much seen "from my experience" in other clicker games.
The game itself except from its obvious differences is still a clicker game and there is not really a lot of difference if you look at it from the bigger picture but with that said the game is well made for the most. The art is funny the "math" and progression is ok balanced but there is some major flaws in my opinion. First of all is this seems to me, after been playing it maybe a little too much a pay to win game. You are able to upgrade almost everything with diamonds and the only way of getting diamonds is by unlocking new levels with the girls’ affection of you. and you arent able to change what you buy of course with these diamonds so you can’t really experiment on what to buy so if you buy something wrong are you kinda ♥♥♥♥ed. Time blocks are almost useless to buy for diamonds compared to what you get from speed boosts instead.
With that said the major way of getting better is by resetting and getting prestige boost that decreases the time needed to level up your skills and the speed, which you get money from the different jobs. This way of progressing is really common nowadays and has evolved to this through the last couple of years. But some of the major problems with this way of progressing and which also affects this game is the way you are most effective. The way you generally are most effective when resetting in clicker games is that you play the game until you reach a point where you begin to slow down your progression and things don't go as rapidly. In this game there isn't going long until you are forced to reset because after that point it's not really "worth it" to waste time on getting more boost. So I’m not a big fan of the way you grind for progress I know this is the way it is in all clicker games but it could maybe use some tweaking.
The two ways of progressing in this game is by getting as high as you can and get some diamonds or grind some prestige boost so you progress faster.  You progress this way in almost every clicker game because it’s one of the easiest ways to make a lot of content with a minimum of required work since it just makes people replay it. There is not necessarily a problem with this but it can easily get boring or too much and i think it has in some perspectives in this game. But with that out of the way it’s a fun and good clicker worth checking out but be mindful of its flaws. :)

A short, fun, guilty pleasure type of shoot-em-up action game wtih 80's cliches. This game will leave you feeling like a true cyber badass with its over the top weaponry and abilities. Although a relatiovely short game (four hours straight run), it has a great 80'S action hero vibe with tons of robot badies to blow up in creative ways. Definitly worth a look if you're into 80's VHS movies, cyber punk visuals, funny movie spin-off jokes, and pure explosive goodness.

You know what's awesome? The 80s, specifically 80s action movies, with their simple no-nonsense plot lines about badass dudes saving the world from ultimate destruction, with synth heavy rock blaring in the background and explosions around every corner. Remember those? Blood Dragon definitely does, in fact it does such a good job of paying homage while simultaneously parodying them that it almost feels like it's a recently unearthed time capsule, built with technology far ahead of its time and hidden until the public was ready for it. That time is now; Blood Dragon is here and it's flipping sweet!
As Sargent Rex "Power" Colt, former army vet killed and then brought back to life Robocop style as a superhuman cyborg, it's up to you to put a stop to the tyrannical plot of your former commander, who plans to harness the blood of the cyber dragon to bring about a new age for humanity no matter the costs. The plot is cheesy, over the top, full of outrageous one liners and more explosions than a Michael Bay film, and outrageously fun for all of it. I can't remember the last time I laughed so hard playing a game as with Blood Dragon, which perfectly nails the balance between self aware cheese and playing up the ridiculousness of itself.
And of course, Blood Dragon plays exactly how you'd expect, by which I mean to say it makes you feel like the incredible cyber soldier that you are, liberating the remote supernatural island bit by bit as you pop off robots, save the helpless nerds, and face off against cyber dragons (essentially giant dragons that shoot lasers out of their eyes). For a budget game, Blood Dragon is surprisingly expansive, with the island being surprisingly large and chock full of side missions, collectibles, and cyber animals for you to hunt. It's not on the level of Far Cry 3 proper, but the size feels perfect for the sort of game it's trying to be, without any bloat and a fantastic ending which I won't spoil but is one of my favorites of any game in years.
If I was going to nitpick, my biggest complaint would be that the constant darkness contrasting with the neon color palette can be rather hard on the eyes after awhile, making this a game best played in short bursts if you don't want to go into self induced blindness. Other minor issues arise with the somewhat weak gunplay and the difficulty of trying to maneuver any vehicle around the island (I eventually gave up driving and just sprinted to my destination) can be bothersome at times, but never made enough of an impact to lessen my enjoyment.
Blood Dragon is a game designed to allow you to relive the glory days of silly action movies, updated with modern sensibilities to be nothing but unadulterated fun. It doesn't take itself the slightest bit seriously, and focuses all its energy into building itself up as a love letter to nonsensical action and soundtracks that you can't help but love (the music might be the best thing in the game, period). As long as you don't go into it expecting anything deeper than "kill the bad guy" and take it for what it is, Blood Dragon will shower you in it self indulging awesomeness and have you begging for more.

Date: 2/11/16
Review Number: 15
Game: Detective Case and Clown Bot in: Murder in the Hotel Lisbon
From (Creator Publisher): Nerd Monkeys
Played On: Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: 89 cents for the next ten hours
Total Time played:45 Minutes
Review:
Back in the old days of my youth, and DOS 5.1, I was rather a fan of Sierra games.  One of the original point and click adventure companies, they made their bread and butter in the early years over series like King’s Quest and Leisure Suit Larry.  I would spend hours playing King’s Quest 5 or Conquests of the Longbow, hunting and clicking, talking with random people, and trying to find that one clickable person that would move my adventure on.  I ate up that stuff, primarily because as a youth, I felt the writing was brilliant.  It should come as no surprise then that I am still fond of these sorts of games, though honestly I play fewer now that I have less time to devote to games.  Therefore I was somewhat pleased when another point and click adventure game came up on the randomizer.  After playing for around 45 minutes, though, I remember why I stopped playing these sorts of games; the return on investment in terms of time is rather low.
Now, this is not really a criticism of the game.  Indeed, behind the very clunky pixelated graphics and overly simple point and click interface lies the makings of a great game.  The humor is varied and entertaining enough to keep me interested, and the underlying murder mystery seems just interesting enough to be worth seeing through.  Even the addition of a sort of interview mechanic was interesting to me.  Unfortunately, after playing through as long as I did, I barely felt like I moved the story along.  This inevitably is the folly of gaming as you age: when you are young, you can waste away the hours playing games without consequence, however the older gamers must balance their gameplay time with work schedules, relationships, and other such real life things.  I find myself wanting for more before realizing that if I dont get to bed there is no way Im going to be able to drive eight hours tomorrow, and that sucks, because it means that I am old.  Enough about me though.  I love this game, it's cute, if not entirely put together, and everything about it makes me want to invest far more time than I have into it.  Hopefully you’ll find the same.
Game’s Fate: Uninstalled.  It's not that I’m not interested, I just have too many point and click adventure games I want to get to first.  Maybe later, when I have the time to spend on games as opposed to writing reviews about them
Buy/No Buy: Buy, especially now, but even after the sale ends, if you enjoy point and click adventure games.

Shatted Planet is not very good. Yes the typo was intentional. It's light roguelike, aka roguelite game with some persistent upgrades that you buy in between the missions. Basically you just grind stuff and levels until you can manage worse enemies and there's absolutely no way to finish the game without it. In that sense the game plays out like Rogue Legacy: you grind until you win. Rogue Legacy was funny and more interactive though since in Shattered Planet you just move around, grid based, turn by turn, clicking enemies few times more to kill them, die, upgrade and repeat. It's quite nice game to look at and simple enough to entertain for couple of hours but after that it's pretty useless.

It's a lot of fun. Like a lot of people I got it as part of the Humble Bundle and it was a bit of an unexpected star. Sure there are a lot of more detailed and deeper Roguelikes out there (Tales of Maj'Eval just to name one), but this is a really fun turn based blast that's attractive to look at and simple to play.
Is it worth £9.99. No. I'd say it's a fiver's worth of fun. But fun it definitely is.

Binary reviews (thumbs up or down) are not ideal for cases like this, but all in all I can't recommend Shattered Planet. While it's technically competent and visually attractive, with a nicely articulated sci fi theme, it unfortunately has little depth and a progression system solely based on grinding. I wasn't aware of the game's tablet roots when I picked it up, but they show through clearly in the design.
The game is a roguelite in the truest sense of the word "lite." The mechanics, stats, and equipment system are all very rudimentary, with character progression limited to three attributes and a couple of additional skills. Equipment is limited to a helmet, active weapon, and a few consumables. Progress is made by playing the game, dying, then spending earned points (scrap metal and crystals) to upgrade these basic stats and purchase new starting equipment. In practice, this means playing slightly remixed versions of the same few levels over and over again while slowly building up the necessary strength and resources to progress. Skill and tactics don't really come into it, it's all down to a repetitive turn based grind to slowly push through to new material while constantly replaying the old.
All in all, there's little to recommend Shattered Planet over roguelikes of greater depth and variety. It was fun for an hour or two, but by then I'd seen all of it that I cared to.

This scribblenauts game is different from the others because of the new approach it takes towards gameplay. The game encourages continued creativity throughout levels by reducing the rewards you receive from repeated use of them in an area. And while it doesn't punish you for not having a large vocabulary, you won't be able to 100% this game by reusing the same dozen words in every level. You'll even be penalized for certain word choices (i.e. Invincible) if only some of DC's writers were held to the same standard.
Another change is the combat in this game. I often felt that the fighting in other scribblenauts games was a clumsy mess, which often lead to me opting for the non-violent solution. No more will you be forced to join the pacifist ranks with the likes of that vegetarian Gandhi. You'll be able to cross swords with the best of them. But watch out, because weapons have durability now as well, so feel free to visit
for some ideas.

But the thing that completely kills it for me is the writing. It's painful. English isn't their first language and it shows in every way it can.  Either I don't get their sense of humor or they don't really have one. This is one actual conversation:
Case: I still haven't been paid yet
Secretary: Ok sign here and here
Case: HAHAHAHA
Clown-Bot: Beep Boop
* Cue laugh track *
... Wait what? Is this supposed to be funny? Some sort of anti-humor about misplaced laugh tracks? Is them being poor supposed to be some sort of running joke? It actually stoops so low to as to try to be self aware about how unfunny it is as if that is supposed to make it acceptable. When you reach that point you have failed.

I am a huge fan of the original Deus Ex and I really enjoyed Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I was prepared to give this one a lot of slack knowing some of the flaws from other reviews. But the biggest flaw, despite arbitrary microtransactions, questionable optimization, odd blurry faces for certain characters, and a fairly weak story is the fact that the game suffers from awful pacing.
The game starts off promising enough: a huge multilayered deserted building for you to creatively sneak or shoot your way through. The AI, though still a bit on the dumb side, provides a fair challenge and is better at pathing and searching rooms. This means that even though it's the first mission, you can't just jump from cover to cover without having to think critically on how you move past clusters of guards. The sequence finishes with a VERY visually appealing sandstorm, with an unfortunately dumb resolution. Still, it's a great way to start the game and if it featured more of these sequences, I would have considered this game one of my favourites despite the other flaws.
Unfortunately, there are only about 5 areas in the entire game that ever get this complex or interesting. Compared to the original Deus Ex, or even Deus Ex: HR, this is incredibly lacking. After the stellar intro sequence you get introduced to Prague which acts as a sort of 'hub world'. This is where things start to grind to a screeching hault. Despite the beauty of Prague with excellent interior and exterior design, the actual play area is far too cramped and limited. I expected a healthy dose of narrative, but these areas are 90% narrative and 10% exploration and gameplay. You have very little in terms of actual space and freedom, which forces you to complete the game's lacking story instead of going off on your own and discovering interesting tidbits about the world.
The biggest problem with Prague is how it isolates certain key areas. I'm not sure if this was a design or optimization choice but the map makes it seem like Prague is bigger than it actually is. Trully, the area is separated into 2 sections: one ridiculously small and the other considerably larger, with every other destination either being a one-off location or a separate entrance to the larger portion. Each of these areas are separated by a long load time. I could imagine how long it must be for non SSD owners.
Even though the game is at its best when you're sneaking/hacking/exploring, there are some small gripes. For one, the Praxis point system seems half baked. I didn't do every sidequest or find any praxis points in the wild yet I was very close to maxed out near the end of the game. I could only imagine what happened to the poor suckers who actually bought points. Also, I'm not a fan of the new hacking system. Aesthetically it's great and when it works, it works pretty well. However, almost 'requiring' items to be successful with some 4 or 5 rated security terminals seems absurd to me.
But the real sour feeling: Why are unskippable credits still a thing? I get it. Your team worked hard on the game and you're proud of your accomplishment. However, not everyone has 20 minutes of free time to throw away to see names of people they haven't met scroll by slowly. As an insult to injury, they snuck a cutscene in the middle of the credits (which I missed part of because I had no idea) and give you an acheivement for watching the whole thing... I could imagine someone who decided to let the credits run not knowing about the cutscene and completely missing out unless they noticed the acheivement.
Consider this a 'mixed' recommendation. Only get this game on a sale, understand that the game gets better past Prague, and understand that this isn't a 'full experience' and you might find yourself enjoying Mankind Divided. But if you're not a fan of Deus Ex or stealth games, avoid this one completely.

The game is quite plain and gets boring very fast.

There is nothing overly bad about this game, except that it is boring.  Between expeditions, the game gives you the option to spend discovered resources from previous expeditions to buy random items, rent-a-pet and improve your character. However, the process of expending these resources has little strategy or intrigue. Some people may like gambling via purchasing random items, but it simply leads to a cache of stored items for your character to choose from and turns from gambling to hoarding. Likewise, the linear progression of character advancement is dull, but a necessity in order to explore the planets: the grind certainly feels like a grind. The game has some humorous aspects to it in the form of your boss’ dialogue and the zany items. Also, the colour pallet for the planets’ are visually appealing, but the repetitive narrow paths connecting each location lends itself to a successfully repetitive strategy for dealing with the monsters and advancing throughout the planet. After quickly finishing the first of three planets in “story mode,” getting bored with the daily’s, and finding the second story planet equally as dull I decided to uninstall the game. If you enjoy grinding character advancement, bad humour, and rogue like explorations then Shattered Planet is the game for you.

Fun game that could have been so much more. It's a simple rougelike with an interesting theme, but sadly there's no substance to it or any meaningful gameplay choices. Mechanics are about as complex as "let the enemy move to you and therefore waste their turn", beyond that it's just a drawn-out game of numbers as you try to sustain through endless levels that don't really get any harder.
Problems:
-The pet AI is horrible and doesn't even seem inconsistent. I've died several times because my pet baited me to death, until I learned to just carry around 5 of them so I could let them occasionally die of their stupidity without also losing because of it. The pets will aggro and suicide on enemies you wanted to just walk past, or sit around doing nothing in the middle of a fight. The option to give them directions would cure half the frustrations of this game.
-There is basically no item progression. You'll go into your run with top tier equippment every time after the first couple runs, and then when you get to a certain area you'll pick up some slightly better equippment that always spawns on the ground in plain sight, every single run. I didn't even bother checking the shops because of how absurdely unlikely it is to find anything better than what you started the run with. Therefore when an enemy drops an equip item, you're pretty much always just going to toss it.
-The secondary items are hilariously unbalanced. There's a whole character built around using guns, but the only useful one is the teleport gun (which is an instant kill because of how easy it is to teleport things off the paths, has the lowest cooldown of guns, and I find it most every run). That's fun for a while, but gets dull once you have two of them and never actually have to fight anything again. The Shovel, the most basic item, seems completely useless until you realize that you can use it to quarantine the spreading time constraint mechanic on every single level. So we have those two, and everything else seems more or less pointless.
-Eventually the levelling system just stops being rewarding. Once you've unlocked the characters, it just gives you pieces of gear that you'e already seen and might even have handy, and which you can only use once.
-No endgame. Once you've pulled off 3 or 4 solid runs you can level up your character and just rampage through everything. The main game mode is endless, but it's more a challenge of attrition and there aren't any ultimate legendary mythril items to keep it fresh.
The good:
-The flavor text is hilarious.
-The turn-based format is the best-executed I've ever seen.
-The atmosphere is well done
Really, this game could have been amazing, it just needed to be balanced better and have more sustanence.

This game should be marked as "free to start" rather than free to play. It has in-app purchases that go up to $100 for diamonds that you will need to keep playing as you level up. Why do you need them? Because the amount of time needed for actions rises sharply and after even half an hour of play time it becomes tedious to wait. You do slowly earn diamonds for achievements, but they will never be enough to make the game more enjoyable.
You can reset your game to earn "speed boosts" that very slightly increase the time needed for each action. You will have to do this many, many times in order to make the game play at a reasonable pace.
The entire design of the game screams "mobile game friendly" - this is the type of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ knock off app you pick up because the Play Store or App Store pushed it as an Editor's Choice. You open it a few times a day while in the bathroom or waiting around and play for a couple minutes then move on with your life. It has no long term interest unless you just like clicking the same button over and over. *
* If you DO like clicking the same button over and over and waiting on a reward, pick up DLC Quest and do the Grindstone part without unlocking the DLC for it to speed it up. That would be on par with this.
Now on to the rest of the game:
The music is simple and makes for decent background music if you like generic anime soundtracks. The graphics are basic and offer nothing special. It looks like all the other generic mobile games out there and offers nothing unique. Yes I realize this is a game on PC but it still looks like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile game.
Most all of your game play will be clicking back and forth between characters or screens every few seconds so you can click the next action. There is minimal payoff for your actions other than repetitive generic dialog from the characters.
The first character you meet is a ♥♥♥♥♥ who doesn't really like you but fear not! All you have to do to win her heart is spend a ton of time and money apologizing to her and she's bound to let you peek at her panties!
The other characters you meet so far have been about as deep as a mud puddle. They spout their stereotypes, you spend tons of time, money, and probably diamonds on them in the hopes they might (begrudgingly) go on a date with you. Despite the very positive reviews on this game, you're better off spending your time doing anything else. Pick your nose, pluck arm hairs, learn to paint with your feet. This is actually a hard decision for me since I have mixed feelings on the game.  This game tries to be like a combination of L.A. Noire with the interrogations and Sam & Max with the humor, and the two main characters in some ways, but most of the humor felt flat to me, and that was the one reason I was curious in it.  Most of the good humor is usually from seeing the sights, like (SPOILER ALERT!!!) the hazmet team taking pictures at the crime scene, Clown Bot breaking the fourth wall, or just talking about "the player," with everybody else calling him "broken," and some of the outrageous interogation animations, which the bartender is probably my favorite, but other than that, most of the jokes just weren't working for me, so I don't see what the audience thinks is funny, and yes, there is, in fact, an audience watching the whole thing.  I though this was game, not a bad sitcom.  As far as the story goes, on the other hand, it's actually decent once you get past the bad jokes.  Heck, I even kept thinking and second guessing on some parts of the game.  I haven't seen too many bugs, but it's best to be careful with this game, as there was one part where, no matter what I did, I can't control the character, though exiting out of the game and restarting it did the trick.  There's also a mini-game where, and I'm not making this up at all, Clown Bot does stand up comedy.  If you tell the joke right, you can catch the flowers the audience throws to you for extra points, but tell the joke poorly or freeze on stage, you have to dodge the tomatoes, or beer bottles, or toilets, or people flying towards you, so you won't lose points.  Ironically, since some of the jokes are still kinda stale, this mode is actually pretty hilarious just seeing what people will throw at Clown Bot.  So in the end of the day, I would give this game a 3 out of 5, that is if Steam did a star system other than a recommendation "Yes-or-No" system, but for now, I wouldn't get this game expecting a good laugh, like I did.

Detective Case and Clown Bot is a Point-and-Click adventure game made in modern times, but with the aim of bringing back the nostalgia of an era since forgotten, complete even with pixelated graphics and a 256x192 resolution.
You take control of Detective Case, a slightly misogynistic failure of a detective, and Clown Bot, a sentient robot that is aware that it is in a video game (and will occasionally make references to this fact) who wants to be a clown. The aim of the game is to solve a recent murder and any other mysteries that appear as you make your way through the game.
On paper this game sounds like it has potential, while Point-and-Click games are generally lacking in compelling gameplay or stellar graphics, they often make up for it with good storytelling, witty humour, or even sometimes heart wrenching tragedy or drama. However Detective Case and Clown Bot fails on all these fronts, the murder is incredibly straightforward to solve and the humour isn’t so much delivered as forced down your throat to the point of becoming painful. With only 5 areas in the game you find yourself backtracking to and fro, picking up objects that will later be used as evidence and interviewing potential culprits.
The interviews are really the core of this game’s “gameplay”, you ask each suspect 3 questions, linking a speech option to an item in your inventory until they crack and spill the beans. However there are no repercussions for failing an interview other than the annoyance of restarting it, something you will find yourself doing repeatedly as the speech options given to you are all phrased incredibly similarly, but only one is the correct question to ask.
In short the game has a linear, predictable plot, uninteresting characters, forced humour, tiresome gameplay, and a world too small to “explore”. Perhaps the only saving grace of this game is that achievement ♥♥♥♥♥s- cough cough –I mean achievement hunters like myself can find solace in being able to perfect the game in under 5 hours.
If you’re looking for a Point-and-Click adventure game why not rather look into Telltale Game’s modern rendition on the genre like the Walking Dead Season One and Two and Game of Thrones, or just Google “Good old Point-and-Click adventure games”, look I’ll even do it for you:
, just don’t waste $7 on this game, you’ll regret it.

I liked Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and I was expecting to enjoy this game as well.
Despite the rather mixed reviews I decided to buy this game, hoping that the issues surrounding the game's launch were finally fixed.
Boy was I wrong.
At the time of writing this, I have requested a refund. The FIRST refund I ever requested here on steam, and I've bought a couple of *really* ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games over the course of the years.
The reasons for my refund request are a multitude of technical issues - and just plain bad design - including, but not limited to:
- Terrible mouse reactivity; the in-game setting for mouse sensitivity actually controls mouse acceleration. It is not in a playable or enjoyable state, no matter the setting. It still has not been adressed by the developers, and I sincerely doubt it ever will.
- Terrible optimization in DX11 and DX12, even after several months and patches. Playing on the following system @1080p/60Hz either results in less than desirable image quality (i.e. due to temporal AA and sharpening, which results in an image that is grainy, over-sharpened and blurry at the same time!) or low frame rates (<35 fps) and even higher mouse lag (i.e. when using MSAA):
Windows 10 64-bit
Intel Core i7-6700K @4.5GHz
16 GB RAM
GeForce GTX1060 6GB
- Some keys on the keyboard can not be bound, i.e. the backspace key (as it is used to delete keybinds). This is a PC game, in 2016; non-bindable keys are NOT acceptable.
Truth be told, after playing through Rise of the Tomb Raider, which is a fantastic Sequel to TR2013, I expected Square Enix to release a worthy sequel to DX:HR. Unfortunately all we got was a complete mess.

DLC quest is an indie title developed by GoingLoud which uses satire based around the current state of video game development and the monetisation of additional or in some cases "cut" content for titles.
Gameplay
- 2D sidescrolling platformer similar to titles such as Super Mario Bros.
- New abilities are unlocked by purchasing DLC (done with in-game money).
Visuals
- 16-bit retro style graphics
- Colourful landscapes
Sound
- Retro soundtrack which fits well with the titles art style
- Varied music which changes as the player progresses to each new area
Extras
- Steam version comes with additional campaign "Live Freemium or Die"
- 20 awardments to unlock in-game and 22 steam achievements to unlock (20 based on the awardments, 2 hidden)
Overall, the title is fun to play and contains a lot of references which many members of the gaming culture will understand. Both campaigns are short in length and can be completed within one sitting but if you want to play a cheap fun little title then I recommend you give DLC quest a go.

PROS:
- Campaigns now have more varied non-stronghold missions than the simple ol' Annihilate condition.
- Dark Eldar and Sisters of Battle are rather interesting new factions to play, both with rather unique mechanics.
- Strongholds in campaign are harder than ever, with a different difficulty focus - rather than having an initial difficult wave and becoming gradually easier, difficulty of waves ramps up over the course of the game.
CONS
- Aerial units for the older factions were very clearly added as a promotion for Games Workshop itself, which was releasing kits of flyers at the time; unfortunately, they add rather little to the game (thematically there were far less iconic than many other potential options), are poorly adapted for the game engine (mechanics-wise, they are simply units which hover, and are rendered as such) and feel forced and limited in scope by the minimalistic single-aircraft-added-to-each-faction theme. (Flyers should have been in development longer to avoid them being "floating vehicles", and several should've been added for them to make any impact. Soulstorm was released before the rise of DLC as a common occurence, but a few aircraft added by patch would've gone a long way.)
- Campaign is more mind-numbingly tedious than ever, with the decision to scrap persistent buildings between games removing what little element of meta-strategy exists and the Ancient Gate mechanic essentially reducing campaign difficulty outside of Strongholds.
- The campaign plot is convoluted (cut off by a Warp Storm which allows every race bar Tyranids into the system? Huh?) and the characters rather dislikeable.
VERDICT:
Play it for Skirmish/Multiplayer (previous expansions and mods theretofor lacked Dark Eldar entirely!) or use it for mods (Inquisition Daemonhunt surpasses the base game in quality of models and design, and the Witch Hunters Mod puts the Sisters of Battle of Soulstorm to shame!), but don't expect an exceptionally engaging campaign mode or major gameplay changes. The campaign system of Dark Crusade was novel then, the unit additions to previous factions satisfactory and the Tau Empire and Necrons factions quirky enough; but for Soulstorm, the novelty had worn out, and the result lacked the lustre of previous entries. The game is no worse than previous entries (albeit no better), but its value is subjective based on how much you value the meagre gameplay changes and modestly great new factions.
That said, it's definitely still over-the-top to say the least, and skirmish or multiplayer with mods is still crazy.

Going in blind only to find one of the most unique roguelikes I've ever played.
Story: 7.5/10
The story is interesting and new for a roguelike. You are a clone generated on some sort of space station. You teleport to planets on a quest to scour and repair these
. You also have an alien scientist that helps you learn and explain the situation along the way -- I don't want to ruin any of it. xD
Gameplay: 8/10
All you need is a mouse to control this game, and it's incredibly functional. There are multiple types of classes to choose from, at first just the Renegade and the Assassin. Each planet you travel to has increasing "distances" or levels, that each get harder, to collect items, scrap, and crystals. You mostly use scrap to level up stats and crystals to craft or buy items. You can also recycle items for scrap. You move around and attack by clicking, with only two equipment slots -- a helmet and a weapon. Your inventory can consist of health items, projectiles and potions.
Graphics: 8/10
An appetizing take on graphics choice for this type of isometric view. It's very reminiscent of something like Shadowrun, but a little more cartoonish. The different sprites for customizing your clone is very dynamic as well. Definitely a unique style.
Sound: 6.5/10
The atmospheric music fits the game well, but for a game with a pace like this I'd expect a little more action in the soundtrack. Still the mood of the music is so very appropriate for the melancholy of the worlds you're immersed in. The sound effects are a little repetitive and could be expanded upon as well.
Overall: 7.5/10
A solid game with
of replayability and character customization. For any fan of roguelikes this is definitely a title you need to pick up and take a look at for a slightly different take on the genre. I think with maybe a few DLC releases, possibly some new music and weapons/armor/worlds, this could become a definite standout game. You won't be disappointed in this title.

Very nice rogue-like game where exploration is fun and rewarding above all else.  Adorable art style and object references,  Smooth and interactive gameplay and UI, solid mechanics and RPG element, it is a very enjoyable game.
Shattered Planet's biggest strength and weakness is its progression system.  Between each run player can and should purchase permenant upgrades which increases the raw strength of the player.  This provides consistent progression after each run which can be very exciting.  However this also incentivise grinding to obtain more power in order to face tougher challenge instead of relying on luck and skill to overcome obstacles like a true rogue-like game.  Since the upgrades do not change the way you play, the game can become stale quickly.  Also the system imposes a cap on the game; you'll only play to purchase all upgrades and explore all of the contents.  The result is you receive a more finite experience than other rogue-like games, which can be a good thing for some players.
All that said, I would still recommend this game to just about anyone.

This game should be marked as "free to start" rather than free to play. It has in-app purchases that go up to $100 for diamonds that you will need to keep playing as you level up. Why do you need them? Because the amount of time needed for actions rises sharply and after even half an hour of play time it becomes tedious to wait. You do slowly earn diamonds for achievements, but they will never be enough to make the game more enjoyable.
You can reset your game to earn "speed boosts" that very slightly increase the time needed for each action. You will have to do this many, many times in order to make the game play at a reasonable pace.
The entire design of the game screams "mobile game friendly" - this is the type of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ knock off app you pick up because the Play Store or App Store pushed it as an Editor's Choice. You open it a few times a day while in the bathroom or waiting around and play for a couple minutes then move on with your life. It has no long term interest unless you just like clicking the same button over and over. *
* If you DO like clicking the same button over and over and waiting on a reward, pick up DLC Quest and do the Grindstone part without unlocking the DLC for it to speed it up. That would be on par with this.
Now on to the rest of the game:
The music is simple and makes for decent background music if you like generic anime soundtracks. The graphics are basic and offer nothing special. It looks like all the other generic mobile games out there and offers nothing unique. Yes I realize this is a game on PC but it still looks like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile game.
Most all of your game play will be clicking back and forth between characters or screens every few seconds so you can click the next action. There is minimal payoff for your actions other than repetitive generic dialog from the characters.
The first character you meet is a ♥♥♥♥♥ who doesn't really like you but fear not! All you have to do to win her heart is spend a ton of time and money apologizing to her and she's bound to let you peek at her panties!
The other characters you meet so far have been about as deep as a mud puddle. They spout their stereotypes, you spend tons of time, money, and probably diamonds on them in the hopes they might (begrudgingly) go on a date with you. If you somehow manage to impress them, they'll even comment on how they can't believe you showed them a good time and maybe let you see their panties.
Despite the very positive reviews on this game, you're better off spending your time doing anything else. Pick your nose, pluck arm hairs, learn to paint with your feet. The game is not worth the time sink unless you really want to find a way to automate playing it so that you can do something more meaningful. LOTRO can be complex to learn (I'm a minstrel and I play infrequently.) and the store can be daunting. I enjoyed meeting Tom Bombadil (and helping him with a few things) and participating in a few festivals with the Hobbits.
If you are looking for an MMO where you get obscenely powerful and faceroll all the content hit up something different. At first, and this was nearly a year ago, the game wasn't too bad. The grind was time consuming, but seemed fair. A few bugs cropped up from time to time but nothing that was knee-jerking. Now...
