I use a lot of complex sims (X-Plane, Orbiter, etc) and enjoy the challenges involved in system startup and flying.  However this game is really clunky and unpolished at the moment.  I watched tutorial videos and followed the very limited written Startup totorial, but could never actually get the ship running.  So I ran out of patience and will come back later after they get some more work done.
The game needs an auto-start mode.  For instance, the Boein 767 I purchaced for X-plane has every system realistically modeled, so I can do a button-by-button startup secquence just like the one in this game.  But if I want to work on flying the pattern and touch-and-gos, I can just auto start the damn thing and just go flying.  This is what this game BADLY needs.  The choice to do the startup yourself, or to step into a running ship.
Unfortunately a lot of software developers keep falling into this trap - of realeasing a game to "pre-alpha-still-in-developement" mode way too early.  You can release a game whenever you choose, but the consequences are lots of negative reviews.  My suggestion is - in the future - hold your game until it gets to the point it is playable before releasing it.

Featuring probably the highest amount of tech-y abbreviations ever used in a sim game, Rogue System is basically a DCS spaceship simulator that makes Elite: Dangerous look like an arcade game.
In terms of raw content Rogue System is still bare bones. While the promise is, there be much more content to come in the near future, so far we're dealing with only six tutorials, one single-player mission (target ring rescue), and sandbox mode. It's undeniable that Rogue System is an early bird even for Steam's Early Access.
However, all the main ship systems have already been implemented and the game is in a playable and rather polished state for what
there. The recent EVAS update even allows you to exit your ship and explore space in just your space suit. Ship combat is still absent however.
In terms of controls, the game works fine with mouse and keyboard alone. For immersion reasons, however, you can throw any hardware you might have at it—be it TrackIR, your HOTAS, pedals, etc, and the binding options are competent. I, for one, am completely fine with using my T16000M (on the left) in combination with keyboard and mouse (on the right).
The game has a long way to go still in terms of development, so don't expect even a half-finished product. I reckon what is there is worth getting at a reduced price at least (e.g., in a flash sale). Once the game is nearing completion, I do believe, though, that the regular price tag is fully justified.

If you're into simulations and space games, then this game is pure gold. It is early access, so there is not a lot of content yet. That being said, I already had loads of fun just working my way through the tutorials, and playing the 2 included missions (one of which is a sandbox mission that allows you to explore freely).
The developer clearly intends to give this game a realistic feel. All visible buttons actually do something relevant (some functionality is yet to be implemented), and the way that your ship's systems (inter)act feels very convincing. Even the most mundane tasks, such as starting the ship, communications, and powering down the ship are simply a fun and interesting experience, which really sets this game apart from any other space sim I've played.
Also, the game gives you some proper challenges. If you want to make your way from one planetary body to another without burning up all your fuel, you'll have to have (or develop) a basic understanding of orbital mechanics (this game is not like Elite Dangerous - another game I like very much - where you just point your ship at something and fly straight to it). So there is definitely a learning curve, and the sense of achievement that you feel when you manage make your way to antother station and dock makes it all worth it.
As I said, this game is early access, but if you're into serious simulation and space sims / sci-fi, then I can definitely recommend you to give Rogue System a go. You'll be supporting a very promising game.

This game is the space flight simulator that i was searching for.

Each ship system has been deeply thought and makes sense, and when you understand the way it works, you can find new means of working with it.
It's in alpha, for sure, so don't expect a lot of content; for now there are several tutorial, one mission (but a fairly hard one!) and a sandbox scenario to explore the system and practice piloting. I'm still amazed to see how long i spent on this game (40h) considering the content. I played less longer on a lot of finished game...
Moreover, the dev is deeply involved in his baby, and what he plans for the - not that far - future is really great.
Is it expensive? Yes, a bit. Is it overpriced? No. You have a stable and very deep space simulator, plus you help the dev - which is alone in this - to be able to work on it more faster and to recruit people. If it's still too expensive for you considering what it has to offer, keep at least an eye on it to see when it will fit your wishes and worth your money. As for me, i think that everyone who's fond of space should have it.

Warning: The game is supposed to run fine on Win 10 now, yet there are multiple instances in the game where the frame rate will just drop abysmally due to an AI issue (as far as I know the AI tries to locate you when you attack it and this can cause to these drops). Apparently this has always been the case. You can just google it. There are some "fixes" for it online, but none worked for me. This makes playing on anything but easy completely pointless in my opinion, since your main weapon requires precise aiming. It's also just not fun, so consider that before you purchase the game.
On to the actual review: Apart from the problem above the game runs absolutely fine and offers some of the best stuff the FPS genre has come up with. It completely sticks to the theme of you being inside an actual computer. That means that all the terminology and all the game's gimmicks have been adapted to fit that theme. For example you're collecting build points to improve yourself, the user. You need to aquire a certain number of build points to get to a new build version, i.e. a level up and so on. You'll also not use weapons and skills, but systems, which you can aquire in containers or from enemies. These also come in different release versions (alpha, beta, gold) and need to be slotted into your character, while the available slots change with each new level. There are systems for quieter walking, higher jumping, getting a zoom function, a sniper rifle, a "shotgun", etc. However, it is perfectly viable to just use your main weapon, the "disc" throughout the entire game. It is also the only weapon that does not consume energy and energy is important to download new systems, emails (only for fluff) and permissions, which you need to open doors, activate switches, etc. They've really made it feel like you're actually in that computer.
Other highlights are the level design, which is vastly different each time, and the pretty good music. Yes, the graphics are a bit outdated, but also kinda timeless. Fighting against the "Kernel" and his programs never gets old. The further you progress the more difficult the enemies become. There aren't a lot of them in total, but anti virus programs, corrupt programs and resource hoggers all fit the theme and all behave differently.
The game also features some light cycle passages, which are, frankly, unplayable due to the non-fixed camera. Controlling the camera with the mouse at such high speeds while making frequent turns and having your view obstructed by structures just makes these all but impossible. THANKFULLY you can skip these parts of the game after you've died about 3 times. The game will just nicely ask you. Which is great, since, you know, light cycling has nothing to do with an ego shooter anyway. It's great that they're in the game, but the implementation is really bad.
Apart from that I can't really say too much negative stuff about the game. Maybe the difficulty is a bit too high, even on easy, since enemies still do a ton of damage and the game is not really comparable to other ego shooters. Think about your main weapon as a slow moving projectile that returns to you when you hit something, but flies off into the nether if you miss, meaning you have to wait an eternity to get it back...Switching weapons also takes an eternity and like I said, using the same resource for weapon discharge as you need for progress in the game seems rather stupid.
The story, on the other hand, is nothing to write home about. It's bland and it's presented in an even blander way, but the setting at least makes up for it.
For 10 bucks, however, you'll easily get 10 hours of fun out of this old classic. And there's always discounts.

Tron 2.0, a game that serves as a sequel to the 80's movie "Tron".
No one expected a release like this, it's unique and a prime example of doing movie-based games right.
Story:
You take the role as Alan Bradley's son; Jet Bradley, to find your father after he's been abducted.
Jet gets unwillingly digitized and must fight his way through the digital world to find his father and escape back to the real world.
Gameplay:
An FPS with some simple RPG elements. Upgrade your stats, assign weapons, armor and utilities.
Make sure to spend every available stat point when you gain a build-level up.
There is a variety of enemies, but not more than four major types. Each have their distinctive colors and weaponry.
The levels might get confusing sometimes, but make sure to explore the levels and find as many upgrade notes (hexagonal thingies) as you can. There is also some platforming, but mostly only for exploration and useful abilities.
Your main weapon is the good ol' disc, costs no energy to use and can block enemy discs.
Then there is the rod, ball and mesh. All of these weapons have subweapons, which means they can transform into something completely different. For example, the rod has the "LOL", which turns a hugging-range tazer into a long-range sniper rifle. That is one of the most awesome things ever in video game history. Oh, by the way, there is light-cycle battles!
Audio:
Music is top notch for those who like electronic. Also, a little fun fact: in the combat music of Thorne's server (chapter: Alliance), there is a voice that speaks out pi as the music goes on. Just give it a closer listen!
Closure:
There is nothing much to say actually. I recommend watching the original Tron movie first to get an idea about the story. They pretty much hit the nail on the head, since this game feels more like an interactive movie than a generic FPS.
Give it a try if you're into the unusual shooters, into Tron or just like extremely colorful level design.
PS: the German version of this game has sometimes cheesy voice acting and some sounds are even missing.

It does provide a rich exposition of a world in crisis and Adam Jensen's role in it and I think the replay value is strong.
I'm surprised by how many♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off reviewers have logged more than 100 hours playing this game yet still not recommend it.
Would I recommend you buy this?

Do i also think that perhaps they could have delayed this by a year, extended the plot into more sophisticated avenues and introduce a stronger villain? Yes.
But I can also understand business interests by development studios. I understand producing plot driven single player games is not as lucrative as other game types like an MMO these days and that each project like this is a huge undertaking.

Mankind Divided is a serviceable sequel to Human Revolution, but it struggles from a number of flaws that I will just list here because I need to get this off my chest:
-The story is GARBAGE. I'm not going to spoil it, but to have this as a followup to Human Revolution is a massive disappointment. HR wasn't perfect either, but it had a compelling setting and some good moments. Mankind Divided however keeps introducing characters that are never fleshed out nor do they matter for the most part. The story is a hamfisted sequence of missions that don't feel like they make any sense. The whole premise of Aug/Natural segregation in society is nothing more than an excuse to keep the story going. And to top it all of, this game has probably one of the worst sequelbait endings I have ever seen. I will stop here because I'm just gonna keep going about how the narrative in this game is ♥♥♥♥ed.
-The gameplay has a lot of issues. Human Revolution already had terrible AI behavior and this game is no different. You're way too powerful in this game and your enemies too weak, so it becomes very easy to evade combat situations (or overcome them). Sneaking around areas still feels statisfying, but it leaves a bitter taste knowing that you could just shoot or tazer your way through all of the game without it feeling like a real challenge.
-A whole bunch of technical issues that hurt the presentation. While the graphics and especially the architecture look really nice, the animations are somehow worse than HR, complimented with the terrible voice acting you "love" in Deus Ex. The audio mixing in this game blows. If you have a 5.1 or 7.1 system, cutscenes or background noises will sometimes be louder than the characters talking so more often than not I had to turn on subtitles or else I would not have understood what was said. This is a real dampener to the experience. The soundtrack by Michael McCann sets the tone well as always but I couldn't get into it for said reasons.
I was really excited for this game and I actually had some fun playing through this. But because of the reasons I listed above and ESPECIALLY that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ending I honestly can't recommend this game. Not even to Deus Ex fans because the story and characters are not worth investing 20-30 hours into this game. It's an okay stealth action game but nothing else. Human Revolution in 2011 atleast felt refreshing, but it seems like Eidos Montreal didn't go with the times because aside from better graphics, this was a step backwards in almost all the other categories.
On top of that they hit you over the head with stupid microtransactions, ♥♥♥♥ Square Enix.

I rarely play MMOs anymore, so I will avoid talking about combat and such in this review. Instead, I will focus on other elements of the game.
So, congrats: you've just found the portal to Middle-earth. LOTRO does a wonderful job recreating the world. Despite the graphics, I still had loads of fun exploring whenever I wasn't off killing orcs. Some places, like Lothlorien, are gorgeous and breathtaking. Others, like Angmar, manage to get under your skin and make you feel just a tiny bit repulsed. The atmospheres of each region are wonderfully conveyed.
Tolkien gave us a fleshed-out world, and instead of drastically changing the lore, LOTRO adds onto it. Granted, the LOTRO-created lore is plausible within Middle-earth, so I'm usually content to let it slide. As an added plus, a lot of it is interesting!
I haven't been able to get far into the main storyline (nearly through with Volume 2), but I can vouch that it's engaging. While the Fellowship is off doing their own thing, your character is tasked with helping the Free Peoples of Middle-earth. Side quests are the usual fetch/kill quests, so nothing really notable there. You can choose to run around in groups of people (appropriately named "fellowships") or just go solo.
And that leads to what I reckon is my only complaint. It's not really a free game. You have to buy quest packs for some regions, so it's a lot harder to level up quickly when you've run out of things to do solo and don't have money to spend. That's how I got bored.
Servers are usually populated with a fair amount of people, with most hanging out on the roleplaying servers. Something that made LOTRO really stand out for me was the kind community. I've met a large variety of players ranging from high schoolers to parents. Many offered to help me out whenever I needed it. There will be the rare troll in the chat, but you can simply ignore them. Everyone's there to have fun and nerd out over Tolkien's works.
If you're a major fan of Middle-earth and don't mind some tweaks here and there, I recommend this game. 7/10.

Any fan of Lord of the Rings--casual or otherwise--will enjoy this game immensely. Every server is still highly populated (although some areas may seem barren because really, who wants to spend all day in an area that has litterally one building for miles?) and filled with people of all ages. I've met high school freshman and college graduates. The people playing this game are extremely nice and mature. I've only had two encounters with genuinely mean people and I never had to deal with them alone even if I was playing alone.
There are lots of quests to do solo and lots to do in groups as little as 2 and as big as 8. There's also a mode where more than one fellowship can play together or somehing I'm pretty sure but I have yet to hit the appropriate level so I can't confirm. If none of your friends wan to play with you worry not! Most everyone is approachable and everyone has common ground. Unlike WoW or GW2 where you could start playing not knowing if you'll ever care about the lore, everyone on LOTRO likes LOTR. Some prefer the books, others prefer the movies, but you all have that common ground.
There are RP servers but if you don't only want to roleplay, there are an abdundance of roleplayers running around on the normal servers to satisfy your urges when you get them.
Gameplay itself is also fun. I wouldn't say it's the most outstanding thing in the entire world. You'll find similar mechanics in other MMOs and it's not any more or less engaging than those other MMOs. Depending on your class you'll get to see some really cool animations, though.
The main storyline is also very engaging and very fun for fans of LOTR. I remember obsessing over it when I first started playing, haha.
So yeah 10/10 I do recommend.

This is coming from someone who never played (or heard of) the first Trine and played with a friend on the Medium difficulty. I’ve played it a bit in single player before doing that, and I wasn’t terribly impressed with it.
Trine 2 is basically a playable fairytale; it’s not a very interesting story, but it’s set in a very charming and magical world. The playable cast are the traditional Mage-Warrior-Thief combo, but they each are quite charming in their own way (like the world of Trine itself). Amadeus (the Mage) can create boxes and planks, Pontius (the Warrior) is a great fighter and can use his shield to both fly and protect himself and his allies, and Zoya (the Thief) is, quite refreshingly, an archer with lots of nifty tricks up her sleeves. All three are rather stereotypical: Amadeus is a smart coward scared of his wife, Pontius is a gluttonous stereotypical hero more concerned with food and saving princesses and Zoya is a shifty, greedy woman. Sadly, they don’t seem to really interact all that much during the game except during moments where the player has little (if any) control. It’s a shame because the personalities clash so much that it makes for some fairly amusing dialogue.
I can happily say that while this game is a sequel to Trine, it never feels like you missed anything. Sure, there are some little references to it (as far as I can tell, at least), but it’s a standalone story in its own right. Sure, it’s nothing special to begin with, but it’s refreshing to play a little fairytale instead of this big complex story with multiple plot twists. It took my friend and I about 8 hours to finish the main game (I’ll edit this when we do the DLC) and it never was too hard, though I would recommend playing on Classic and not Unlimited, as that really does force you to work together and not independently. However, I would also highly recommend playing the game with two players instead of three or one for reasons I’ll delve into later.
This is mainly a puzzle game where you have to find a way to go from point A to point B with all the tools given to you, such as boxes, pipes, fire, portals and more. However, there are a TON of hidden little nooks and crannies scattered throughout the game, and since it’s mainly EXP (because yes, there is a levelling system), it’s actually rewarding in a concrete way. There are also hidden paintings, which are basically concept art, and hidden poems, which are foreshadowing the story. Not necessary, but certainly fun to hunt down.
Notice how I said this is mainly a puzzle game. There are little combat breaks in the game that seem to separate puzzles, which is a welcome addition. However, they lead to a problem within the mechanics of the game and they’re why I can’t recommend playing this with three players (on Classic). To properly explain, however, I have to address the levelling system. It’s quite simple: pick up 50 hidden doohickeys and you level up, gaining a skill point for your account that can be used for either Amadeus, Pontius or Zoya. Amadeus will be able to create more objects, Pontius mainly gains combat abilities and Zoya gains different kinds of arrows that can assist in both utility and combat. As a result, Amadeus will not be very useful during combat, while Pontius and Zoya will be very useful (especially Pontius). The problem here is not quite Amadeus: it’s Pontius.
See, the bulk of the game is puzzle-based, so Pontius can’t really do much but stand around and wait for the others to clear the way to the next battle. Furthermore, his special ability (breaking rocks and wood) becomes obsolete as soon as Zoya gains explosive arrows, which are much more flexible since a lot of the hidden EXP bottles are hidden up high. Therefore, the player stuck with Pontius (in a 3P Classic situation) would be mostly useless and Amadeus finds himself helpless during battle (he can help, but not as much as the others). As a result, I found that playing with two players, one dedicated to Amadeus and one dedicated to Zoya, led with the most satisfying game experience as we could switch to Pontius whenever needed instead of having deadweight with us. We didn’t even need to get Pontius’ skills until Zoya (for me) and Amadeus (for my friend) had all their skills unlocked.
While the game is very, very forgiving (except, I’m guessing, on Hardcore), having lots of checkpoints that fully heal every character as often as you wish, there are still some annoyances (provided you don’t mind how forgiving the game is, which I didn’t). This mainly comes with the few ‘boss’ battles that appear throughout the game. They always take the same form: a big goblin with a massive club. Furthermore, this goblin kills anyone in a single hit and takes a fair bit to kill compared to other enemies, which is quite annoying. Also, I can’t imagine fighting the last boss in single player, though it’s a great fight where, once again, Pontius isn’t very useful.
Visually, the game is actually pretty stunning, being very colorful. Lots of shadows and lighting make the game ‘pop’ and seem alive. You can clearly see everything on the screen even when it’s dark, which I feel is crucial in a puzzle game as the main challenge shouldn’t be finding the pieces, but figuring out how they fit into one another. The music is also very pretty, being very soothing most of the time and kicking up the tempo and intensity when needed. However, none of the songs really stick in your head, instead blending into an immersive soundscape.
The whole game, being a playable fairytale, has a delightful cartoony feel to it, from the character designs to the story to the sounds and visual design. While the shallow combat seems a little tacked on and only created to give Pontius a purpose, the combat scenes are so short that it shouldn’t be counted as a huge negative.
I would highly recommend this game for 2P coop players and cautiously recommend it for 3P coop players and single players, as I feel the former would leave one player bored (assuming they play on Classic, as Unlimited is simply too easy as far as I’m concerned) and the latter feels like it’s missing something. The game isn’t too hard either, making it perfect for both casual and hardcore players, though it does seem more casual. Nevertheless, it’s a nice little game that’s definitely worth your time.
Do note, however, that the trailer (quite sadly) shows more of the DLC than the game itself. I’ll edit this when my friend and I get through the DLC, but know that it’s like a sequel (or a part 2) to the game; Trine 2 itself has 13 chapters and the DLC adds 7, to give you an idea. Who knows, maybe my complaints are fixed in the DLC?

quick preliminary review -
Short - fun but potentially frustrating (due to strange controls and combos along with obvious unfairly over-powered characters) game that has excellent graphics and sound, and multiple game modes.
Note internet connection was fine no issues other than the obvious internet ping and your own computer graphics limitations.
Long -

No internet lag/connection problems (relatively speaking), multiple game modes along with King-of-the-Hill's, player matches, ranked matches, rooms etc.
Overall somewhat fun game but, - As Always for Nether-Realm Games -- > there are overpowered characters (usually bought..) who have incredibly superior movesets to the 'normal' types.
Typical 'spam' issue where people will start by picking okay (normal) characters, then as they get 'frustrated' (by you beating them) they inevitably pick the 'op' guy, and out comes the repetitive tactics out of desperation (and the increasing frustration level ensues..).  This is typical of NetherRealms past game injustice where some characters are 'okay', and you'll play people who lose with 'okay' characters then they get mad and start picking the 'op' guys, and of course start cheap-shotting you and winning.
This is very typical of NetherRealm games and relates to them being an Illuminati company and knowing how to create frustrating ego-driven scenarios that lead to anger and 'Wrath'.   (which has a corrupting 'demonic' effect on society..)
Graphics are amazing, on a 15 foot (that's right, feet, 8 feet high+14 foot wide) diagonal (projector) 'screen' there are no pixels or anything just deep rich visuals from beads of sweat to scratches on metal, it's a feast for the senses.
Sound is top-notch too very few games have such deep rich 'thuds' and 'cracks' as you pummel your opponents, sound is movie quality is this game and a real treat.
The variety of characters and stages allow you to play both at night in a 'dark' mood, but also there are lively characters and sunny stages for day-time play.  This is a bonus as it's a great game to have in the background throughout the day while working on other stuff, that's a huge plus for it.
Drawbacks include that extremely frustrating gameplay aspect where people pick the 'comeback op' character who has all over-the-top movesets, making it incredibly annoying to win consistenty then all the sudden start losing as players get desperate and pick cheap characters.
I'm on the line with the technical aspects of the gameplay as sometimes it can feel solid and rewarding, other times it feels totally way off base especially compared to almost any other fighting game.  I feel much of it has to do with the button-block dynamic that tends to 'drag' after blocking somehow leaving you open to more shots, which is incredibly annoying, frustrating and rather anger-inducing (lol).

Note I have a near-flawless blocking ratio in games like sf2 yet here it can seem incredibly difficult to simply block then hit someone back at times -- VERY, very frustrating.
Overall I -Would- recommend this game because at least it tries to be somewhat realistic (in the graphics etc), varied game modes and overall effort they put into trying to make a wholistic game experience.
Be aware that this is an 'addictive personality/frustration' type game, where the good satisfying feelings almost always come packed with the frustrating angry moments later - it's an adrenaline rush game and not good for relaxing or trying to stay positive (lol).
Overall it is what it is and in a world full of fruit-cakey anime fighters it's dark realistic tone alone makes it stand out from the crowd,
definitely worth a buy and if you have reason to hesitate get it on sale.

This game is going to be great for people who love detail and having to know the backend of the systems. I'm also very impressed with the dev communication with the community on the forums.  This is going to be a great game!

The best Tron game. Keeping to the old trippy neon virtual world shown in the classic Tron film but adding a new model of light cycle and new weapons. In this world you will fight against security programs, programs corrupted by a virus, users working for a rival corporation, and data worms which are technically viruses themselves. The disc has been updated with a newer and cooler design featuring the Triforce. A flying assistant runs you through the basic stuff but it is not a bit. It is a byte. Upgrades to your disc will give you different ways to handle each level. 0011000111/10 would digitize again.

Rating: 7/10
Overview: First Person Shooter/RPG
The Good:
+ It is highly recommended to use the Killer App Mod which increases resolution and widescreen support and makes the game playable on modern systems.
+ The visual aesthetics fit perfectly with the theme of the game and universe and despite being almost 15-year-old game, still holds up well.
+ The RPG mechanics are well done; Leveling up allows you to upgrade health, energy, weapon efficiency etc. You can also install perks (called subroutines) that grant bonuses like more damage, better defense etc. These perks can also be upgraded giving better stats.  You only have a limited amount of space to install them so you must pick and choose carefully. These perks can also become corrupted making them less effecting and requiring you to clean them.
+ A variety of unique weapons, some of the more powerful weapons requiring energy to use.
+ A very lengthy campaign that is held together by a good story
The Average:
+/- Certain mechanics are poorly explained in the beginning of the game
+/- Some levels have confusing level design and it isn’t always clear where you are supposed to go.
The Bad:
- Certain levels can be very frustrating
- Frustrating boss battles
Conclusion:
I knew nothing about this game going into it and I am pleasantry surprised how well this game holds up. A decent game for a FPS/RPG hybrid.

This ... game ... is ... awesome !!!
It's not the biggest open world sand box FPS. It took me around 11 hours to get everything, and it's much more linear than most. However it's fast pace actually helps to make it feel really intense and action packed; it never drags.
I typically hate things that try to be cheesy 80s retro (I love retro stuff, I just hate it when it's faked in a cheesy way), but this game actually pulls it off pretty damn well. It is funny, it is entertaining, and it doesn't push any jokes too far to the point where they just stop being funny. Most of all it's still an FPS to it's heart, not a comedy.
The only downsides is that it feels a bit sluggish compared to most FPS games, and the hard difficulty is not really that hard. There is also an upgrade which is super easy to get early on, high explosive rounds for the sniper rifle, which makes most of the game trivially easy. This is to the point where it removes some of the challenge (it would just be better if it was a tad harder to get).
But they are small gripes to an otherwise incredible FPS.

So back when MKX was in its glory days, I was watching a few live streams on the game and I fell in love with the combos. Back then fighting games didnt appeal to me because they were so damn hard to figure out but something about the combos in MKX made me fall in love with. So I decided to pick up the game which later got me into more fighting games (Injustice, Street Fighter, the rest of the MK francise) and I have loved it ever since. I regret not getting into the game earlier because now its dead and its being replaced by Injustice 2, which is sad because I love Mortal Kombat X and I recently decided to learn the mechanics more and become a great player. That being said my love for Mortal Kombat isn't all the great because while the game is fun I find it a bit boring at time doing the same thing over and over. When I first got the game I played the story which I loved and I decided to learn some characters but after a while it got dull and I stopped playing, mainly because once you finish the story there isn't much to do aside from Online (which I didn't bother with at the time seeing my skill level was pretty low), Towers (that get boring after a while), and unlocking items from the krypt (which requires grinding alot to get credits). I later decided to get back in the game after visiting the Razer store in San Francisco which still had a few people playing the game on the xbox one and I saw some better players hitting combos really well and I wanted to reach that skill level. In the end I keep coming back to this game to hone my skills and practice new combos but for a casual player this game might get a bit boring since the online community is dry apart from a few high skill players and there isnt much to do other then towers or grinding.  That said, this is a great game still and I'd highly recommend getting this game if you want to get into the fighting genre because this has, hands down, out of all the games I played, the best combo system.

The Mean Greens – Plastic Warfare reminds me a lot about Army Men back in the day. The concept, the graphics, sounds, and most importantly the maps make this game a childhood memory that has come back from the plastic graveyard. The graphics is using the Unreal 4 Engine, and then the attention to details on the army men, maps, and background are all done very well. The sounds and music fit the theme perfectly. The UI is simple and clean – ammo, objective status, health, etc. The gameplay is smooth and feels similar to the old CoD titles but with a 3rd person view.
You also have a variety of guns, but some of those guns are in need of a tweak (either buff or nerf). You can use the environment to eliminate your opponents. For an example, you can use the foosball to run someone over with it while making a score for your team. Another map has cars racing around and you can bait them (the enemy) onto the track and watch them get flown off the table.
Unfortunately, the game is multiplayer only and finding a game is pretty much slim to none. When I did manage to find a game, it was smooth and I didn’t notice any lag/disconnects. I’ve heard of some players doing special events or scheduled days to play this game so that way people can actually have a full-fledged match going on. Adding bots could help out the multiplayer scene. If someone is playing with bots and someone joins their game, they are then placed on the opposite team and they replace one of those bots. When someone else joins the game, then they join one of the teams and replaces a bot; etc.
An enjoyable game, but i'd like some proper mod support, bots, and a server list.

Straight to the point, get this game.
is a phenomenal product and is packed with entertainment value from its bountiful loot system to its nutty amount of community support. Most of my experience with it is solo, but my limited amount of co-op experience has been even more fun. I couldn't tell you a thing about the story but the gameplay is so smooth and so satisfying that I'm willing to overlook that.
is all about its gameplay. Destroying hordes of enemies, raking in ludicrous amounts of loot, constantly upgrading and changing your gear to fit your playstyle, talents on talents on talents to offer a wealth of different playstyles, and though it may lack depth it certainly has width to spare. There are so many items and so many different possible skill builds in this game that it's nigh unimaginable to even think of how long it would take one person to collect them all. Each class offers similar but different means of approaching the gameplay, and if that's not enough, there's a respectable array of mods for the game that add even more to an already incredible experience. There are some interface and gameplay shortcomings I was disappointed with, but I'm completely willing to ignore since I've yet to encounter an issue I've had with the game that can't be solved with a mod.
Quick and simple, this game has very little lore and story appeal from my experience. If that's your thing, stay away from this one. Though the worlds look and sound gorgeous, riding upon an endearingly mushy aesthetic, there isn't a lot of meat to them for players to gobble up.
If you're not familiar with the hack'n'slash, ARPG, whatever you wanna call it genre, then I would also mention that this is a great entry. It does a solid job of explaining itself, its difficulties are very fair, its classes aren't terribly convoluted, and the progression is extremely straightforward. For those well-acquainted to the genre,
offers a complete experience and there's really no reason to skip over it unless you can't get over the generous price tag.
All in all great game. It doesn't exactly break barriers on its own, but the mod support is magnificent and the game itself is still a stellar romp through a lovingly crafted world.

If you're looking for a hardcore space sim, there just isn't anything else like this available. The game is in very, very early stages right now, but I think it has a lot of potential. If you like the concept, have a few dollars to spare, and want to support development then I would encourage you to take a look. I've put a lot of time into the game (even if this isn't reflected by the steam hour count) and still haven't managed to successfully finish the sample mission, so it's been worth the investment for me at least.

Really like firing this game up to relax. There's not a lot to do in it yet. If you like systems management and clicking buttons, you can definitely get a few hours out of this already just learning the ship systems in detail, and then take another few hours trying to do the Ring Rescue mission and optimizing your results. You can also try your hand at orbital transfers, and if you want to visit all the major bodies you can add at least another two hours.
Beyond that, however, I think it also offers a kind of atmosphere that I've not seen in any other space game. The sound design is minimalistic, but very effective, and seeing a planet's surface rotate along below you through the pixelated view on your monitor (no windows on a military spaceship, obviously), while you yourself are also floating and spinning in your cockpit gives me a majestic feeling I've not had in any other space game.
Of course it'll not last long before my ship suddenly starts blaring warning noises at me as it's losing energy because I fried the FCS cores due to sloppy setup back at the station and I frantically get back in my pilot chair and start pushing random buttons in a futile attempt to do something - all I end up doing is jettisoning the entire fuel cure, putting the ship into an awfully fast spin and on the monitor I see the planet rushing by a few times per second. At least the annoying fault noise quickly stops as I run out of energy and everything turns dark and silent - just what I need to relax again.
It's a cool space flight sim but no updates have been done to this for months and I can't seem to find a devlog anywhere.

It's hard to justify putting $30 down on an early access title that fits in a small niche such as this one, but while I played my first couple hours I realized this niche was exactly what I was looking for.
I remembered a couple years ago I was playing KSP in a cockpit-only career, with modded in multi-function displays and exterior cameras aiding me. It was great, but I was itching to go deeper into the cockpit than that. Rogue System scratches that itch, it's KSP without the rocket building, just focused on you in the cockpit of a spaceship.
Or rather it's not, because it's going further than that! It's clear that the future of the game includes expanding the interior of the ship to contain mutliple compartments, and gameplay will apparently get much deeper than it is right now.
If you're into KSP, and into detailed flight sims, then you'll probably enjoy Rogue System.
This is the best starship simulation I have ever seen. Highly recommended for simulator freaks.

This game has a ton of potential, but as expected from a 0.2.x early access state, there is not much content.
What it currently has is a ship with a set of deeply interconnected systems, a great system of orbital mechanics, and vast potential. Learning the startup procedure and how to operate the ship systems was deeply satisfying. The tutorial missions do a good job of covering what you need to know to get the ship running, transfer bodies, and dock with stations. However, a previous understanding of orbital mechanics is probably required.
There is not much content to speak of yet, and I would catorgorize this as a toy where you play with a ship more than a game, as the game has not been added yet. But this isn't a knock on it, as the ship is really fun to play with.
I really look forward to wathcing this game grow, it has a great base to build on.
Lovers of KSP and Orbiter will love this game.

I've played it with a HOTAS, but it's not required and you can play the game with keyboard and mouse. Actually I switched to KB+M for more precise maneuvers.

-Immersive environment due to good sound and level design
-Fun main missions and side missions, everything feels condensed, no fillers like in other RPGs
Cons:
-Story and characters, has its moments but otherwise falls flat, really lacks the nuance of the previous games, you’d expect to encounter some sort of moral dillema when it comes to choices and the faction you choose to asssosciate yourself with but the choices were all easy for me in the end
-Game length is overall pretty short
-Bugs, glitches, crashes, performance issues and frame dips
-Lacks weapons for the non-lethal playstyle, would’ve preferred something more than a tranq rifle and a stun gun, especially since the tranq rifle is mostly useless due to how the levels were designed.

Loading screens vary from Jensen standing on a tube line to him walking down the tube line and messing about with his augmented arm. Overall I am divided on whether or not to recommend this game or not. There is little wrong with the game but the feeling of emptiness at the end left me with a void in my soul. There will be a sequel is what I got from this game. Blood Dragon takes Far Cry 3 back to the future with its 80's inspired retro futuristic mayhem. You're Sergeant Rex Colt, a Cyber Commando who has a simple mission...save the whole damn world.
The core Far Cry 3 gameplay is still here, but given new life as you sneak about enemy outposts stalking prey for a silent takedown, assassinating targets with a well placed arrow, sniping pilots out of helicopters or simply picking up the biggest gun you can find and going to town on enemy Cyborgs like some crazy 80's action flick - complete with ridiculous story line, cheesy dialogue, neon visuals, synth soundtrack and more explosions than you can shake something highly explosive at.
There is certainly more fun to be had for those that enjoy a more sandbox like environment as you almost always have options available for how you approach a given situation (the exception being a few missions that require you to kill a target with a specific weapon to succeed), whether you want to take things slow and stealthy or go in guns blazing the world is set up to allow for different playstyles.

The game doesn't take itself seriously, poking fun at things like tutorials and collection quests (although it still puts you through them, annoyingly), it even has a laugh with its loading screen tips. It's well aware its a game and can suit quick pick up and play action or longer play sessions as you clear out outposts, hunt wildlife or just cause on the fly chaos. One drawback is the number of enemies, in many cases there just seems to be too few that even the largest of outposts can be cleared in under a minute...but it is usually a fun minute!
If Far Cry 3 was a decent bottle of wine, Blood Dragon would be a few pints and a lot of shots. It may be a reduced game at a reduced price, but its not reduced the fun to be had. It's a more distilled Far Cry 3 experience that will suit both FPS fans that have yet to play Far Cry 3 and those that have, but want more of the same with some 80's flair on top.

A quiet, ambient, exploration platformer based in Tibetian theology. The graphics are bright, detailed, and colorful, similar in some ways to other pixel platformers, but has some nifty water effects I haven't seen in other games. Ignoring that, the game itself is a short explorative narrative where talking heads spout a line or two of Tibetian wisdom while you roam around the moutains. Snow and multi colored butterflies flitter downwards as you hear the wind pass chimes and mournful notes between rocks. The sound design is quite good, and the platforming is solid, although you can be hung up on geometry now and then.
The premise is simple: fine the tablets, reunite them with the appropriate shrine, visit the talking heads, and explore and absorb. Much of the game is getting from point A to point B, but it's the journey - the idle absorption between those points - that you are meant to entertain and merely enjoy, perhaps to think about a little.
Like other exploration games, it has little replayability, but it's a neat little game, however short it is. Like life in a way.
Enjoy it while you can.

An absolute classic, certainly a must-play for Tron fans.
This game perfectly builds upon the world established by the first film, and recreates the feel of the setting in a way you'd never have imagined possible for a game to do back in the days when the original Tron came out.
It takes the original world and builds upon it with themes from shows like Reboot, itself heavily inspired by Tron, to flesh out the world in so much more detail, and even goes so far as to establish long-standing concepts in the franchise going forward, from the new bikes being a precursor to what we saw in Tron Legacy, to establishing the sickly green colouration with broken edges for virus-infected programs which has persisted in the more recent (And sadly far less substantial) Tron: Evolution movie tie-in game. The plot for the film even borrowed from Tron 2.0 in several areas.
The game solidly utilises a lot of concepts which more first person titles have begun to adopt more and more in its storytelling and worldbuilding, and delivers things like emails, etc. in a way which perfectly makes them fit within the narrative flow and setting.
Its character progression system is very well realised, particularly with the concept of memory capacity of the system a given level is set within encouraging experimentation with builds, such as when you enter a PDA and are suddenly limited in just how many skills you can bring with you, due to its incredibly low hardware specs not being able to run some of your less optimised software.
The game is a core part of the Tron franchise, and sadly, like other great aspects like the animated classic Tron: Uprising, has often been woefully overlooked.
And it has Bruce Boxleitner.
Because of course it does.
It may not be Deus Ex, but if you're looking for a first person game with more than just shooting, graphics which still pass the test of time due to the visual style they went with ageing well, with gorgeous audio, gameplay which is absolutely solid, with some replay value in the potential builds you can go with, and a story and world which capture the essence of what Tron should be  which so wonderfully immerses you in the setting - this is definitely worth picking up.
But seriously, get it on GoG or something so you don't need to sort out the infinite crash loop on startup that it only has with Steam.

I played this game back when it was released after years of yearning for more TRON. It was all that I could ever hope for and more. It nails the aesthetic and feel of the movie while providing a visual upgrade, bringing the world of TRON into the new millennium.
A lot has changed since the 80s. We have the internet, PDAs are becoming obsolete and the old mainframe systems are being phased out. All of this is reflected in TRON 2.0, providing a believable backdrop for a sort-of-continuation of the original story.
While the story in this game is no longer considered canon, it's a much better sequel than the new movie. This will always be the true sequel in my eyes.
The gameplay is based on first person shooter conventions, but you have a lot of different tools at your disposal. In addition to the iconic disk, which can be used both at range and as a melee weapon, you have a host of typical projectile based weapons, variations of these and subroutines that grant you special abilities (perks).
The controls are sharp and responsive and help you feel grounded in the computerized world you inhabit. It controls just as well as any recent game I've played, if not better.
All in all, this game is a fantastic realization of the TRON universe in interactive form. It has tons of charm and nerdy references and details, plus a great story that absolutely stands up to the original.
If you're a fan of TRON, you have probably already played this game. If you haven't, you need to play this game.
If you aren't familiar with TRON, I highly recommend playing this game (and watching the original movie). In doing so you'll be treating yourself to quite the unique experience.

A cyber-punk knock-out, or, depending on your playstyle, a cyber-punk slaughtering. I chose the latter. As a game, Mankind Divided is marvelous at giving you bandwidth in playstyle; from pure stealth, assisted by a light refracting nano-cloaked layer to a bulldozing tank, protected by a carbon nano-weave armor, Mankind Divided is deftly designed to augment either playstyle with finesse.
While this is not a true open world game, but rather one that employs hub-zones that have levels (generally underground spaces, laboratories, etc) that fork off the main hubs, there is still a decent amount of open space to rummage through. Satisfactorily, this game is absolutely packed with detail, validating its smallish map relative to other modern games of this type, and also greatly rewarding those persistent enough to check every nook and cranny.
The mission structure, for the most part, is open-ended, with seldom direction hand-holding that has become prevalent in modern gaming. These mechanics nicely complement the intricate level of detail; mission structure asks you to pay attention to directions and, gasp, often require you to read a log, diary, etc, for further insight on what to do. But, even with an intelligently designed game world, it does occasionally suffer from extended back-tracking, particularly late in the game, when you are wrapping up various incidentals in the game world before going in to the final act. This aside, though, the game is paced quite well; striking a nice balance between character exposition and gameplay.
The gameplay is at its best by its own divergences; the game greatly encourages creativity and further rewards you for it. Gunplay, if you choose this route, feels great. With responsive combat and interesting weapons, plus the various Jensen-enhancements, gunplay is exhilarating as you weave between enemies, laying a wake of slaughter. Or, as mentioned, if you move silently, using stealth augments to knock out the enemies or slip past them, the experience is certainly different, but the results to the game’s conclusion may be vastly different. Choose wisely.
With such wonderful gameplay and world-design, if there is a complaint to leverage at Mankind Divided, it’s how terrible the lip-syncing is and that many of the character models look remarkably stiff – both potentially pulling you out of the games otherwise amazing experiences. These nitpicks are somewhat disappointing, especially when the game is considered against other large budget, high graphical fidelity games of 2016.
Now, Mankind Divided begs your time, but requires your attention. If you can give both, you’ll find the utmost satisfaction with this game.

Ive started a second playtrough, going for some more achievments, but after the second mission I dont want to play any more, because there are so many little lacks of gameplay, which are making the game somehow unenjoyable:
- Keyboard inputs arent recognized well, often a key must be pressend twice
- achievments like foxiest of the hounds are near impossible to get, due to a lot of problems/bugs
- going by stealth is a LOT harder then going for combat, especially if youre looking for items
- hacking sucks. Probability calculations of the game are totally wrong (15% detection chance would mean 15 out of 100, but Ive counted 50 out of 130 so far, reaching up to 78 out of 85 for the 60% nodes), and hacking gui is terrible, you cant see anything.
- graphic is very nice if you play on ultra settings with high-end GPU. But if you do not have a GTX1080, there arent much options for fast frame-rates. Reducing overall quality from ultra to low speeds up the fps by approx 50%... but image quality sucks. Most likely unplayable on my radeon cards
- where are the boss-fights? Only one boss in the entire game? wtf... saved tons of ammunition and upgraded all weapons only to find out, that there is a kill-switch for the final-boss. Never fired a round.
Good stuff, recommended!

I've played Rogue System since 0.2.01.07, and before that I was following the development for a year or so. Everyone has already summed it up pretty nicely: DCS in space. The developer is devoted and the development model minimizes the risk of a feature-creep. The game has a publisher and therefore is (minimally) funded, so this minimizes the risk of staying in the development-hell or being a vaporware.
If you want to purchase it because you want to actually play a game right now: don't. Right now it's not much more than a glorified tech demo. You can finish all the tutorials in a few hours. You can mess around in the "sandbox" mission and there's one extremely difficult rescue mission which puts everone's skills to the test, but sooner rather than later those who think there's tons of content right now will get disappointed.
However, the things which are in the sim are amazing! You just have to learn what every system does or you might "accidentally the whole ship" by disengaging superconductors while MTS is up & running, suddenly releasing several million degrees (at this point it doesn't matter if we use Kelvins, Celsius or Fahrenheit...) plasma is melting the rest of the systems. One accidental press of a button can do that to you. Darwinism is real.
Rogue System is going to make Space Sims Great Again. Screw arcade pew-pews meant for casual gamers, 500+ pages long manual, systems schematics and checklists are coming!

I like havoc space sims like Pulsar and RS feels like a more mature/serious version of it with a much more complex cockpit and flight physic. So if you like to push buttons and manually dock instead of using the auto pilot then thats the place to be. As you can see on various screenshots the cockpit seems quite funktional at this stage and looks decent. Same goes for stations etc. You cant expect highres textures and the hud looks like... ugh it needs work but it is enough to deliver a pilot feeling.
But don't ya think you hopp in and fly like hawkx in space! Think more about good old Moonbase Alpha and slow space travel like the cryo space travel of colonial marines in Alien. Currently i gave up to try flying because for me its not intuitive at all. I need to call Buzz Aldrin for some detailed briefing sessions / check lists to get the bird up and i will need some some time to get the docking done without scratching the paint. So its more like a i want and need to learn the game than just hopping in for some rounds arena commander.
So this is also part of the thumb down. If you expect a fast entry you might be disappointed. And if you want to make use of your ~2h refund option be aware you may have not seen much till you hit this deadline. Its a time consuming game - which might be also true for just getting a grip on the basics. (If you're not already a DCS hardcore pilot with self made cockpit at home) Its also in Sapce... so don't expect a fancy soundscape. I hope these things will come but currently the acoustic experience is limited.
But somehow i will not refund even that i know i might have to wait ages for updates to see hte full core game or even a finished game. I think the complex control of the cockpit will be a great feature combined with a multi crew - which is even further afar. But Elite didnt deliver like promised, Star Citizen is also not there... so why not trust Michael Juliano coding in his shed?!
The few things i've seen so far feel more like a space shuttle simulator - and yea it feels good despite being non intuitive for me. What i'm not so sure about is the combat aspect. Since i'm not sure if a space shuttle with a mounted gun might be a fancy fighter... Well its just being used to stuff like elite, wincommander and the like. Then combining war/fighting with such a detailed flight sim like RS is... Perhaps the game is just about that - freeing your mind for something new.
Of course for judging many aspects of the game i've seen and experienced not enough yet. But i think its still of value to drop some words to those who didn't find enough info about the game and who are not sure what they will get. And as often it's like you've just died and you see the gourgeous light at the end of the tunnel in the haven of games if your're a sim fan. But at haven's gate there's still bureaucracy and some nasty construction work going on and you can't tell yet if the elevator goes up or down.

Rogue System may be very early on in development but if you love or at least have ever dreamed about having your own (as close to reality as possible) spaceship that you take command of then this is for you and I encourage you to support the game.
So what's there?
Well as of this moment you have one ship, you can push all its buttons, fly around a small solar system, find and dock with small "stations" of sorts. It's a very detailed spaceship simulator with the potential (and developer vision) to be a true space sim a lot still needs to be done and I'm closing to saying it's a diamond in the rough but even as it is now it's still very well polished.
If you're the kind of person who'd happily sit and spend hours with truck sims, flight sims etc. then this is one you should add to your collection... if you like sci-fi and space of course :)

I've been following this since it's very early stages, long before Kickstarter, and I was always impressed by the simulation depth and all its details.
As others wrote before, it's not yet done, there is not that much to do in terms of missions. If you watch the early videos of the prototype -- which was more or less just meant as a proof of concept -- you will hopefully see the potential of Rogue System. If someone asks me about Rogue System, I give the standard answer: DCS in space, which is meant as a compliment and is in my opinion well suited to categorize the simulation and its target audience.
Sadly, it's just more or less Michael, the programmer, and the audio artist. But I'm absolutely willing to wait and support their efforts because of the very transparent communication to the community and the near perfect atmosphere. There might be games/simulations with better graphical quality or more content as of today, but I never felt that immersed and that alone, operating a tiny ship in a large universe, as in this simulation. It absolutely manages to transport a very special atmosphere, a feeling of being in space, handling some complex system.
Keep on Michael, thumbs up, fingers crossed!

The story exists purely a motivational device to send you around a house solving puzzles to break into safes. The graphics, voice acting, dialogue, and music are both inoffensive and do not deter from the main focus: the puzzles.
The puzzles are a good variety of really great logic-based problems: no random guessing, time limits, insta-death, etc. Some cannot be solved immediately, as you need a component, hint, or mapping, that is generated from another puzzle's solution, but after a while I began to recognize when that was the case.
Tip: Right click to open your inventory and to see a map of the mansion indicating unsolved puzzles.
I would NOT recommend this game to someone who hasn't tried their hand at logic/puzzle games before, as it would probably be a very frustrating experience - the hand-holding/hint system is essentially non-existent.

Turns out, it's a best HL2 mode in ages. Its good side includes:
1. Atmosphere of original game maybe overdone - genious light\shadow play, cool overall design, good use of original materials mostly. And even this you can double by using all the possibilities of customised Source engine.
2. Good findings, especially new gravity tool and simple, but fresh mechanic of hiding in unlit places.
3. QR codes, tablets, memorable gnome, hidden magnum - things to explore with enjoyment.
But there are some minor bad sides:
1. Tablet storytelling. 3 dimensions has a lot of interesting narrative techniques, but their potential haven't been used.
2. Game is too intensive, like an fruit extract, and that's why it's too short. HL2 had a good balance of calm and active gameplay. There you will meet two new outstanding mechanics, but you won't have enough time to get used to it - only a bunch of puzzles and final fight. It's not quiet easy to make your mod, that's right, but it feels like a row of testing cells. Need a place to walk through and explore between puzzles - maybe, that would be a good room for some plot events?
3. Strange end. Without spoilers, I will say, it was a bit unpredictable. You are running, fighting, everything - CLACK - and it's over. It's not about a shortness, but these dozens of cool stuff deserves better - a dot, an eplanation point - but not this comma on the end of line. Maybe, it's one of reasons it looks so short.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is an ambitious title in control, but unambitious in its execution. You control two characters with one controller, each analog stick controls a character, with one shoulder button assigned to them for contextual actions. This is a unique take on control, and is very much welcome. The story itself is run of the mill, but fits the control scheme and brings in some nice and creative storytelling.
The caveat is, the game has this particularly unique control scheme, but does not take it to any unique extremes. The gameplay is unique, but usually keeps it very simple. This is not inherently bad, and in fact, I believe it was the intent. It allows the game to be more of an "adventure", something that just engages the player through the execution of actions, rather than a "game". I personally would have liked to see more dynamic and complex puzzles with some of the mechanics the game introduces.
That being said, the game is quite good in most capacities. At a 3 hour playtime, I might be hesitant to buy it at full asking price, especially more than 3 years after its release date. Check it out!

I'm a sucker for these clicky freemium games.  I'm "that guy" who buys nothing and grinds all the way - or buys the "speed increase" item and grinds the rest.  This is a bit like a Newgrounds dating sim, without the nudity (or so I've read).  Art is great, plot is a cute twist on the normal dating sim, and the gameplay is simple to learn.
BALANCE ISSUES: The time requirements and item costs are VERY unrealistic - hope the devs fix this before final release.  One would need to spend $1000+ of real world money buying "diamonds" to advance in this game, or use a tool to cheat to access late-game content.
In a recent update, devs increased the speed multiplier max to 2400 - playing for about an hour can earn you 1x additional "prestige" to up the multiplier.  Even at max multiplier, it would take a VERY LONG TIME to grind job and skill levels - over a year to advance a skill?  YIKES!
Once the balance issues are fixed, this title will be a nice time-waster for those looking for a distraction.  Lonely neckbeards will approve of the art, the devs will make cash, and your mouse will need to be replaced from all the clicking on these poor gals!
I'll update when balance issues are fixed, but I can't recommend the game in its current state - reaching higher levels basically REQUIRES cheating at this point.

Trine 2 is a charming, beautiful 2D platforming & puzzle game.
You basically control a 3-in-1 hero, that you can switch whenever you need it (or when your current one died, for whatever reason). You may switch between a utility-type magician conjuring boxes and planks, lifting monsters or other interactable stuff, a rogue-like thief with an awesome grappling hook and a bow for ranged engagements, and a knight for melee fighting, blocking and devestation.
The game relies more on puzzles and art than combat, even though it has it's fair share of the latter, too. It's pretty easy on it's medium setting, but you can ramp up difficulty by playing on hard (+ hardcore, which makes checkpoints one-time revival points only).
I can definately reccommend this game (and the predecessor Trine) to every 2D platformer fan, who doesn't hate puzzles and timed jumping.

The mechanics and gun play are for the most part, good. But thats all there is to this game really.
At least from what I've played, the game is heavily in favor of the Germans to start off, its not like the Germans get tigers while the Americans are running around in gokarts, but its still pretty bad. In a 10 battle anylisis, I discovered that the Germans, even when place into an inferior position, will most likely be able to come back with ease. Since the maps switch the sides the teams start on, I was able to further confirm this as when the Americans were placed into an inferior position, they stood absolutely no chance of making a comeback. That was my experience at least.
Another issue I've discoverred is that the starting poits on the maps for each team tends to be one sided. One side always seems to have the advantage over the other. For example, on the Encounter Depot map, if your team starts on the southern starting point, you are pretty much guranteed to win, unless you are the Americans, in which then the Germans will on occasion be able to pull something off. Why is this? For other maps, I cannot say, but for the one listed in the example above, I can. In the Encounter Depot, the southern starting point is in a far superior position than the northern starting point. While both are roughly equal distance from the capture point, the southern starting point is closer to the side of the depot's building and the majority of its entrances. The building the cap point is in on this map is very hard to break into if the enemy team is in control of the building. The northern starting point really only has one point of entry, which is only aceessible through a courtyard on the Northern side of the depot. This courtyard adds extra distance between the building and northern starting point allowing the team that started on the southern starting pint to take ontrol of the building with little to no resistance. On top of that, the courtyard creates a chokepoint in itself that is a struggle to control from the northern point. The east and west entrances to the deopt are essentially irrelevant and serve mainly as firing posts for the team that is in control of the building. The southern starting pint is also in such a postiton that makes it so the team on the southern starting point can easily outflank the team on the northern flank due to the deoots favorable orientation to the southern starting point. I can go further into detail, but i believe that this point has gotten across now.
The grind in this game is not as bad as people made it out to be which is a good thing, but then again, im only rank 2 so I'm not sure how much say I have when it comes to how grindy Heroes and Generals is. This in short, means, take this section as a grain of salt.
I have only 3.5 hours on recrd which isn't too much, but the patterns in gameplay were easily picked up in that time frame in my opinion. These are just my experiences in it, and it is entirely possible that I just got really bad luck, but the evidence against that, is, in my opinion, substantial

This action, I believe should take the form of rebalancing the Germans and the Americans to be 50/50, and while maybe not a total rework of the maps, heavy revisons are needed for them. Examles inculed maybe moving the Encounter Deopt staring pints to the east and west instead of north and south. This game, being a World War II game, could also benefit from some historical battles as well.

There’s a lot to be impressed by in The Mean Greens; Plastic Warfare. This thought began to occur to me when, after a good 15 to 20 minutes of waiting in the multiplayer lobby with no other players in sight, I began to realise how perfectly cheesy the music playing in the background was. It’s a delightful medley, one perfectly suited to taking pride of place in any respectable escalator, even down to the way it’s instantly forgettable from the moment you walk away. As time went by and many more minutes passed without a soul to be seen, it’s perhaps the only thing that kept me sane in those intensely dark moments of loneliness.
There were other things that did a great job at maintaining my sanity, however. The colourful menu screens were also helpful; the perfect tease for the vibrancy and craziness I could expect to be thrown into, once I’d mastered the arcane magic required to summon people at will to actually play the game with me. It gave me the same pleasure as knowing there’s a cake waiting in the fridge for when you arrive home from work; that anticipation of knowing that there is something to look forward to in your future. The fact that your journey home takes 15 years and the fridge is permanently locked kind of puts a dampener on proceedings, but hey… At least you know there is the tiniest possibility of getting cake. Or actual gameplay. This metaphor might be getting a little confusing.
The unpredictability present in The Mean Greens was another fun factor that kept me on my toes, and not knowing what would happen when I tried to search for a match proved to be gripping stuff. I could end up actually finding a match (unlikely), find myself in yet another lobby, or even be met with a loading screen that looks like it's loading into a match, only to freeze and crash back to the main menu at a moment's notice.  It all proved to be incredibly uncertain and exciting, something that not many other games could offer in the same weird way. It wasn’t just trying to find a match which created such spontaneous moments, either. Imagine my surprise and delight when I tried to set the game to windowed mode, only for the screen resolution to completely mess up as a result. It created a situation where I was completely unable to click on anything, and was therefore required to force quit to desktop. I never knew what was around the next corner!
Persevere with this randomness for long enough, however, and with a little luck you might be placed into an actual match with a smattering of other desperate players – all of you finally free to play the game you’ve paid for. Unfortunately, this is where things kind of start to fall apart, because the gameplay just isn’t very fun. Take a good minute or so it to digest the poor quality soundtrack constantly on loop in the background, and then another minute to scour the map and find someone to shoot at, and you’ll soon realise that combat fails to provide any satisfaction.
For instance - shooting your gun doesn’t have any weight or sense of impact to it, making you feel as if you’re shooting marshmallows rather than bullets, and the simple task of knowing if you’re damaging someone or being damaged therefore becomes far more difficult than it has any right to be. Even getting a kill gives very little fanfare or rewards, therefore making all your efforts beforehand in taking the time to kill someone feel a little wasted. It’s disheartening, to say the least.
Each map being a different game mode is also a nice idea in theory, but for one reason or another simply doesn’t work when put into practice. There’s one mode that sees you capturing flags on a speeding toy train. This sounds exciting, but it fails to feel action packed in the slightest, due to the way every death puts you so far away from the action it can take upwards of a minute to actually get back to where you were.  Another mode presents almost precisely the opposite problem; you’re meant to float on rubber ducks to capture flags, but considering you can pretty much see and snipe anywhere from the spawn area (Up to and including the other team’s spawn), there’s really no incentive to ever move from your starting position. On it goes, map after map, the sparse amount of players only making games drag out their limited welcome even further. It’s enough to make you long for the lobby screen again.
With all sincerity, however, let me close off this review with an observation; there’s nothing wrong with ambition. Indeed, the developers of The Mean Greens should be commended for taking on the challenge of a multiplayer only shooter, especially when you consider how saturated the market is with them. The problem comes in the fact that I simply can’t help but feel that there should have been a moment where a healthy dose of realism was infused into proceedings. There should have been a realisation that this game, even with all best wishes, could have ended up as the barren wasteland that is has turned out to be. Measures such as the inclusion of bots in the future may not save this game or even make it somewhat appealing again, but at least they would create something that's remotely playable playable. As it stands, however, this isn’t something that will keep you entertained.

Alright, know that I have already watched this show twice, and my hours on record isn't representative. It is very easy to get spoiled about this show, so avoid other reviews if possible.
To address the most common problems with anime first, here is what the show doesn't do. The show doesn't do fan services, doesn't have dumb nosebleed scenes, doesn't have excessive slow-mo, no excessive flashback, and no filler episodes (except for one re-cap episode). It is a very normal show, and I would recommend it to anyone as a "first" anime, right after Hayao Miyazaki films.
Plot wise, there is no "beating the enemy into joining", and I feel like this disserves its own sentence. The fights are mostly uninterrupted, the story is easy to follow, and makes sense. There are no time jumps, no time travel plots, and no convoluted♥♥♥♥♥pulls. The characters don't enter monologues during fights, or spend multiple episodes screaming/in a speech. Lastly, no romance plot.
Oh, that fishing rod you see Gon (green cloths) holding? He doesn't use that past the first story arc, except once in the second story arc. Seriously, no bamboozle, he stops using it, and it's never seen again.
Now, ignore the last picture on the slide. She is a joke character that only appears for about 5 minutes. The show never gets inappropriate or awkward, except for the clown in picture 4, but that's not done for laughs. It's safe for work in that regard.
Now that that's out of the way, this show is not suitable for children. The first few episodes are easily G rated, with splotches of PG-13. With every season however, the show gets progressively darker. It builds up to it slowly, and you wouldn't even notice it if I didn't tell you about it. By the time we enter the fourth story arc (Yorknew city), the show start straining what it means to be "PG-13". However, it doesn't stop getting darker, easily surpassing PG-13 in the later story arcs. It becomes full-on  Game of Thrones, except you already know the real main characters.
All this being said, the show has some common tropes due to its age (1998). For example, the blond-haired boy (yes, I know) in picture 6 is (not spoiler): from a murdered clan, out for revenge, and has eyes that turn red when he's angry. Please note that this show is older than Naruto, so it's not a rip. Either way, all the characters are all well-written and unique in personalities, motivation, and abilities, even prototype Sasuke.
Now, you may have heard about Togiashi, or how the show is also known as Hiatus X Hiatus, but rest assured that the anime has a complete ending, and doesn't split from source material.
And one more thing, this is a slight spoiler, but it's nessisary. if you are uncomfortable with children being wounded, dismembered, or otherwise murdered on-screen, then don't watch.
