Okay, I want to preface my review by saying that I love The Lord of the Rings and just about everything involving Middle-Earth.
But, that said, I find myself questioning why I downloaded this game.
I can hear it now, the people clamoring to tell me that I just need to give it chance.  However, that won't be happening, and for one good reason: the game does not work on my computer.
A bit of information about my computer, since I know it is highly important to the working of the game:
-Windows 8.1
-AMD A8 2Ghz Processor
-4 GB RAM
This would seem to be enough to play the game.  This is certainly enough to play a game that is arguably more taxing, namely Star Trek Online, which runs smoothly with only a few hiccoughs when my Internet connection slows.
Now, for my review of the game.
*Gameplay: 0/10*
The Lord of the Rings Online, unlike Star Trek Online, does not run smoothly.  In fact, it barely runs at all.  After nearly three hours of downloading the game, I open it to discover another five hours of updates before I can play the game.  Once I open the game, I stare at a black screen for five minutes, waiting for something to happen.  Then, I am introduced to a cinematic cutscene with audio that is jerky and lags.  The video runs slowly, and I sit through another ten minutes of this.  I reach the character creation screen, and I finally have the game run smoothly.  There are no problems here.
My character created, I enter Middle-Earth, and then I walk away from my computer to take care of some pressing issues.  I come back just as the the load screen disappears and my character shows up in a small room with only one other person present, Elrond.  Just an FYI, I created an Elf Hunter.  It is a level 1, since this was about as far as I got in the game.  I try to approach the wise Elder, only to learn that my actions have a serious lag time of five seconds.  Anyone who plays a MMORPG can tell you that even one second can be the difference between surviving a battle and dying horribly at the end of a goblin spear.  But I persevere.
For another ten minutes, which is how long it takes me to reach the first door portal in the game.  I step through, and the game crashes.  Hard.  As in, I barely managed to get the Task Manager to open in order to End the game.
*Graphics: 6.5/10*
The graphics are not amazing, but they aren't terrible.  I really didn't get enough play time to determine much, but from what I did see, they earned an average score.
*Story: N/A*
I only played for a short time before I was done, so I can't even begin to guess what the story is about.  I caught something about a Dwarf and some artifact that belonged to some wraith or something... yeah, I've got no clue.
*Player Interactions: N/A*
With this being an MMORPG, or so I've heard, there should be player interaction at some point.  I never saw it, for the sole reason that I never got out of the tutorial.
*Final Verdict: 0.5/10*
tl;dr - I honestly want to play this game, but as it currently stands, I never will unless I find someone in the real world who has it and will deign to let me play for a couple of hours.

So, another Deus Ex. I was looking forward to this one for ages, but by the time it finally came out my excitement had fizzled. Good thing, too, because turns out it's a bit lacking. Don't get me wrong - it's still a good game. It's still Deus Ex. But it's missing something.
I think one big failure of this game was to set the whole thing in Prague. It just doesn't have the same kind of cyberpunk mystique of New York, Hong Kong or Hengsha. And it's not the fault of Prague as a city - it's the fault of the level designers. Dreamfall Chapters was also set in a futuristic Prague, but that looks and feels way more exciting. But perhaps the level designers were hemmed in by a storyline, which - barring the opening scene and final level - is inexplicably almost entirely set in one town. That's not the Deus Ex we know and love. Where are the black helicopters flying me all over the world? There's barely even a conspiracy - no betrayals, no suspense, no moral questioning - the bad guys are the bad guys are the bad guys. This is the most pedestrian Deus Ex yet, storywise.
Fortunately, there are side missions. And the side missions make the game. There are some awesome creepy cults and freaks and serial killers and AIs that evoke all the best parts of the original Deus Ex and Human Revolution. There aren't any stupid boss fights (well, except in the main mission, which we already established sucks). There is dark comedy, tragedy, seediness and sleaze hiding in the gaps, if you look for it. You can sneak around and hack stuff and stun people and yay. The game gives you way more power-ups than you could ever hope to use (i finished the game with 20+ unused praxis and tons of grenades and hacking softwares), but just ignore the built-in God mode and you will probably have a great time.
Quick word of warning if you have a slow hard disk or slow internet connection - changing areas has a load time of 10+ minutes on my machine, and whenever you quit the game (or it crashes) you won't be able to play it again for an hour or so while the savegames sync to Steam. Probably not a problem if you have an SSD and fast internet, but i do not.
Overall it's a fun game. It's worth the money. But it's definitely a step backwards from Human Revolution. I just hope Eidos Montreal get whoever wrote the side missions this time gets to write the main mission next time. Oh yeah, and lose Adam Jensen. He's a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥

Deus Ex Mankind Divided is as thoroughly deep and entertaining as it's predecessor, Human Revolution. The new augments, setting and theme does indeed reflect today's reports in a rise of xenophobia and intolerance, however I can't help but feel that Square Enix's claws dug into the developers and forced them to shorten the game for the prospects of a threequel.
The gameplay is fantastic and Michael McCann nails it with the techno cyberpunk soundtrack (see Splinter Cell Double Agent / Human Revolution) but the game is over too quickly. Replayability is at 100%, but the ending seems rushed.
I recommend you buy this game. But do not purchase the consumables (DLCs), they are a ONE TIME USE. Which is Square's fault, not the developers. You can play through one whole game and unlock 90% of the augmentations. Do not purchase Praxis Kits.
Also, avoid the Breach mode. Again, another Square Enix decision to implement a useless game mode into a game that is already entertaining enough without it.
I love the Deus Ex series, and while the same high quality standard is there for Mankind Divided, it is unfortunately over too soon.

Much like Metro Last Light, Trine 2 is a shining example of how to do a sequel. I loved the original game but found the balance between the 3 characters to be a little out of whack. Trine 2 managed to keep the characters essentially the same, but fully balanced their skills out via gameplay mechanics.
In the original game I’m fairly certain I used the thief 80-90% of my play time. For a game whose core mechanic is switching between 3 different heroes to solve different puzzles, this really takes away from the point of the design. Trine 2 introduces a physics based fluid system, steam and fire piping, much stronger AI, and a much better assortment of enemy variety. The result is that I’ve had to use each character almost equally to work my way through each level. I still default to the thief out of habit, but I frequently needed to utilize the others talents in very intuitive ways. For a game that is largely the same, this small change makes this sequel both a welcome revisit to the world and art style while making the gameplay feel highly polished, fresh and new.
Whether you played and enjoyed the original Trine or not, Trine 2 should definitely be on your radar. As a standalone title it is fantastic and as a sequel it’s even better.

Let me put it this way... no wait, ♥♥♥♥ that, you have to get this. First of all, it's absolutely immersive. The visuals and the soundtrack (and sound effects) are making the game INCREDIBLY immersive. Second of all, the story is beautiful. It could be made a movie. It's an epic fantasy adventure with a few plot twists and surprises, and LOTS of interesting creatures around. Third, the game's puzzles are p e r f e c t. They are neither too hard nor painfully obvious. You just need to look around for a few seconds every once in a while and the gameplay is still fluid af. And I wouldn't call it a puzzle game either, most of the "puzzles" only revolve around the game's unique mechanics anyway. The last thing I would like to mention is that you will most definitely feel amazing when you finish the game. Even if up to that point you weren't sure whether you like it or not, I can guarantee you that you will love the final part of the game (which is also visually, again, incredible).
In short.
Pros:
- Amazing visuals, best at the final part of the game
- Immersive sound effects
- Emotional and quality soundtrack (I can't stress how good it is)
- Not a single word you can understand, but a very rich and emotional story (IMPORTANT!)
- Reasonable length (4-5 hours of gameplay)
- Easy achievements (but best collected AFTER you finish the game so they don't distract you)
- Fantasy elements (contains all kinds of creatures)
- Unique gameplay mechanics
- Very fluid puzzles that are neither too complex nor painfully obvious and are barely noticable.
Cons:
- Quite expensive (although you can get it for $4 on sales)
- Short? (depending on what you want, I like them shorter) (I've said earlier, 4-5 hours)
Don't be prejudiced because, trust me, you WILL love it.

This is a rather unique game. There is no dialogue really, everything is in another language. The story is told through actions such as pointing, showing objects, nodding etc. The characters and locations are well designed and give a genuine fantasy setting which oozes history and lore. But this isn't really where the game excells, it's the control method and puzzles that shine the most. You control both characters in the story with individual controller sticks and triggers. It can get a little confusing, especially if the characters move across the screen and you get confused about which stick controls which character. That said, the puzzles require you to move each character quite precisely at times, rotating objects held at each end by the two brothers or pushing a lever one way whilst pulling it another. The puzzles aren't hard, they aren't really there to tax the mind but when combined with the control method, it can provide a fun little challenge of timing and precision. The game is a couple of hours long but it's very high quality. Perhaps wait for a sale if you want your money's worth in terms of time spent but if you're looking for a good story and neat little challenge, this is worth the asking price.

Normally when thinking about movie-licensed games, people tend to air on the side of caution. Several of said games are nothing more than cynical copy-paste gameplay cash-crabs to exploit the current movies hype and as predicted, these games are usually f"*king terrible.
Now, what happens when a resourceful and experienced developer gets their hands on an old franchise and attempt to revitalize it? "Why, such feat has never been accomplished!" I hear you cry.. But, what if I told you it had been already done? Almost 12-years ago in fact...
Personally I never owned the original release of TRON 2.0, but if I had the option I would have. This is a wonderful action experience faithful to its source-material, complete with hammy acting and generic plot.
For some reason I cannot help but to love the art-style of 2.0, maybe its that colourfull low-poly feel that everything has. Much like the old TRON film, (Which I have watched and find decent.) there is a great deal of flat-colors highlighted with crisp straight lines of contrasting neons and the way that is represented in the game is equally nice. The added transparency effects and other details including glow and lighting, faithfully augment the art-style.
However, I must not be blinded by the bug-light of pretty art-style, oh nonono... I must also talk about the gameplay, for this is an action-title. Therefore, talking to a length about it, is only logical..
Well, the action in TRON 2.0 is very similar to Monoliths Aliens vs Predator 2. (One of my personal favorites..) On the fact that most of the weapons feel the same, the disc, "rifle" and "shotgun" to be precise. Don't take this as a negative criticism, I in fact enjoyed the familiar feel that I got from the weapons and with that was quick to adapt to their pros and cons. The most notable difference between the two games is that TRON seems to encourage movement around the area, when AVP2 (most notable on the Marines side) is a very narrowed linear experience.
that freedom of movement is also seen in the levels, they are rather expansive for what they are and encourage exploration. However, in a very limited way. However, there seems to be only one way to approach the situations and with that narrow the players possibilities on engagement.
In a few instances, the narrow passages became very crowded from the attacking forces and I died a few times. However after moving around instead of sitting on my thumbs up my peripheral-port, I finally found a way around the encounter. However with some scripted events, these little annoyances mount up rather hastily.
In all, the action in 2.0 is very satisfying although a bit repetitive. Certain parts might appear impassable, but there are ways around it. But I'd still recommend to save the game at the start of every level, just in case something goes wrong or some valuable equipment is missing.
Is there anything else to talk about? I can't really talk about the plot, since I'm doing my best to avoid story spoilers for those who want it in their games. (Like me) But, let's just say if you want a... hmmh... DECENT sequel to the old TRON flick, you can give this one a look. It might not be the best, but it's still better than the borefest of EVOLUTION...
DEVOLUTION.. There, I managed to keep it in this far..
TRON 2.0 is an enjoyable little action title, even with its minor shortcomings. And manages to deliver a rather decent in-universe spin-off of TRON.
For those looking for a worthwhile action experience, that gives the movie-licensed games credit. Have a look at TRON 2.0.

It's been 25 years since John Madden crashed through the front cover of your video game like a moppy-haired Kool Aid Man. That's 25 years of digital touchdown celebrations and the Cleveland Browns making it to the pretend Superbowl, just like in their dreams that never come true. For an anniversary so important it warrants messing up a long-established naming scheme, you’d think EA Sports would do more to celebrate it than just put in some retrospective trivia in the loading screens. Unfortunately Madden NFL 25 is more of a run-of-the mill upgrade than a big anniversary edition, but it is still a great version. Madden NFL 25 makes a lot of small improvements that build on last year’s big Madden NFL 13 revamp to create one of the finest football gaming experiences available.
The differences aren’t huge, and hard to spot at a glance, because most are under the hood. Over a few games, though, it becomes apparent that Madden 25 doesn’t screw up as much. The Infinity Engine 2 physics got a lot of tweaking, and players look more realistic than ever in action. Each tackle feels and looks different, with players tumbling to the ground in myriad ways, but this year they do it without the crazy splaying legs and linebackers comically tripping over a downed receiver after a play. The cartoonish goofiness that took us out of the experience is gone, and Madden feels one step closer to replicating the look and feel of a real NFL broadcast.
The other noticeable enhancement to moment-to-moment play is a much better set of tools for the running game. Maneuvers like spins, dives, stiff arms, and hurdles have all been improved and expanded, making great running backs and tight ends more awesome to play with. If you’re playing with a superstar athlete like Adrian Peterson, you can use a new Precision Modifier to really amp up the moves – if a player's stat in, say, Hurdles, is high enough, he can leap greater bounds, jumping over diving defenders. It's tough to pull off, and can only be done with the superstar athletes, but it's so satisfying when it happens.
All of the modes from last year's game return, with some new tweaks that add another fun layer on top. Like in Madden NFL 13, each of 31 online players can decide if they want to play as a coach or as a single player (created, real, or legendary) in Connected Franchise. But now Franchise lets you play in Owner Mode, putting you in control of an entire team's staff, finances, and stadium. For the most part this is just a lot of metagame menus on top of Coach Mode, and deciding the price of hot dogs and jerseys isn’t the kind of thing that’s going to be long-term fun for most. But there is some cool stuff in here, most notably the ability to move teams to new cities. I was pleasantly surprised that when I decided to move my St. Louis Rams I was encouraged to pick Los Angeles, and when I did the mode's faux-Twitter stream mentioned the return of LA's prodigal sons. Owner Mode is a novelty to some extent, but it's a well done novelty, and adds a new way to play the already expansive Connected Franchise.
With its incremental but noticeable improvements, Madden NFL 25 is the best football game experience I've had to date. It shines on a technical level, but the real issue with the series is that other sports games have improved so much faster that Madden 25 looks and feels dated by comparison – fake Twitter streams and pre-game montages are already old news. It would be better if EA Sports did more that was new and interesting rather than bringing back features discarded in previous versions. But the real meat-and-potatoes gameplay is better than ever, and when it comes down to it, we’re here to play some damn football. Madden 25 brings it with bone-crunching intensity.

Rogue System is a hardcore space simulation, the best way to put it is DCS in space or ArmA for spacecraft. This style of game comes with a steep learning curve, but rewards players that take the time to understand the game. Rogue System has you pilot a ship with near unlimited access to the systems it has, you will balance cooling systems and manage power and feel like some kind of spacecraft god whilst doing so. For now, however, I'll talk about what the game is currently.
Well.. coming from a KSP and ArmA fan.. yes, the orbital mechanics are accurate and managing the ship is satisfying when you have the hang of it. All controls in the game are rebindable and I have no problem hooking up various controls to my X55 Hotas. But it is hard to think of more that the game has right now that is good. As it stands there are few missions to participate in with a sandbox *fly around and do whatever* being most of the story for now.
Not strictly speaking.. it's in a
early state which is another way of saying barely any missions, one work-in-progress ship and infrequent updates. Rogue System has solid foundations for a hardcore space sim but it'll be a
time in development before we see any kind of final release. Bugs are present and most of the game is still concept art. Which make it hard to get you to pay the £23 price tag.
At this stage most likely no for most people. Rogue System will become a great sim if it does what it says it will at the end of the road, but if you want to buy this game to enjoy a space sim. Wait untill it's finished, however, If you want to support the developer in their endevaours then feel free to purchase. I will personally be upvoting this game, as I feel that it has great potential given time.

I will just say this, if you like DCS, if you like Kerbal Space Program's adherence to realistic space physics and orbital mechanics, if you like Orbiter, then, this game is a good home for your virtual near future space flight fantasies.
Like most today, I am a cynic when it comes to all these seemingly unfinished E.Access games. However, last year I had the opportunity completely by dumb chance to tryout RogSys and it was and has been tremendous fun despite its early state.  So far the dev has been a very professional and open communicator with his customers/players/community. I believe he's been at this game for over 3 years and has not shown any sign of giving up, so I'm confident at the very least we'll see a playable proper campaign, if not more.
It's in very early stages so READ the duscussions and reviews, visit the forums and WATCH some videos of what it's like first.  A lot of the foundation work is in, but there isn't too much as of this writing in the typical "gameplay" sense as the dev is still obviously in very early access stages. Most of what you CAN do is:
- operate the Flying Fox support spaceship from full cold startup and shutdown, docking, managing systems etc.
- practice the tutorials,
- rescue a drone target ring,
- explore the solar system,
More gameplay features (eva, repairs) and missions to be added in upcoming updates.
Additional expansion modules will be feasible with multiplayer, multi-crew ships and freelancer style play, if we get more players to buy in and support the dev hire additional help.
The $30 price may be steep for its current state, but as with anything early, it is going to keep on updating and more goodies will be here eventually. Keep this one on your wishlist at the very least!

Note: I bought this from the website when it was released in the eAccess program (about 6 months ago?) I spent about 40 hours in it.
If you want realism, clickable cockpit controls, logical manuver methodologies, orbital mechaincs, in your space game - look no further. Docking manually in this sim feels like the great accomplishment it is. The cockpits remind me of a DCS study sim for a modern combat jet. This has the right to be called a simulation - There are many proceedures and contingences to memorize and perfect, and there is are few 'magic' sci-fi systems - it all seems plausable.
There is not a lot to do yet except run though the tutorials and practice docking, navagation and manuver in a limited system, but seeing the developers progress over the last period prior to Steam EA release, I believe he will deliver a great space sim.

It's basicly set up like a high quality flight simulator, but in space. Every button is clickable and serves a purpose, and if done in the wrong order will cause system failures. The orbital dynamics are spot on. The one ship (so far) is set up very well to learn on, and the tutorials are of good quality. There isn't much to do, but the syastem available is well done and is fun to just buzz around.  Definately looking forward to what gets added.
I would definately recomend this for anyone who love flight sims and space sims.

This game disappoints on almost every front. A spiritual sequel to the 1997 game Safecracker by Daydream Software, this game puts you in the shoes of a professional safecracker tasked with finding the will of a recently deceased oil baron hidden inside his mansion. Now, let's go over the standard review claptrap:
Graphics: Good-looking, but terribly bland. For a purported eccentric, this mansion is generic as hell apart from the occasional interesting bit, and it just puts me to sleep. Thumbs down.
Sound: Once again, the music is serviceable, but terribly generic. Half of it feels like it's trying to fit into a horror game, but this isn't even close to being a horror game. Thumbs down.
Puzzles: The game's strong point, but even then, it doesn't fail to disappoint. Half of the puzzles are painfully uninspired, and even those that are fairly interesting fail to provide a meaty challenge (apart from one that is just unreasonably annoying to go through) and are instead leave you with a fairly resounding "meh". And to add insult to injury, the 1997 Safecracker had more interesting puzzles. Thumbs down.
Plot: Yes, this game apparently feels its plot is important, and honestly, it's a joke. Way too little time is given to flesh the characters out, and in the end, the game expects us to make a decision based on our judgement of those characters we don't have a bloody clue about. Thumbs down.
Overall: A complete disappointment, outclassed on every front by its predecessor, and it comes along with technical problems to boot. Not recommended.

Another pleasant surprise in a bargain. I thought it would be a safe cracking simulation game, but in fact it is a nice collection of puzzles with pleasant graphics, a plot, and a British accented narrator. Similar concept as in The 7th Guest, only absolutely not spooky and without cinematics or lenghty animations in the puzzles. The graphics are pre-rendered, with a 360-degrees free look system which worked surprisingly well for me. The game is not without humour, solutions to puzzles are sometimes so unpredictable. None are sadistically difficult, but some require pen and paper to work them out. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys well designed puzzles. Although it is for Windows only, I play it on a Macbook Pro using Crossover.

Interesting, to say the least. Safecracker is a Point-n-Click style adventure game with a first-person perspective and 3D environment. You play as a professional safecracker hired to find the long-lost will of some guy who owns an oil rig. This game was released in late 2006 and the graphics are pretty stellar for it's time. Clean, sharp textures and smooth lighting. However, this isn't saying much as the majority of the game takes place inside an old Victorian manor. The puzzles are very interesting and require a wide variety of logic and situational awareness.  My only complaint is the somewhat steep learning curve for some of the puzzles. Once downloaded, I reinstalled the game, placed all of the files in to the Tron Folder in the Stream Library -> Common -> Tron 2.0 folder and unpacked / installed all of the programs in to the same folder.
Restart machine and the game has worked ever since.
I had forgoten how damned challenging this game was and how often you absolutely NEED to quick save... like every 3 seconds doesn't actually hurt. This is a game from an era when games were finished, tested and true to their source material and with some of the naration it utterly shows - Hey, they got the original Tron in to the game (Bruce Boxleitner) and it feels like he was enjoying the opportunity.

A very short and sweet Half-Life 2 mod that expands the classical gameplay by adding a few new features. Those include a modified Gravity Gun that shoots Combine Energy Balls which explode on contact with enemies, items or environment. You can utilize that explosion to propel yourself (rocket-jump) to reach otherwise unreachable places. Another interesting gameplay mechanic I liked is the use of darkness and light. Zombies and turrets can't see and attack you in darkness unless you shine a flashlight at them. Speaking of graphics the game's lighting was improved allowing a nicer contrast between light and darkness. There is some story that can be read on tiny papers but it is not that important. What is important is that you can smash Striders with those large shipping containers while jumping around with your Zero Point Energy Projector. It is also commendable that this mod was made by a single developer.
7.5/10

Honestly just don't get it. Really not worth it anymore. The single player is fun, but it gets repetitive quick, around the time Trevor gets to Los Santos. The switching mechanic is slow and unintuitive on keyboard and mouse. Not only that, but the game is frankly unoptimized, especially for how ugly the game looks (at least in my opinion). For reference, I have an i5 and MSI R9 390X. Not the best system, but still there shouldn't be a reason for this game to be playing at 30-50 FPS (yes, it is THAT inconsistent) on medium-high.
Now onto Multiplayer.
Holy balls are the character models ugly. Mind you, when GTA Online first got released, the character customization was even WORSE. People looked like a mix between a crack addicted Ork from Warhammer and Gollum. it was bad. Now, to their credit, it *is* better now, but it is still an excercise in patience trying to make your character even remotely attractive. I only put this first because character customization is a huge thing for me. I love spending time to make my character look awesome. It's almost impossible to do that here, with the combination of ugly character models, bad customization for the ugly character models, and ugly fashion choices. There aren't a whole lot of clothing options that I can really guarantee will look good on anyone (why do the fitted suit pants make your character's feet look freaking massive???). Overall, character customization is a HUGE minus.
Gameplay is...meh. Honestly unimpressed. I honestly think Ubisoft (even though they have their own gameplay issues...) mastered 3rd Person shooting. Ghost Reco: Wildlands and Watch_Dogs 2 have MUCH better shooting and movement mechanics compared to this, and Watch_Dogs 2 has, at least in my opinion, better driving than this game. But that stuff isn't the focus of the multiplayer, no.
The focus of the multiplayer is actually an MMO style grind.
Now, personally, I was never really into grinding. It just seemed tedious and boring to me. And this game proves no different. EVERYTHING is expensive. You get a car, a 2 car garage, a pistol, and the clothes on your back for free, but everything has else needs to be bought. This might sound easy, but mind you, the early game missions pay out maybe a couple grand. The less expensive houses (the next step up from your 2 car garage) are still around $35,000. That's 17 missions if you're lucky, and those missions take up to half an hour at a time. It's probably not going to be 17 missions though, seeing as you're probably going to be spending your money between missions, either on ammo, armor, or character customization.
Going back to the first point about character customization, I have a HUGE problem with character customization being tied to level. It seems like a really stupid decision. Why limit what I can make my character look like? I can understand making certain clothing more expensive so you can't get it right away, like making a 3 piece suit more expensive than sweatpants and a t-shirt, but the game doesn't do that--at least not with base game clothing.
No, the grind really comes to a head with the free DLC. The DLC adds a lot of kind of cool stuff! Like a CEO office, new houses (including mansions!), new cars and clothes, biker clubhouses and more! Too bad most of it is $1 million+. If you buy now, you are NOT going to be able to do that stuff, even though it adds a couple of gigs onto the already monstrous 50 gigabyte install. It's not like you're missing out on much anyway. The new clothing options are still ugly, the new cars are frankly underwhelming (even the ones with guns), and the CEO office, clubhouse, new garages, and now the bunker ONLY add new missions. Missions which get you more money. Which you inevitably use to buy an office/clubhouse/garage/bunker. Which you'll do more missions for. To get more money. And the cycle repeats. The missions aren't fun either. No, they're honestly quite boring, and worst of all, some are almost impossible without either a helping hand or a full crew. "Fun" for the whole family I guess.
So, you obviously want money becuase, really, those guns and cars *do* look *really* fun....so what do you do? Speaking from experience? Find a hacker. A lot of the hackers in GTA give you money and it's awesome. They're really the best part of the game and community because they let you bypass the slog that is the GTA Online experience. So let me start off by saying that this is a free game. So it really doesnt cost anything but your time to play this, and I think its worth the time. Also before I really start saying anything I would like to note that when you boot up the game the first thing you see is a message telling you to play the game in the dark for the proper experience, and honestly its right. Playing this in a dark room is really the way to go, preferrably at night; it really helps the atmosphere. Finally keep in mind this game is not very long. At all. So Transmission: Element 120. Its a Half-Life 2 mod and is set in the universe of Half-Life 2. There isnt much of a discernible story immediately as to how you, Gordon Freeman, got here but It really isnt a big deal as you are quickly tasked with finding a crowbar to advance past the starting area. Before I continue there are some gentle spoilers ahead; anyway quickly the first mechanic is introduced in that mechanical enemies and zombies cannot see in the dark. This is honestly a pretty cool mechanic but I found it wasnt used often. It was really just used twice back to back in the beginning. I dont really mind, the game itself like I said is really short so the dev probably couldnt fit many more parts like this in without sacrificing other parts so fairs fair. It does end up being used in a tense section where you must navigate a pit full of zombies in the dark in order to get to a pulley in the center so you can open the door out. It then leads to Gordon discovering the Element 120 of Transmissions Element 120. You discover a hidden rebel lab where they were testing with zero point energy and 'element 120' in which the result was an especially volatile variant of the gravity gun called the gravity concussion gun.
If you dont care about what it is then skip this part. Unlike the gravity gun which pulls stuff in and then punts it the concussion gun fires a pellet of dark energy that violently throws everything in the vicinity away from it on impact. This leads to the second major mechanic, shooting it at your feet and 'gravity jumping' up to high ledges. Additionally the gravity concussion gun can be used to kill groups of enemies with ease but the downside is that rather than using ammo it uses your suits energy, because your suit uses the energy to cancel out the radiation the weapon gives off.
Afterwards the game proceeds to an area where you have to fight hordes of zombies before leading into the final boss of the game, a strider battle in an old construction site. The strider battle was probably the weaker part of the game for me. Mostly because I ended up accidentally using up all my rockets and while the concussion gun looks like it damages the striders it really doesnt so I ended up spending way longer than I probably had to just killing them broken up by me checking every nook and cranny for rockets and health.
And thats it. The game then promptly fades to white and ends. Credits roll and back to main menu. Told you it was short. Ultimately you cant really complain about its length because while I finished it in around 98 minutes in my first playthrough and now Im clocking in at around 2 hours of play time with my second playthrough the dev clearly put a lot of work into it and is effectively giving it out for free on steam. For a free Half Life 2 mod this was a good game and I fully recommend it to anyone who's played and enjoyed Half Life 2.

is an immersive and atmospheric adventure, where two brothers go on an epic fairy tale journey to collect the waters from the Tree of Life so they could save their father.
In short terms, it delivers everything it is supposed to. It not only introduces themes such as companionship, brotherhood and loss, but also develops them beautifully.
You can play it with a friend or by yourself, since each brother requires only a thumbstick and an action button. You will never be able to solve a puzzle by leaving one of the kids behind, since each one of them have a different ability (the youngest can pass between narrow bars while the oldest can pull levers, or boost his brother to higher places). And even when you're playing alone and exercising your entire brain at once, you'll see how you can never leave one behind since he'll be important later.
The essence of the story might be simple, but its events are delightful. It is really rare to see a story telling so much using no words at all - well, they do speak, but their language is fictional and we end up understanding the whole thing from actions, gestures and expressions.
The scenario and soundtrack harmonize marvelously with what I said above. The game even offers you some benches where you are able to sit and just let your eyes and ears appreciate the whole thing. It's wonderful how even the darkest scenes, which depict suicide, a bloody war or a scary night among the wolves, can still be appreciated.
Talking about the scenario, its exploration will lead you to the achievements, which are seriously rewarding since you'll get a cutscene everytime you find one. Even though I wasn't able to get all of them on my first gameplay, I was more than happy to play through the chapters again only to discover what I had missed before.
If you're refusing to play this game just because you don't have anyone to play with you, since it has to be local, you should play it by yourself. You're missing
by not playing it.
Play it with a joystick! It would just be
without one. A simple one, using softwares you can easily find online, will do the job.
And I know that there are people that don't care about getting all of the achievements of a game, but I can assure you
. Don't worry too much about it on your first playthrough though, just make sure you come back later to experience what you left behind.
I was lucky enough to get it on a sale but it is amazing enough to get it at its full price, considering that it has provided me about 5 hours of gameplay. It is something I would love to play again in the future.

I'm recomending this game because I genuinely do think it's ok. However! I recieved the product on sale for $2.45. I do not think that this game is worth $15. While the imagery is interesting and the world and ideas are lovingly fansiful, I feel like this game fails in a lot of key areas. I still recomend it, because I think that people really should play it, but there are alot of things in it I don't care for.
Gameplay- While the idea of controlling two separate characters is interesting, the simplicity of most puzzles reveal how under utilized the feature is. What the obstacles in this game have in creativity, they lack severely in difficulty. While I certainly wouldn't advocate every game being brutal, I get weary of barriers to progress being so overwhelmingly simple as to not pose any challenge whatsoever. It bothered me because every puzzle felt like part of a tutoriel, a teaser for a more difficult area ahead that would require mastery of the skill. Brothers kind of does that, as the skills do get alot of use.... but, alas, it never feels gratifying upon using them because of the lack of difficulty. Raising the difficulty, in my eyes, would've redeemed everything else aboutt he game for me. (the rest of this is nitpicking.)
Story- Granted, I haven't seen the story in its entirety, and I do want to see the end, but so far, it's pretty ok. It's of course rather minimalist, as all of the characters speak a sort of simlish, but this works for what brothers is going for. The only thing that ruins it for me is, once again, the lack of difficulty. I have a lot of trouble getting connected to the characters and their plight because I'm halfway into the game and it feels like they just went on a short jog. The lack of challenge makes what could feel like an impressive, and at sometimes, opressive and dangerous world become a sort of boring slog. It really feels sometimes like you were lead by the hand through the world, and yet the story tries to act as if you've realy accomplished something. This dissonance ruins the story for me in some ways.
Bugs- There are alot fo bugs. This is a really minor nit-pick though, as it would not damper the game that much were the gameplay better. None of the bugs are that astonishing, but they're just kind of anoying because I already have trouble emersing myself in the story, (because of the reasons previously stated,) so it's really hard to look past it.
In short, do buy this game, as I think it's worthwhile, but at least attempt to wait for a sale. Better puzzles alone might make this worth their price. Otherwise, it's definately worth your time.

So you've successfully started up the A-10C in DCS and flew it around. Congratulations.
But what if...what if I told you that there is an A-10C
, cold and dark and ready for you to get it started? How does that make you feel?
If the answer is "excited", or at least "intrigued", then you've found the game for you.
Rogue System's ships are not quite like the A-10 yet, in fact what we have now is a support ship(with functional space claw, to boot!) and not a warship. But there are other two spaceships planned that are fighters and bombers, and who knows how much else if we get to the expansion modules.
The ships' system will be fully simulated, down to electrical buses breaking and leaving you with no power even though the reactor is still happily producing it. Orbital mechanics will be respected. Star systems will be to scale(yes, we do have time compression).
In short, this is sci-fi as hard as you can get without signing up as an astronaut.
Be advised this is still very much in its early phase. We get some basic tutorials, a test mission to save a space station from uncontrolled deorbiting, and a free flight scenario where we play with the ship in a single star system. Start it up correctly and head to another planet, or mess the systems up until it explodes, it's our call).
Eventually we'll have a full single-player campaign with three different ship types and multiple star systems. This is guaranteed. Then there are Elite-like freelancer, first person combat, and multiplayer expansions planned that will come if the game has enough success.
The best part? All of this is currently being developed by
(Michael Juliano), who has already done an amazing job. Think how better it can get once dedicated help can be hired!
So if any of this interests you, get this early release now. It's the best investment you can make :)

Do not get me wrong, the idea behind it was superb. I've always had a fascinating interest in philosopy, regardless of it's origins. I'd never had a chance to learn about Tebet Philosophy so I anticpated an eye opening of new found knowledge kind of experience.
As for the visual appeal? I mean come on. Pixles? Over done. I'm sorry but trying to be 8-bit or pixlated game has already been done, you might as well be a Toby Fox fanboy (or girl). In a generation where the gaming demagraphic is constantly changing and evolving, on ALL platforms, you can't stick to year old tactics and expect it to always work. But i guess that's why this is a FREE game.
Enough with the smaller details now on to the gameplay. In all of my years as a gamer, not once have i ever felt like i was wasting time in my life playing a videogame(Ironically). This game lasted me about 30 minutes but htat was because i was taking my time observing the game and all it's flaws if i were to find any. And find i did. For a game of these graphics there was a ton of lag. I can't tell you how many times I had fallen to lag trying to jump in a platformer game such as this.  My main problem is just how short this game is. This game could of been so much more. It felt like i was playing a demo of sorts and it just made me cringe. for those who remember the part with opening the giant door, i was expecting a journey ahead. Did i get one? nope. Instead I'm presented with an elevating path (Riveting. -.-) , that would lead me to a person I have to speak to that reminded me alot of Karma. Not sure thats Tebet but maybe thats just a nitpick. I was expecting exposition into the game, but instead i get a wel spoken, but small message, and boom. Game's over. Not even an hour of
Now despite this game's many flaws i did enjoy the philosiphical messages spreaded out across the one map we get to play in. (I'm assuming they were?) But to be honest, i didn't get enough for this to be considered what most call: "A masterpiece". I'm sorry to say that this game isn't even worthy of the "free" section of this store. In fact this game would find better success in minigame websites like
, and whatnot.
Message to the developers: You guys are clearly aspiring to be game designers, which is great and all, but this is isn't the way to go. Truth be told, a friend of mine whose finishing up his last year of highschool this year, is developing his first game, and getting to see it in the developing stages, the game already looks better than this and is probably longer too. And who knows, i might be wrong. you might add expansions to this game and this whole review would be all for nothing and invalid (for the most part.) Anyways your game is....sigh...it's meh.

Before going into details let me tell you this: I played Deus EX and I think it is one of the greatest game ever been created.
So, I suppose, it must be hell of a difficult job to make a sequel game to Deus Ex.
Let's just remember Invisible War!
But man! People from Eidios have done it!
Mankind Divided presents us a beautiful and believable not so distant story with  full of mature oriented themes.
As you can imagine, the more you proceed in Mankind Divided the more things get complicated.  Story becomes so awesome that there will be times that you really have to think hard to figure out  Who's screwing who.
There's no  starks rights and wrongs in this game. Every decisions you make might be wrong as well as right.
So this leaves you with burdensome emotional consequences. And this is awesome!
In terms of visuals this game shines! All those animations, city lights etc looks gorgeous!    I use  GTX 980Ti           with I7 4770 and 16 GB Ram and game runs without hiccup with ultra settings @4k.
When it comes to gameplay, Mankind Divided does not stop the amazing me in this department too. Everything is so smooth. From covering to shooting or from weapon upgrades to aug skills.
You do all this things and more effortlessly as if they are  your natural movements.
Also I have to add, as a rpg fan, Mankind Divided has the most interesting and vigorous sidequests I've ever seen in a rpg game.
Essentially, for anyone who likes Science Fiction, who likes mature themes in a game, Mankind Divided is a gem!
It is like a novel that you never want to finish because it is so elevating to read it.

Overall score of 6/10. Read below to find out why.
I've never really been a fan of F2P games. Most F2P MMOs tend to overdo or implement micro-transactions counter-intuitively or completely wrong (Rift being one of those exceptions). So I figured I'd give LOTRO a try and see how they did.
They failed. They are one of those examples of OVERDOING it. I realize companies' need to make money.. especially on a F2P model. But Turbine REALLY nickel and dimes EVERYTHING. The base game includes 4 zones (3 of which are primarily starting zones with 1 real adventure zone). You can travel to areas you haven't unlocked through the store but don't expect to do much. So many things you take for granted in other games (space, skills, etc.) beyond a bare minimum have to be unlocked. And they REALLY like pushing some of the boosts. Comes with the territory, I know. If you are incredibly patient, you don't have to worry about those things, but expect ALOT of grinding and expect to be incredibly sub-par others that are your same level.
And P2W (Pay to Win)? If you pay for the boosts and unlocks, you are way ahead of the power curve. Pretty much anything can be had if you drop down some money.
Thankfully, sales happen now and again where you can get deals on TP or, during weekly sales, can get things like quest packs or unlocks for half off. Coupled with the lotro store giving away a couple free boosts per week, there's hope if you willing to drop some cash on the game and wait around for a good sale.
The ONLY saving grace is the ability to obtain TP (turbine points) on multiple toons that you can use towards unlocking the MANY features/content available. It's still alot of grinding. But I've managed to setup farming alts and a setup where I can earn about 200TP in about 90 mins. 3 runs and you can buy a quest pack for a zone.
(Middle ground score only because you can grind out the TP's if you really want something and don't want to spend real money, otherwise, the score would be 1/10 because of how overdone and nickel/dimey Turbine is about things)
The storyline is an epic one in the true tradition of Tolkien (NOT the movies). Which means it's dry, long and kinda boring (to me, anyways). The epicness of Tolkien's writing is not in the writing style but it's broad and intricate vision and LOTRO captures that well, at least. There's a big world to explore. And LOTS of things in it.
However, alot of that beauty is mired in meaningless quests for characters you care little about mingled with very boring writing. I'm a BIG fan of storylines, quests/missions, etc. and love to find out what's going on with everyone. But, for some reason, LOTRO quests are written so Tolkien'ish that the character dialogues seem overdone and I find myself not really interested and just skip reading it (for the most part). Additionally, there is no real feeling of storyline progressions (aside from the big main epic one). All the sub-storylines go all over the place and don't have real conclusive endings to them. Just an "I thank you for helping me, kind sir. Goodbye" with NPC audio chatter of "Oh won't you listen to my woes?"
(Just for the fact there's ALOT of quests, at least.. not for the writing at all)
Graphics-wise, LOTRO is partially old school. Harsh, blocky edges (especially in notably older zones) and weird or cheaply done world animations (can you say Shire waterfalls?) and blurry textures/skyboxes plague the game. Characters, are overly, bland looking, lifeless and blocky.
, despite all that, the world is really beautiful. Maybe it's because I come from the old school world of Meridian 59, UO, and EQ1. It may be outdated.. but there's still beauty in it. The way the grass shifts when you run through it or the gentle babbling of a nearby brook while you walk through a meadow neighbouring a dense forest. Newer zones and areas get an updated treatment with cleaner textures and more polys per object/models. So at least the graphics gets progressively better. But you can tell some TLC went into some of the earlier zones albeit old-school looking.
Nothing remarkable about the sound. The background music is appropriately themed, albeit very looped and repetitive. There's some voiceovers (mainly for cutscene introductions) and NPC chatter. The NPC chatter voiceovers are.. annoying, in some cases. "Excuse me! How rude!" from a Hobbit lady I JUST helped. "Oh! Won't you listen to my miseries and woes?" from a human I just helped by saving his wife from being eaten by orcs. Maybe he DIDN'T want her returned? the voiceovers give a little bit of life to NPC's but they are rather short, repetitive and inappropriate.. hence..overall annoying. I'm spoiled by games like TSW that did voiceovers incredibly well.
(what can I say? there's sound/bgm/voiceovers, at least)
Quest mechanics are your typical MMO fare. Fetch this, kill that, escort that. There's just ALOT of them. All over the place. And there's nothing more infuriating than a SLOW npc that you need to escort. It's an MMO staple. It works. But I haven't come across anything that stands out like a TSW puzzle or WoW NPC event. No world bosses for the community to band together and defeat (RIFT). No random events that pop up and surprise you (ESO). There' lots of quests, occasional instances (with the ability to vary the party requirements or the level of the mobs), skirmishes (repetitive scenario training grounds), epic battles (if you unlocked rohan for post 50), 100 levels worth of adventuring, the ability to play "bad guy monsters" called Creeps in PvP level 100 combat against regular players, etc. Lots of different features, not all incredibly exciting.. but there's something to do, at least.
(for LOTS to do, but not alot of enthusiasm to do it)
Each server is going to be different. I chose Landroval (US-RE.. roleplay encouraged) and the world chat community is.. talkative. Helpful at times and immature/mature some times depending on the time of day or weekday/weekend. Community-run roleplay events tend to go on frequently with spatterings of actual roleplay going on in various populated areas. It's not bad. Most F2P games are packed with immature freeloaders. I can only suspect that the old style nature of the game and the nickel/dimey nature drove some of them away. That's ok. go play Archeage, CS:GO or Dota2, kids.
Connectivity-wise, I don't get much in the way of lag. Ping times are ok, even during holiday events. Though, I do get some odd lag bursts that I can't pinpoint as network-related. One of my friends have severe issues with LOTRO's port switching tech which leaves her able to chat, but unable to move until she gets kicked. At which point she has to go through the hassle of editing the conf files to manual change the ports because the auto-port switching doesn't work quite well (we suspect her ISP is throttling/blocking some ports). Graphics-wise, I don't run into much lag except in heavily forested areas or scripted scenes with raging fires, overall, I'm running around with 40-60fps easy. I personally run into a SERIOUS issue with the LOTRO store. It's laggy, slow-loading, doesn't reflect your current TP's properly and sporadically I get an access denied and nothing loads in it. Ok.. if you don't want me to spending money, Turbine, you could just tell me.
(for numerous technical issues)
LOTRO gets an overall score of
. It's not spectacular, but it's not god-awful either. Although it has some saving graces, I'm going to have to give it a thumbs down. Too many little things make this game not as enjoyable as it could be. Sorry.

Yes the game is old, but so are the books that the game's based on.
The lore is there, and the areas are there, almost as good as the books. The main story (epic quests) has you following the fellowship (or running parallel), working in the background to fight the rising evil, aiding the good cause.
You will quest around landmarks from the books like Weathertop, and you can find little touches like the petrified trolls in the Trollshaws.
It may not have the best graphics (but certainly not the worst either). I grew up with a Commodore 64, so gameplay is more important than graphics for me, but things like the use of lighting to set the mood works really well for me, as does the weather.
It is F2P, but that doesn't mean it doesn't cost a thing to have all content available.
The good thing is that the store credits (Turbine Points) can be earned in-game, and that you can buy almost everything that is included in the VIP status with it. The only notable exception is 'fast travel' which you really will miss if you haven't got it, as the game is BIG.
The bad thing is that earning TP quickly is a grind, although it can be sped up if you have some high level characters.
Combat is old school skill clicking, which you either like or dislike.
Crafting is extremely simple; you have the mats, you make the item. (with a % to critical success). I would have liked something more involving, like EverQuest II's crafting perhaps.
Crafting does require interaction with other players, as you won't be able to get all materials you need yourself for the crafts you choose.
If you are into PvP, then this game is not for you.
There is some sort of PvP (PvMP), where some players have a character on the evil side, and some players play their regular 'good' side characters. There's one map for it, and the PvP crowd varies wildly per server.
If you are into endgame raids, then this game is not for you. There is no (new) endgame content. There are scaling instances, which are essentially the same from L20 upwards, except with harder enemies.
There is some new endgame content in the making though.
Most of the population is helpful and mature, but, as this is an online game, there are some trolls and trouble makers on the chat channels. Although vocal, this is a very small group compared to the helpful people.
Oh, one major bad thing: The download is HUGE, and the update process is extremely slow compared to other MMOs.
Overall: If you like the Lord of the Rings lore (whether from the books or the movies) and like to explore Middle Earth yourself, then this is the only game to play.
It's free up to around L30, after which you need to unlock quests for other areas.
Whether you pay for it with money or with time is up to you, which is a fair deal IMO.
And remember, the journey is more important than the goal.

i'm half convinced this game was killed by hype back when it came out in late 2015. mean greens was a flavour of the week game on many popular forums because its beautiful graphics and nostalgic feel captured the imagination of a lot of people who watched toy story or played with the little plastic army men themselves as wee ones.
but when people went to play it, there were really big problems with the gameplay. overall it was clunky, and that's being generous. really it was bordering on unplayable, with rocket launchers and disconnection screens dominating every game. not only that, there was no visceral indication of doing damage -- things just died without any audio or visual cues, and this along with the wonky hitboxes made those brief & glorious moments where you weren't getting spammed with rockets or disconnection screens underwhelming.
this caused a ton of people to stop playing the game, even those people who gave this game a positive review, which is many. if you scroll back to december 2015/january 2016 reviews, many of them are positive, but then you check the time played and its often less than 5-10 hours, which is a poor showing for a multiplayer game that you think is good enough to write a positive review for. the gameplay just wasn't there, and people realized that.
now that there's been seventeen patches, i'd like to think that the gameplay has been improved. i feel like a lot of the problem of the gameplay comes from its map design, which puts visuals in front of being fun (many of the maps are linear with giant sightlines and tiny choke points, which means good luck trying to get to an objective if you're losing). but maybe from all the updates, things are fun to shoot at.
we'll probably never know though, because as of the last thirty days, the average size of the player base has been 12 people. there is no server browser, so it's near impossible to even find those 12 people. there are no bots, no single player; these things wouldn't be a problem if there were people playing, but it seems required for this ghost town game at this point.
the game had a ton of promise coming out with its beautiful visuals, and it still has some promise even now. it is such a pretty game to play. but no one plays it, and that makes it hard to say if any of the updates fixed the problems that the game had on release.
until they put in some single player aspect into the game, you should spend your money elsewhere.

Did I finish it: Yes, some years ago. Replayed recently, but haven’t finished yet.
Yes, it’s old. Doesn’t matter, you can still get it on Steam, and I have it installed. That’s the list I’m starting this series with, just for lack of better ideas.
My feelings about this game are kind of mixed. Before this one, if somebody had told me there was going to be a sequel to a movie I liked, but it was going to be a videogame, I’d have vomited blood. Movie/game tie-ins that respect neither medium are pretty common, and back then it was normal to believe it impossible to do better. To go as far as making an actual sequel would seem preposterous. By using a franchise where it seemed natural to try, they made a good game and paved the way for other people to try it with other properties. It’s fair to call it a classic on this basis. On top of that, it certainly had excellent graphics for the time, as evidenced by the fact that back then, I had to upgrade specifically to play it. That presentation has aged very well, aided by the style inherent to the series and an excellent fan-made upgrade, which is a necessity if you want to play today.*
Despite that, I’m not sure how vociferously I’d recommend somebody who doesn’t have it to buy it now. If you’re a fan of the series, definitely do it. I love Tron: Legacy, but this is what the original’s creator intended the sequel to be, and it has more soul if you ask me. Even if you’re not attached to Tron that much, the setting is beautifully interesting and the story they tell in it is good, if you can stomach all the corn the dialogue and its somewhat flat delivery will force you to eat.
The trouble (which some might see as a bonus) is that its gameplay is representative of the period. Regardless of how pretty the graphics were, gameplay in FPS got stuck for a while after Half-Life. Everyone knew Find the Key maze shooters were dead, and were trying to jam in-engine story presentation in at the same time as they were struggling with what to do next in terms of game and level design. Between that and the characteristically dumb AI of the time, the result was an odd mash of jumpy arcade action, (which I’ve always had a smaller appetite for than most) frustratingly Xen-ish platforming, and not-criminally-bad stealth opportunities. Tron is just such a transitional work, so if you’re not nostalgic for Goldeneye, you won’t enjoy it the same way. I think it’s worth playing even by modern standards, mind, it’s just that how much you’d be willing to pay might be affected by that.
Bottom Line: $30 for me, $15 if you’re not a fan or supernerd.
* If you get it, you’ll need the Killer App mod to get it working on modern systems.

Tron 2.0 is a very old first person shooter developed by Monolith Productions and published by Disney. Though hailing from 2003, it does have the necessary components that allow it to hold your interest even with todays gaming giants.
A little bit of background; Tron 2.0 is one of several games I frequented as a young child in the early - mid 2000s. It was also the first game to introduce me into a beautiful world with a good story line, thus sparking my love for video-game lore. I thoroughly enjoyed this game, through out all of its flaws and perks and even twelve years later I still cannot stay away. This review may be a tad biased, but I also believe that reviews should reflect upon ones experience, whether it be positive or negative.
As far as gameplay, it's not entirely up to par from modern games of today but it is not exactly lacking either. You have all of your basic functions; crouch, walk, lean over to the side, strafe and jump (There's no sprint.) Additionally all of your keys are rebindable which was a nice consideration. You do have a difficulty slider from Easy, Normal, Hard and Insane. Replayability shouldn't be much of an issue. Aesthetically the game does an incredible job of immersing you inside the digital world of a computer, from the sounds of your foot steps to the views of the many levels this game has to offer, and even as far as some of the termonology used in the games dialog.
The sound track is amazing and as I've said it before and I'll continue to say it, this game by far has the most unique and nicest looking game-worlds of anything I have played to this day. I'm not sure about you, but I am a fan of the innards of a computer. Neon lights, blocks, digital bridges, circuit boards and all. I cannot help but stop and look around for a solid five minutes when I enter a level. It's just very pleasing to the eye, even if it is a world designed in the early 2000s.
You play as a character who gets digitalized into a computer to fight off a virus. Your character can acquire build points to level up attributes such as health, energy, and processor (How long it takes your character to defrag or clean a corrupted subroutine). There are four types of weapons in the game, with three sub-types of those weapons to choose from. For a 2003 game published by Disney, I would not say the story is great, but it is not by any means bad either. It drew me in pretty easily early on, but I found it had some consistency problems towards the tail end of the campaign.
Aside from the age and story, and lack of previous success in it's earlier years, another and perhaps more fatal flaw is that it's relatively difficult to get this game to work for Windows 10. I'm not sure about previous versions of Windows and other operating systems though, so I will focus on what I had to do to get Tron 2.0 to run on my Windows 10 machine.
Before I get on with the how-to for Tron 2.0 on Windows 10, I will say that I recommend you to pick this game up. It's worth a run through the world to see the sights and hear the sounds, and a play through the story as well. It's relatively cheap, you can replay it easily at a higher difficulty, It's really a lot of good fun. Give it a go!
There are two+one items you will need to download and install to get the game to run (Links at the bottom of the review until if and when I am asked to remove them). The first item you will have to download is a seperate launcher. Simply place the new launcher into the folder that this game installs to, replacing the default launcher, is all you need to do for the first step. Secondly there's an unofficial patch that you'll have install as well but it's nothing too complicated. Just download and run the installer, and you're done. At this point, you will be able to run the game, and should do so before you continue reading this review / how-to.
Finally, there is an optional mod that gives you extra features, including resolutions for 16:9 and 16:10 monitor ratios. The mod comes as an installer and is relatively straight forward to use. If you choose to download this optional mod, you must be warned that it might hang up at a certain part of the install due to you having any logitech or razer software / driver on your computer running. I found the easiest way to get the mod to install is to restart your computer and boot up into safemode. Run the mod installer once you're logged in and you should be able to finish the install with out any further issues.

TRON 2.0 is one of those games where for the first few hours you're thinking, "Eff yeah, this game is great! Why don't more people talk about it?" Then you get to a frustrating light cycle section and your confidence in the game is shaken. But then you have a few more hours of well-designed levels, fun new weapons, and interesting story, and you're back on board. And then you hit one of the three or four really bad boss fights and you start to suspect maybe there's a reason you don't hear so many people talking about this game. But you keep at it because the art is super cool (and has aged quite well for a 12-year-old game), the music is great, and you loved TRON as a kid and feel you owe it to 12-year-old you to see this thing to the end. And you do, but not without making some compromises, like finding the cheat codes to top off your health from time to time (the boss fights are really tedious) and even skip a section here and there (I admit, I'm rubbish at the light cyle sections).
In the end, though, I'm really glad I stuck with it. I was surprised at the depth of the character ability progression, which was really ahead of its time. Every shooter does it now, but I can't think of anyone doing it back in 2003. But I think the best thing I can say about TRON 2.0 is that it evokes the movie so well that I had a big nostalgia grin on my face for most of the 17 hours it took me to finish it. What more can a TRON fan ask for?

Overall just a retread of Human Revolution. Nothing in your set of starting goals was accomplished and ultimately the villain was obvious from the moment you saw him (Even before that if you saw the trailer, I was hoping for a bait and switch). The narrative ended anticlimactically and felt like a part 1 of 2 rather than a solid entry on its own merit.
As for gameplay, the only changes the made from HR reduced difficulty or moment to moment decisions. Being able to hack from a distance with a "Hit the light" minigame and shut down turrets became mandatory simply because it was far easier than the alternative of actually sneaking up to the terminal or bot and hacking it. The broken invisibility from HR was never fixed, you can still just spam biocells to perma invis now and that's all you need to do in the later half of the game. The enemy AI doesn't allow them to use any widely available augments to counter your own usage, letting you fly through the game with ease so long as you don't make too much noise without the noise cancelling aug.
The last thing I want to address in this review was subject matter, Apartheid was a huge societal divide and we're seeing echoes of it with the rise of xenophobia within several nations. To use augmented citizens as a stand-in for those subjected to various prejudices could've worked, had the game itself committed to portraying the prejudice and systemic oppression as anything more than a minor inconveniece for you. We didn't find Apartheid abhorrent because you had to ride in a different, albeit equal train car and occasionally get called a bad name. It was a constant state of dehumanization from a federal level. Several times I made it a point to break these policies expecting some form of backlash that never arrived, the worst was getting told "Not to do it again." I believe this was to not shackle players with gameplay that might not be "Fun" but then why attempt to tackle ugly subject matter such as this?
MD was disappointing as a story, game, and analogy for contemporary politics. I'll be pirating the next game because I paid full price day 1 for a complete narrative, not this.

This one's a bit of a nostalgia trip. Safecracker is a puzzle/adventure game using the classic Myst formula. You wander between fixed viewpoints in a mansion, and you click on puzzles to solve them. It seems out of place in this decade, but I had fun with it anyway.
The nice thing is that the puzzles are, for the most part, good, and that's really all that matters. The puzzles, with a few exceptions, are clever and well-made. In general, they require some real puzzle-solving skills. Bring pencil and paper for this one.
Now, for the bad. The big one is that with many of the puzzles, you don't know if you're missing a part of it or if it's just hard. Sometimes the hardest part is figuring out where to go next. The mouse controls pretty poorly, which can be a huge hassle. It doesn't run that well on Win7: check the Steam forums for fixes. Story is almost non-existent.
I beat this in a few hours. I wouldn't pay $5 for it, but if you like puzzles, get it when it's on sale.

Is there even a point to writing reviews on Free to Play games? It's not like you're losing anything other than time by downloading and trying them. On top of that, Crush Crush is an idle game. So your loss of time will only prove to enrich your experience with the game. What a genius business strategy! Nobody loses.
Except, somebody does lose. I do. Because now I'm wasting time writing a review for a game that nobody will read. But this is a labour of love and I will persevere, dammit, because this game is great and I want to make my voice heard.
Honestly, I was a little disappointed that there were no Candy Crush-esque sliding puzzles involved. Those puzzles are actually what kept me enjoying HuniePop, and LOOK AT THE NAME. Crush Crush. What a wasted opportunity. The name comes from the way you physically or mentally CRUSH your crushes. Your crushes being every girl that you meet. Whether you run them down in the street, destroy their perception of reality or tell a bad bear pun, the girls are CRUSHED by your actions. And a few hours later, they'll be your passionate lover.
If I became passionate lovers with every girl I've ever wronged, I'd have at least 1 girlfriend. This game is unrealistic.
It's a semi-standard idle game. You do jobs and hobbies which take time and give rewards, and once you reach certain milestones, your relationships with your crushes advance. The time system (which limits the amount of stuff you can do at once) mean you have to check back regularly to do some micro-management. That might seem bad for an idle game but it actually keeps interest levels high. I almost feel compelled not to let the crushes down, and I keep coming back every couple of hours to cash in the millions of dollars I've earned flipping burgers, managing a restaraunt, bounty hunting, doing coding and being a professional athlete (all at the same time) to buy the girls a 59 million dollar pair of shoes and poke them with a stick.
The dialogue is actually hilarious. I've been left close to tears by some of these scenarios. They're all downright absurd and outrageously funny and just download the game already, it's free.
Micro-transactions. We love to hate them! Spend a little money, get a little in-game currency. Well, this game's premium currency is Diamonds and they're pretty expensive. However, the natural progression system in the game means they actually aren't necessary!
The main things Diamonds do are:
Diamonds can be earned for free (You get some every time you advance a relationship with a girl.) A bigger time metre can be achieved by earning in game achievements (which the game has by the bucket-load) and you can speed up progress bars by 'Prestiging'.
Prestiging does what it sounds like. It resets the game (except for Diamonds, Diamond purchases and the time bar) and gives you a permanent speed boost.
Who needs diamonds anyway?
I love this game. It's one of the most interesting and interactive idle games out there, to my knowledge, and I highly recommend it.

Sims 3 is a fun, enjoyable game that I have spent countless hours playing.
I would like to be able to 100% recommend the game, as it is a virtual world with unlimited options and customization, however, there are also reasons why I wouldn’t recommend it.
I’m choosing to not recommend it, and this is not because the game itself isn’t good, it is because of the numerous glitches and issues that come along with the game.
I have been a fan of sims for years, and have Sims 2 Pets for Game Cube, Sims 3 for Wii and Sims 3 for PC. Out of these three, Sims 2 was the only one that didn’t have a lot of glitches. There were some small ones, but nothing that makes the game unplayable.
However, in both the Wii version and PC version of Sims 3, while the game starts out being relatively glitch free, as you progress through the storyline, the glitches gradually become more frequent and begin to affect the fun of the gameplay itself.
As of three or four years ago, I had to stop playing the Sims 3 for Wii, because every time I would try to load the game, within two or three minutes in live mode, it would freeze completely.
I purchased Sims 3 last year during the summer sale, along with the Pets expansion. There was a special offer that meant I was able to buy both for way less than the normal price. That was the only reason I even considered buying the game.
I love Sims, don’t get me wrong, but given that I know how many glitches were in Sims 3 for the Wii, I wasn’t willing to spend full price on a game that may or may not be playable at some point in the future.
To give you an idea of the types of glitches I have encountered, I will first of all list all the expansions that I have currently.
I have:
Sims 3 Pets
Sims 3 Generations
Sims 3 Supernatural
Sims 3 University Life
Sims 3 Seasons
Sims 3 Ambitions
I got the other expansion packs at the beginning of this year, again on sale.
The game, while it often lagged a lot, worked relatively well until the beginning of February, when a strange and very frustrating glitch occurred.
I was trying to get my sim to walk to the fridge to get some food, but every time I tried to issue the command, the bubble indicating that they can’t go there came up. My fridge was in the same exact spot as it had been since I started playing that save file. I couldn’t figure out why my sim couldn’t get to the fridge, given that there wasn’t anything visibly in front of the fridge door. So, after trying to remove the invisible object, I decided to move my fridge one spot to the left. I issued the command to my sim again, and they simply walked over and completed the task. However, the fact that there was some kind of invisible object blocking access to half my kitchen still remained, for which I couldn’t find a permanent solution.
There were other annoying glitches as well, but for the PC version, this was the one that really made me frustrated, because while I could just move houses, I had everything in my current house the way I wanted it and I didn’t want to have to buy a new house because of some invisible object. This, in addition to the numerous issues I have encountered with the Wii version as well as the PC version is what caused me to get so frustrated.
Sims 3 would be an extremely fun game, but the enjoyment of playing it is greatly diminished by the glitches that interfere with the gameplay.
In conclusion, I do not recommend the Sims 3 game, unless you are willing to deal with the problems that will more than likely occur the more you play the game. I wish the developers of the game would have taken more time and effort to smooth out the issues instead of trying to get it done quickly in order to be able to sell it to the public. Quality is always more important than quantity.
